Cardiac fibroma.description: A rare benign primary cardiac tumor composed predominantly of fibroblasts and dense collagen. It usually arises within the ventricular myocardium, particularly the left ventricle, and may be discovered incidentally.

Cardiac hemangioma.description: A benign vascular cardiac tumor composed of proliferating blood vessels. It can occur in any cardiac chamber or myocardial wall and is sometimes detected incidentally.

Cardiac lipoma.description: A benign tumor of mature adipose tissue that may arise in the myocardium, subendocardium, or pericardium. Many cardiac lipomas are asymptomatic and found incidentally.

Cardiac myxoma.description: The most common benign primary cardiac tumor, usually arising from the interatrial septum in the left atrium. It may cause obstructive, embolic, or constitutional symptoms, although occasional cases are incidental.

Cardiac sarcoma.description: A rare malignant primary cardiac tumor, such as undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, or angiosarcoma. These tumors often invade adjacent myocardium and commonly produce progressive cardiac symptoms.

Splenic infarction.description: Ischemic injury of splenic tissue caused by impaired blood supply, often appearing as peripheral wedge-shaped, poorly perfused splenic lesions on ultrasound or MRI.

Splenic abscess.description: A localized bacterial or fungal infection within the spleen that can cause fever, left upper quadrant pain, and focal splenic lesions on imaging.

Splenic vein thrombosis with secondary s.normalized_text: Splenic vein thrombosis with secondary splenic infarction
Splenic vein thrombosis with secondary s.description: Thrombosis of the splenic venous circulation can impair splenic blood flow and may produce splenic congestion or infarction; MRI may demonstrate abnormal vascular signal near the splenic hilum.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection with ext.normalized_text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection with extrapulmonary splenic infarction
Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection with ext.description: Mycoplasma pneumoniae commonly causes an atypical respiratory infection and can rarely trigger thrombosis or splenic infarction through inflammation or transient antiphospholipid antibodies.

Infectious mononucleosis with splenic in.description: Usually caused by Epstein-Barr virus, infectious mononucleosis can cause fever and splenic enlargement or, rarely, splenic infarction due to transient hypercoagulability.

Amoebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histoly.description: An extraintestinal complication of amoebiasis in which Entamoeba histolytica forms a hepatic abscess, often months to years after travel to an endemic region.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A localized bacterial infection of the liver, commonly caused by enteric organisms and associated with fever, inflammatory-marker elevation, and a low-attenuation liver lesion on imaging.

Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkho.normalized_text: Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkholderia pseudomallei infection)
Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkho.description: Melioidosis is an infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, endemic in northern Australia and parts of Southeast Asia; it can cause pneumonia, sepsis, and abscesses in the liver and spleen.

Hepatic fascioliasis (Fasciola hepatica.normalized_text: Hepatic fascioliasis (Fasciola hepatica or Fasciola gigantica infection)
Hepatic fascioliasis (Fasciola hepatica.description: A liver fluke infection acquired from contaminated water or aquatic vegetation; the acute migratory phase may cause fever, abdominal discomfort, and focal hepatic lesions.

Septic portal vein thrombophlebitis (pyl.normalized_text: Septic portal vein thrombophlebitis (pylephlebitis) associated with intra-abdominal infection
Septic portal vein thrombophlebitis (pyl.description: Pylephlebitis is infected thrombosis of the portal venous system, usually arising from gastrointestinal infection such as diverticulitis, appendicitis, or colitis; it may coexist with hepatic abscesses.

OPA1-related autosomal dominant optic at.normalized_text: OPA1-related autosomal dominant optic atrophy plus syndrome
OPA1-related autosomal dominant optic at.description: A mitochondrial disorder caused by pathogenic OPA1 variants, typically producing slowly progressive bilateral optic atrophy and sometimes additional neurologic features such as spastic paraplegia, ataxia, neuropathy, deafness, or cognitive symptoms.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic.normalized_text: Hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic atrophy, such as SPG7-related disease
Hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic.description: Hereditary spastic paraplegias are genetic disorders characterized by progressive degeneration of corticospinal tracts, causing lower-limb spasticity and bladder dysfunction. Some complicated forms, including SPG7, can include optic atrophy and other neurologic features.

Primary progressive multiple sclerosis.description: A chronic inflammatory and neurodegenerative central nervous system disease that can cause gradually progressive spastic paraparesis, sensory disturbance, bladder dysfunction, and optic pathway injury. Oligoclonal bands support intrathecal immune activity.

Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with a.normalized_text: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with an MS-like neurologic syndrome (Harding disease)
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with a.description: A mitochondrial DNA disorder in which hereditary optic neuropathy coexists with central nervous system demyelinating or MS-like manifestations. It is more often associated with maternally inherited visual loss and can include spasticity and bladder symptoms.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder affecting the optic nerves and spinal cord, often causing optic neuritis and myelitis with motor, sensory, and bladder dysfunction. It is commonly associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies, although seronegative cases occur.

Wilson disease (ATP7B-related hepatolent.description: An autosomal-recessive disorder of impaired copper excretion caused by ATP7B mutations, leading to copper accumulation in the liver, brain, cornea, and other tissues. The reported homozygous ATP7B c.2333G>T (p.Arg778Leu) pathogenic variant, Kayser-Fleischer-type corneal findings, and basal-ganglia MRI abnormalities strongly support this diagnosis.

Herb-induced liver injury (drug-induced.description: Liver injury caused by medications, supplements, or herbal preparations. Chinese herbal medicines can cause hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed-pattern hepatitis and may produce jaundice and severe itching.

Autoimmune hepatitis.description: A chronic immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease that commonly affects girls and young women and can present with jaundice, impaired liver function, and progression to cirrhosis if untreated.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis.description: A chronic cholestatic disease characterized by inflammatory fibrosis and stricturing of the bile ducts, causing impaired bile flow, itching, and jaundice. It is less common in young females and is often associated with inflammatory bowel disease.

Progressive familial intrahepatic choles.description: A group of inherited childhood and adolescent cholestatic liver diseases caused by defects in bile formation or transport. It typically presents with persistent pruritus, jaundice, and progressive liver injury.

Azathioprine-induced Sweet syndrome (acu.normalized_text: Azathioprine-induced Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis)
Azathioprine-induced Sweet syndrome (acu.description: A neutrophilic inflammatory skin disorder that may be triggered by medications, including azathioprine, and classically causes abrupt fever, neutrophilia, painful erythematous plaques or nodules, and arthralgia.

Azathioprine hypersensitivity syndrome.description: A potentially severe idiosyncratic systemic reaction to azathioprine, usually occurring within days to weeks of initiation, characterized by fever, malaise, rash, arthralgia, and inflammatory-marker elevation; it is not necessarily dose-related.

Serum sickness-like reaction.description: A medication-associated immune reaction causing fever, rash, and symmetric joint pain or swelling, generally developing one to two weeks after exposure to a new drug.

Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis (d.description: Inflammation of small cutaneous blood vessels, often triggered by medications, which can produce palpable purpura or painful erythematous lesions and may be accompanied by fever and arthralgia.

Adult-onset Still disease.description: A systemic autoinflammatory disorder that can cause high fever, inflammatory polyarthritis, neutrophilic leukocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers, and a transient salmon-colored rash.

Traumatic retropharyngeal hematoma.description: Bleeding into the retropharyngeal/prevertebral soft tissues after neck trauma, causing expansion of the posterior pharyngeal wall and possible airway obstruction.

Laryngeal trauma with laryngeal edema or.normalized_text: Laryngeal trauma with laryngeal edema or hematoma
Laryngeal trauma with laryngeal edema or.description: Blunt injury to the larynx can cause mucosal swelling, soft-tissue hematoma, vocal-cord dysfunction, and progressive upper-airway obstruction.

Traumatic pharyngeal wall hematoma.description: A localized hematoma within or adjacent to the pharyngeal wall after blunt trauma can narrow the pharyngeal airway and produce dysphagia and voice change.

Cervical spine injury with prevertebral.normalized_text: Cervical spine injury with prevertebral soft-tissue swelling
Cervical spine injury with prevertebral.description: Cervical vertebral fracture, ligamentous injury, or associated prevertebral hemorrhage after trauma may produce marked prevertebral swelling and dysphagia; absence of tenderness does not fully exclude injury.

Retropharyngeal abscess.description: A deep neck space infection causing a collection behind the pharynx, with posterior pharyngeal swelling, painful swallowing, neck stiffness, and risk of airway compromise.

Insulinoma.description: A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes insulin autonomously, causing recurrent fasting hypoglycemia. It is the most likely diagnosis given endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia and a hypervascular pancreatic lesion.

Factitious hypoglycemia from sulfonylure.normalized_text: Factitious hypoglycemia from sulfonylurea or meglitinide exposure
Factitious hypoglycemia from sulfonylure.description: Hypoglycemia caused by use of insulin-secretagogue diabetes medications, which increases endogenous insulin and C-peptide and can closely mimic insulinoma.

Non-insulinoma pancreatogenous hypoglyce.description: Diffuse pancreatic beta-cell hyperfunction causing excessive endogenous insulin secretion and recurrent hypoglycemia, usually without a discrete insulin-secreting tumor.

Insulin autoimmune syndrome.description: A rare cause of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia caused by insulin autoantibodies that bind and later release insulin, often associated with certain medications or autoimmune disease.

Adrenal insufficiency.description: Insufficient cortisol production can impair glucose maintenance during fasting and cause fatigue, weakness, neurocognitive symptoms, and hypoglycemia.

Slipping rib syndrome.description: Hypermobility or subluxation of the false-rib costal cartilage, most often involving ribs 8 to 10, causing intermittent pain from intercostal nerve irritation. The ultrasound appearance of abnormal relative position/motion of the lower ribs is supportive.

Intercostal muscle strain.description: Overuse or minor tearing of an intercostal muscle caused by repetitive forceful trunk motion, heavy exercise, or twisting.

Costochondral or interchondral joint spr.description: Mechanical irritation or sprain at the junction between a rib and its cartilage, or between adjacent costal cartilages, often following repetitive loading or forceful trunk movement.

Rib stress fracture or stress reaction.normalized_text: Rib stress fracture or stress reaction
Rib stress fracture or stress reaction.description: A repetitive-loading injury of a rib that can occur with sudden increases in training intensity, producing localized pain that worsens with activity.

Intercostal neuralgia.description: Pain caused by irritation or compression of an intercostal nerve, producing sharp, stabbing, or burning pain along the course of a rib. It can occur secondary to chest-wall movement or rib/cartilage instability.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.normalized_text: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.description: A clonal myeloid neoplasm characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia, dysplastic or immature eosinophil precursors, cytopenias, and possible organ infiltration, including pulmonary disease.

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia.description: An eosinophilic lung disease causing subacute respiratory symptoms, blood or bronchoalveolar eosinophilia, and peripheral pulmonary infiltrates; it usually responds promptly to systemic corticosteroids.

Hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES).description: A syndrome of sustained eosinophilia with eosinophil-mediated organ damage after secondary causes have been excluded; the lungs, heart, skin, nervous system, and gastrointestinal tract may be involved.

Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.normalized_text: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene rearrangement
Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.description: A group of clonal hematologic neoplasms driven by rearrangements involving genes such as PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, JAK2, or ABL1. They can cause marked eosinophilia, anemia, marrow abnormalities, and pulmonary or other organ infiltration.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: A systemic eosinophilic vasculitis typically associated with adult-onset asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis, eosinophilia, transient pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy, skin lesions, and possible renal or cardiac disease.

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma

Rosai-Dorfman disease.description: A rare non-Langerhans-cell histiocytic disorder characterized by accumulation of activated histiocytes in lymph nodes or extranodal organs. It can cause systemic inflammation, anemia, abdominal lymphadenopathy, and involvement of the kidneys or gastrointestinal tract.

ALK-positive histiocytosis.description: A rare histiocytic neoplasm driven by ALK gene rearrangements. Systemic disease in children may involve lymph nodes, bone marrow, kidneys, liver, lungs, and gastrointestinal organs and can produce fever, anemia, and inflammatory marker elevation.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including anaplast.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including anaplastic large-cell lymphoma
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including anaplast.description: A malignant lymphoid disorder that may present in children with fever, weight loss, anemia, abdominal pain, mediastinal or abdominal lymphadenopathy, and extranodal organ involvement.

Crohn disease.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any portion of the gastrointestinal tract, causing abdominal pain, diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, growth failure, anemia, weight loss, and elevated inflammatory markers.

Disseminated tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection may cause prolonged fever, weight loss, anemia, abdominal pain, mesenteric lymphadenopathy, and involvement of multiple organs. Exposure risk can be increased by travel to regions where tuberculosis is more prevalent.

Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: Severe mosquito-borne malaria caused by P. falciparum, common in Tanzania and characterized by high fever, hemolysis, jaundice, renal dysfunction, and potentially high parasitemia. The rapid test and thin blood smear with multiple delicate ring forms, including appliqué forms, strongly support this diagnosis.

Blackwater fever.description: A severe hemolytic complication of falciparum malaria in which massive intravascular red-cell destruction causes hemoglobinuria, dark urine, jaundice, and acute kidney injury.

Leptospirosis.description: A zoonotic spirochetal infection acquired through exposure to water or soil contaminated with animal urine. Severe disease can cause fever, headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, jaundice, acute kidney injury, and dark urine.

Dengue fever.description: An Aedes mosquito-borne viral illness that can occur in East Africa and commonly causes abrupt fever, severe headache, fatigue, gastrointestinal symptoms, and occasionally hepatitis or plasma leakage.

Acute viral hepatitis, including hepatit.normalized_text: Acute viral hepatitis, including hepatitis A or E
Acute viral hepatitis, including hepatit.description: Acute liver inflammation, often acquired during travel through contaminated food or water, that may cause fever, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, dark urine, and fatigue.

Delayed pharyngoesophageal perforation f.normalized_text: Delayed pharyngoesophageal perforation from cervical spine hardware erosion
Delayed pharyngoesophageal perforation f.description: A late complication of anterior cervical spine fixation in which plates or screws erode into the pharynx or esophagus, causing a perforation, leakage, and deep infection.

Esophageal perforation with mediastiniti.description: A tear or hole in the esophagus permits saliva, bacteria, and food material to enter the mediastinum, producing severe infection and potentially extending into the neck and paraspinal tissues.

Infected cervical spinal instrumentation.normalized_text: Infected cervical spinal instrumentation with cervical vertebral osteomyelitis
Infected cervical spinal instrumentation.description: Infection involving cervical fixation hardware and adjacent vertebrae can cause osteomyelitis, soft-tissue infection, and formation of extensive paraspinal abscesses; it may also erode into the esophagus.

Retropharyngeal abscess with extension t.normalized_text: Retropharyngeal abscess with extension to the mediastinum
Retropharyngeal abscess with extension t.description: A deep neck-space infection located behind the pharynx that may descend through fascial planes into the upper mediastinum and produce systemic infection.

Descending necrotizing mediastinitis.description: A severe, rapidly progressive mediastinal infection that spreads downward from an infection in the neck, pharynx, or esophagus and can produce purulent mediastinal collections.

Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous esophage.description: A full-thickness tear of the esophagus caused by a sudden rise in intraesophageal pressure, classically after forceful vomiting. It can produce pneumomediastinum, pleural effusions or hydropneumothorax, and rapidly progressive mediastinitis.

Acute mediastinitis secondary to esophag.normalized_text: Acute mediastinitis secondary to esophageal perforation
Acute mediastinitis secondary to esophag.description: Inflammation and infection of the mediastinum, commonly caused by leakage from an esophageal rupture. Early imaging may show mediastinal air, pleural fluid, and inflammatory changes before fever or leukocytosis develops.

Acute aortic dissection.description: A tear in the aortic intima that creates a false lumen within the aortic wall. It can cause abrupt severe chest pain radiating to the back and may be associated with sweating, nausea, and tachycardia.

Acute coronary syndrome.description: Myocardial ischemia from reduced coronary blood flow, including unstable angina and myocardial infarction. It commonly presents with pressure-like chest pain, diaphoresis, nausea, and autonomic symptoms.

Spontaneous pneumothorax or hydropneumot.description: Air, with or without fluid, in the pleural space that can cause acute chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, and reduced lung expansion. In this setting, a left hydropneumothorax could occur as a complication of esophageal rupture.

Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (funct.description: Paroxysmal episodes that resemble epileptic seizures but are caused by functional neurologic mechanisms rather than abnormal epileptic brain discharges. They are commonly associated with trauma-related and psychiatric conditions; the EEG image is compatible with prominent movement artifact without a clear evolving ictal epileptiform pattern.

Generalized tonic-clonic epilepsy.description: Epilepsy characterized by seizures with abrupt tonic stiffening followed by generalized rhythmic clonic shaking, often associated with loss of consciousness, falls, postictal confusion, muscle enzyme elevation, and occasionally urinary incontinence.

Post-traumatic focal epilepsy with focal.normalized_text: Post-traumatic focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures
Post-traumatic focal epilepsy with focal.description: Epilepsy caused by prior brain injury, in which focal seizures may begin with sensory, autonomic, visual, cognitive, or emotional symptoms and then spread to cause bilateral tonic-clonic convulsions.

Convulsive syncope.description: Transient loss of consciousness from temporary reduction in cerebral blood flow, sometimes accompanied by brief stiffening or myoclonic/convulsive movements. It may occur with arrhythmia, vasovagal triggers, dehydration, or substance use.

Panic attacks with functional motor mani.normalized_text: Panic attacks with functional motor manifestations
Panic attacks with functional motor mani.description: Panic attacks are abrupt episodes of intense fear and autonomic arousal; in some patients, especially those with functional neurologic symptoms, they may precede dissociative states, shaking, immobility, or seizure-like behavior.

Obturator hernia with small-bowel obstru.description: A pelvic hernia in which bowel protrudes through the obturator canal, classically occurring in thin, elderly, multiparous women. It can compress the obturator nerve and cause medial thigh or knee pain (Howship-Romberg sign).

Femoral hernia with incarcerated small b.normalized_text: Femoral hernia with incarcerated small bowel
Femoral hernia with incarcerated small b.description: A hernia through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament. It is more common in women and may incarcerate or strangulate bowel, causing acute intestinal obstruction.

Incarcerated inguinal hernia.description: A protrusion of abdominal contents through the inguinal canal that can trap small bowel and produce mechanical bowel obstruction.

Sciatic hernia with bowel obstruction.description: A rare pelvic floor hernia in which bowel protrudes through the greater or lesser sciatic foramen. It may cause bowel obstruction and pelvic, buttock, hip, or leg pain from nerve compression.

Small-bowel obstruction due to pelvic ma.normalized_text: Small-bowel obstruction due to pelvic malignancy or pelvic mass
Small-bowel obstruction due to pelvic ma.description: A pelvic tumor, metastatic disease, or enlarged pelvic lymph node can externally compress or invade bowel, causing mechanical obstruction and a palpable pelvic mass.

Susac syndrome.description: A rare autoimmune endotheliopathy affecting small vessels of the brain, retina, and inner ear, classically causing encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions, and sensorineural hearing loss.

Multiple sclerosis.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that commonly affects young women and can cause visual, sensory, and brainstem symptoms with white-matter lesions on MRI.

Antiphospholipid syndrome.description: An autoimmune hypercoagulable disorder causing arterial or venous thrombosis, pregnancy morbidity, and sometimes retinal or cerebral ischemic events.

Cogan syndrome.description: A rare inflammatory disorder characterized primarily by ocular inflammation, especially interstitial keratitis, together with audiovestibular disease such as sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo.

Neuro-Behcet disease.description: Neurologic involvement of Behcet disease, a systemic inflammatory vasculitis that can cause headaches, focal neurologic deficits, ocular vascular inflammation, and brain lesions.

MERRF syndrome (myoclonic epilepsy with.normalized_text: MERRF syndrome (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers), usually due to the m.8344A>G mitochondrial DNA variant
MERRF syndrome (myoclonic epilepsy with.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder characterized by mitochondrial myopathy, ragged-red fibers on muscle biopsy, neurologic manifestations, hearing loss, and sometimes cardiac conduction abnormalities. Phenotypes can be incomplete and may present predominantly with axial myopathy and ataxia.

Mitochondrial myopathy due to an mtDNA m.normalized_text: Mitochondrial myopathy due to an mtDNA mutation
Mitochondrial myopathy due to an mtDNA m.description: A group of disorders caused by impaired mitochondrial energy production. Adult-onset mitochondrial myopathy may cause axial and proximal weakness, elevated CK, exercise intolerance, hearing loss, cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia, and abnormal mitochondrial staining on muscle biopsy.

MELAS spectrum disorder (mitochondrial e.normalized_text: MELAS spectrum disorder (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes)
MELAS spectrum disorder (mitochondrial e.description: A mitochondrial DNA disorder, most often associated with the m.3243A>G variant, causing variable combinations of myopathy, hearing loss, cognitive impairment, seizures, ataxia, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, and stroke-like episodes. Mild or late-onset phenotypes occur.

POLG-related mitochondrial disease.description: A nuclear-gene mitochondrial disorder caused by pathogenic POLG variants. Presentations may include external ophthalmoplegia, sensory neuropathy, ataxia, seizures, hearing loss, myopathy, and cognitive decline; severity and age at onset are variable.

Desmin-related myofibrillar myopathy.description: An inherited myofibrillar myopathy that can cause adult-onset axial, neck, and proximal limb weakness, camptocormia or bent-spine syndrome, elevated CK, and potentially serious cardiac conduction disease or arrhythmias.

diagnoses.name: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia.description: An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, often presenting in children with extranodal masses and bone marrow or peripheral-blood involvement. Tumor cells typically express surface immunoglobulin with light-chain restriction, CD19, CD20, CD10, and HLA-DR, while lacking TdT and CD34.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.description: A mature B-cell lymphoma composed of large malignant lymphoid cells that can involve lymph nodes, extranodal soft tissue, and bone marrow. It is less common than Burkitt lymphoma in very young children but may have a similar mature B-cell immunophenotype.

High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC rear.normalized_text: High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC rearrangement
High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC rear.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma with high-grade morphology and frequently MYC-associated cytogenetic abnormalities. It may overlap biologically and clinically with Burkitt lymphoma and can involve extranodal tissue, marrow, and blood.

B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma.description: A malignancy of precursor B lymphoblasts that commonly affects young children and can cause bone pain, anemia, lymphadenopathy, and soft-tissue masses. Typical blasts express TdT and CD34 and usually lack surface immunoglobulin light-chain restriction.

B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable/intermed.normalized_text: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable/intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable/intermed.description: A mature aggressive B-cell neoplasm with features overlapping Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Such tumors can present with extranodal masses, lymphadenopathy, marrow involvement, and a germinal-center B-cell phenotype.

Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Sch.normalized_text: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni
Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Sch.description: Chronic intestinal schistosomiasis can cause egg deposition in portal venules, producing periportal fibrosis (Symmers pipestem fibrosis), hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and portal hypertension. The positive stool examination strongly supports this diagnosis.

Hepatic schistosomal periportal fibrosis.description: This is the hepatic manifestation of chronic Schistosoma mansoni infection, characterized by fibrotic thickening around portal tracts, often with portal hypertension and splenic enlargement while liver function may be relatively preserved.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A pyogenic liver abscess is a focal bacterial infection of the liver that commonly causes prolonged fever, right upper-quadrant pain, and a focal hepatic lesion on ultrasound or CT.

Amoebic liver abscess.description: An amoebic liver abscess, caused by Entamoeba histolytica, typically presents with fever and right upper-quadrant pain and may follow amoebic intestinal infection.

Traumatic hepatic hematoma or liver cont.normalized_text: Traumatic hepatic hematoma or liver contusion
Traumatic hepatic hematoma or liver cont.description: Blunt abdominal trauma can cause liver contusion or hematoma, producing right upper-quadrant pain and focal hepatic abnormalities on imaging.

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.icd11_title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.normalized_text: Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (anterior STEMI)
Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.description: Acute myocardial infarction due to coronary artery occlusion, with ECG findings consistent with acute anterior wall ischemic injury in the precordial leads.

Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary thrombosis associated with a myeloproliferative neoplasm
Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary.description: Acute myocardial ischemia or infarction caused by arterial thrombosis; markedly elevated platelets and erythrocytosis raise concern for an underlying myeloproliferative disorder predisposing to coronary thrombosis.

Polycythemia vera.description: A chronic JAK2-associated myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by increased red cell mass and often increased white blood cells and platelets, causing pruritus after warm bathing and increased arterial or venous thrombosis risk.

Essential thrombocythemia.description: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm marked by persistent clonal thrombocytosis that can cause microvascular symptoms and arterial thrombosis, including myocardial infarction.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) o.description: Acid reflux or esophageal inflammation can cause recurrent nonexertional burning substernal discomfort, often occurring at night and improving with antacids or proton-pump inhibitors.

Scimitar syndrome (partial anomalous pul.normalized_text: Scimitar syndrome (partial anomalous pulmonary venous return with right lung hypoplasia)
Scimitar syndrome (partial anomalous pul.description: A congenital cardiopulmonary malformation in which part or all of the right pulmonary venous drainage enters the inferior vena cava rather than the left atrium, often with right lung hypoplasia, dextroposition of the heart, anomalous systemic arterial supply, and pulmonary hypertension.

Pulmonary sequestration.description: A congenital nonfunctioning lung segment that lacks normal communication with the tracheobronchial tree and receives systemic arterial blood supply, commonly from the descending thoracic or abdominal aorta. It may cause respiratory distress in neonates, particularly when large or associated with other lung malformations.

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.normalized_text: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM), possibly with hybrid sequestration
Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.description: A developmental malformation of the lower respiratory tract characterized by cystic or solid abnormal lung tissue. Some lesions coexist with systemic arterial supply from the aorta, termed a hybrid CPAM-sequestration lesion, and can produce neonatal respiratory distress through mass effect or impaired ventilation.

Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the.normalized_text: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the.description: Failure of the normal postnatal decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance, leading to right-to-left shunting through fetal circulatory pathways and severe hypoxemia. It is often associated with perinatal asphyxia, meconium aspiration, pulmonary disease, or congenital cardiopulmonary malformations.

Meconium aspiration syndrome.description: Respiratory disease caused by aspiration of meconium-contaminated amniotic fluid before or during delivery. It can cause airway obstruction, chemical pneumonitis, hyperinflation, atelectasis, pulmonary hypertension, and severe respiratory failure.

Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangio.normalized_text: Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangiopathy with malignant hypertension
Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangio.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy causing endothelial injury and small-vessel thrombosis, often triggered or worsened by cocaine-associated severe hypertension; renal biopsy may show arteriolar intimal thickening and onion-skin lesions.

Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic u.description: A complement dysregulation disorder producing thrombotic microangiopathy, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia of variable severity, and often profound renal failure; inherited complement abnormalities can cause familial kidney disease.

Malignant hypertensive nephrosclerosis.description: Severe, accelerated hypertension can injure renal arterioles and glomeruli, producing hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis with onion-skin intimal thickening, ischemic kidney injury, proteinuria, and renal failure.

Hepatitis C-associated membranoprolifera.normalized_text: Hepatitis C-associated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (often cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis)
Hepatitis C-associated membranoprolifera.description: Chronic hepatitis C can cause immune-complex glomerulonephritis, commonly with proteinuria, renal dysfunction, hematuria, and complement consumption; mixed cryoglobulinemia often lowers C4 prominently.

C3 glomerulopathy.description: A group of complement alternative-pathway disorders causing dominant C3 deposition in glomeruli, proteinuria, hematuria, progressive renal failure, and persistent low serum C3; familial complement abnormalities may occur.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.normalized_text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) with area postrema syndrome
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune astrocytopathy associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies that can cause inflammatory lesions in the area postrema and brainstem, producing otherwise unexplained persistent nausea, vomiting, hiccups, and neurological deficits.

Area postrema syndrome due to AQP4-IgG-p.normalized_text: Area postrema syndrome due to AQP4-IgG-positive autoimmune brainstem encephalitis
Area postrema syndrome due to AQP4-IgG-p.description: Area postrema syndrome is a characteristic NMOSD presentation caused by inflammation of the dorsal medulla, especially the area postrema, a vomiting center with high aquaporin-4 expression.

Multiple sclerosis with brainstem involv.description: Multiple sclerosis is an immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause brainstem lesions, eye movement abnormalities, weakness, and upper motor neuron signs.

Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein anti.description: MOGAD is an inflammatory demyelinating disorder that may involve the optic nerves, spinal cord, brain, or brainstem and can occasionally mimic NMOSD.

Brainstem encephalitis (rhombencephaliti.normalized_text: Brainstem encephalitis (rhombencephalitis), including autoimmune or infectious causes
Brainstem encephalitis (rhombencephaliti.description: Rhombencephalitis is inflammation of the hindbrain, including the pons and medulla, and may be caused by autoimmune disorders or infections such as Listeria, leading to cranial nerve, motor, respiratory, and autonomic dysfunction.

Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae infective e.description: A subacute bacterial infection of a cardiac valve caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, a Gram-positive rod that is characteristically resistant to vancomycin and often causes destructive aortic-valve endocarditis.

Native aortic-valve infective endocardit.description: Infection of the native aortic valve, usually bacterial, producing valvular inflammation, vegetations, regurgitation, and potentially periannular extension or abscess formation.

Aortic root abscess complicating infecti.normalized_text: Aortic root abscess complicating infective endocarditis
Aortic root abscess complicating infecti.description: A localized suppurative infection around the aortic valve annulus or aortic root, usually occurring as a complication of infective endocarditis and often associated with severe aortic regurgitation.

Lactobacillus species infective endocard.description: An uncommon form of infective endocarditis caused by Lactobacillus species, which can occur in patients with underlying cardiac disease and may show intrinsic resistance to vancomycin.

Bartonella endocarditis.description: A subacute, often blood-culture-negative infective endocarditis caused by Bartonella species, commonly involving the aortic valve and presenting with prolonged nonspecific constitutional symptoms.

Paradoxical arterial air embolism throug.normalized_text: Paradoxical arterial air embolism through a patent foramen ovale
Paradoxical arterial air embolism throug.description: Venous air introduced during venesection can cross a patent foramen ovale into the arterial circulation, causing embolic obstruction of cerebral and coronary arteries.

Venous air embolism.description: Air entering the venous circulation during an invasive vascular procedure can obstruct pulmonary vessels, producing abrupt hypoxia, dyspnoea, chest pain, and cardiovascular instability.

Acute coronary air embolism causing myoc.normalized_text: Acute coronary air embolism causing myocardial ischemia
Acute coronary air embolism causing myoc.description: Air entering the coronary arteries can transiently obstruct coronary blood flow and cause acute myocardial ischemia or infarction, often with chest pain, ECG changes, and troponin elevation.

Transient ischemic attack due to cerebra.normalized_text: Transient ischemic attack due to cerebral air embolism
Transient ischemic attack due to cerebra.description: An embolus of air reaching the cerebral arterial circulation can produce sudden focal neurological deficits that may resolve rapidly if the obstruction is transient.

Acute pulmonary embolism, including pulm.normalized_text: Acute pulmonary embolism, including pulmonary arterial air embolism
Acute pulmonary embolism, including pulm.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial blood flow by embolic material can cause sudden dyspnoea, hypoxaemia, chest pain, and secondary right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale.

Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), rec.description: A rare, usually superficial astrocytic tumor that commonly affects younger patients, often presents with seizures, and is frequently associated with BRAF V600E mutation. It may recur after resection.

Anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.description: An anaplastic PXA is a higher-grade, more aggressive form of PXA that can arise through recurrence or malignant transformation of a previously lower-grade PXA and may show more infiltrative imaging features.

Diffuse astrocytoma, IDH-mutant.description: A diffusely infiltrating lower-grade glioma that commonly arises in the cerebral hemispheres of younger to middle-aged adults and often presents with longstanding seizures. It typically appears as a nonenhancing or minimally enhancing T2/FLAIR-hyperintense lesion.

Ganglioglioma.description: A generally slow-growing glioneuronal tumor, often located in the temporal lobe, that is strongly associated with chronic focal seizures. Some gangliogliomas harbor BRAF V600E mutations.

Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype or high-grade.normalized_text: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype or high-grade diffuse glioma
Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype or high-grade.description: A highly aggressive infiltrating astrocytic malignancy that can produce enhancing mass lesions, edema, headache, seizures, and neurologic deficits. It is less likely than recurrent/anaplastic PXA in this clinical setting but may be considered if there is malignant transformation or rapid radiographic progression.

Classic dermatomyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by distinctive cutaneous findings and symmetric proximal skeletal-muscle weakness.

Antisynthetase syndrome.description: A systemic autoimmune inflammatory myopathy syndrome that can cause myositis, inflammatory arthritis, interstitial lung disease, Raynaud phenomenon, mechanic's hands, and sometimes dermatomyositis-like rash.

Polymyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy causing subacute, symmetric proximal muscle weakness and elevated muscle enzymes, but without the characteristic skin findings of dermatomyositis.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: A severe autoimmune myopathy, often associated with anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies, that produces rapidly progressive proximal weakness and myalgia with muscle necrosis; cutaneous findings are generally absent.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflam.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflammatory myositis overlap
Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflam.description: Systemic lupus erythematosus can rarely overlap with inflammatory myositis, causing proximal weakness, myalgia, skin eruptions, and periungual vascular changes.

Phenytoin-induced osteomalacia.description: Metabolic bone disease caused by long-term phenytoin use, often through increased vitamin D breakdown, impaired calcium/phosphate balance, and defective mineralization of osteoid.

Vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia.description: Defective mineralization of bone due to inadequate vitamin D availability, causing bone pain, muscle weakness, insufficiency fractures, and biochemical evidence of increased bone turnover.

Tumor-induced osteomalacia.description: A rare paraneoplastic syndrome, usually caused by a phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor producing excess FGF23, which leads to renal phosphate wasting and osteomalacia.

Fanconi syndrome with hypophosphatemic o.description: A proximal renal tubular disorder causing urinary losses of phosphate, glucose, bicarbonate, uric acid, and amino acids; chronic phosphate wasting can produce osteomalacia.

Primary hyperparathyroidism.description: Excess parathyroid hormone secretion causes increased bone turnover and renal phosphate loss; severe longstanding disease can cause skeletal pain, weakness, fractures, and elevated alkaline phosphatase.

Acute infective endocarditis of the mitr.normalized_text: Acute infective endocarditis of the mitral valve due to group A Streptococcus
Acute infective endocarditis of the mitr.description: A bacterial infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve, with formation of valvular vegetations. The echocardiographic image is consistent with a mitral-valve vegetation, and blood cultures identify group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus.

Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke from.normalized_text: Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke from infective endocarditis
Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke from.description: An ischemic cerebral infarction caused by embolization of infected valvular vegetation into the cerebral circulation. The brain image is compatible with an acute cortical infarct, likely from septic embolism.

Severe mitral regurgitation secondary to.normalized_text: Severe mitral regurgitation secondary to infective mitral-valve destruction
Severe mitral regurgitation secondary to.description: Backward leakage of blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole, potentially caused by infected mitral-valve leaflet damage or perforation. Color Doppler imaging appears consistent with substantial mitral regurgitation.

Acute decompensated heart failure due to.normalized_text: Acute decompensated heart failure due to valvular infective endocarditis
Acute decompensated heart failure due to.description: Acute heart failure can occur when infective endocarditis causes severe valvular regurgitation, impaired forward cardiac output, and pulmonary congestion. In this case, mitral-valve involvement and severe regurgitation are likely contributors.

Group A streptococcal sepsis with septic.normalized_text: Group A streptococcal sepsis with septic embolization
Group A streptococcal sepsis with septic.description: A systemic infection caused by Streptococcus pyogenes that can produce fever, tachycardia, inflammatory-marker elevation, organ dysfunction, and—in the setting of endocarditis—septic emboli to the brain or other organs.

Cranioectodermal dysplasia (Sensenbrenne.description: A rare ciliopathy characterized by sagittal craniosynostosis/dolichocephaly, distinctive facial appearance, ectodermal abnormalities involving hair, teeth and nails, skeletal dysplasia with narrow thorax and short limbs, and progressive kidney disease.

Short-rib thoracic dysplasia with or wit.normalized_text: Short-rib thoracic dysplasia with or without polydactyly (Jeune syndrome spectrum)
Short-rib thoracic dysplasia with or wit.description: A group of ciliopathies causing a narrow thorax with short ribs, limb shortening, skeletal abnormalities, and variable renal disease that can progress to chronic kidney failure.

Mainzer-Saldino syndrome.description: A ciliopathy usually featuring renal tubulointerstitial disease or nephronophthisis, retinal degeneration, cone-shaped epiphyses, and variable short stature or skeletal dysplasia.

Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia.description: A multisystem disorder caused by SMARCAL1-related disease, characterized by steroid-resistant nephropathy, progressive renal failure, disproportionate short stature/spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, and often immune deficiency.

Ellis-van Creveld syndrome.description: A skeletal dysplasia characterized by short limbs, short ribs and narrow thorax, ectodermal abnormalities of hair, teeth and nails, and frequent congenital heart defects; renal disease is not a usual major feature.

Cancer-associated dermatomyositis.description: An inflammatory autoimmune myopathy causing characteristic skin lesions and proximal muscle weakness; in adults it may be associated with an underlying malignancy, including gastrointestinal cancer.

Polymyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, elevated muscle enzymes, and possible dysphagia, but without the characteristic dermatomyositis rash.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: A severe autoimmune muscle disease causing rapidly progressive proximal weakness and marked creatine kinase elevation; it can occur with malignancy, statin exposure, or anti-SRP/anti-HMGCR antibodies.

Antisynthetase syndrome.description: A subtype of inflammatory myositis associated with antisynthetase antibodies, commonly causing myositis, inflammatory arthritis, interstitial lung disease, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and hyperkeratotic 'mechanic's hands.'

Paraneoplastic inflammatory myopathy due.normalized_text: Paraneoplastic inflammatory myopathy due to oesophageal malignancy
Paraneoplastic inflammatory myopathy due.description: An inflammatory muscle syndrome triggered by an underlying cancer. Dermatomyositis is the most common paraneoplastic inflammatory myopathy and may precede discovery of oesophageal or other gastrointestinal malignancy.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.description: Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children, causing fragmentation, flattening, and possible collapse of the capital femoral epiphysis. It most often affects boys aged 4 to 10 years.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE).description: Displacement of the femoral head epiphysis relative to the femoral neck through the growth plate, usually occurring in adolescents during periods of rapid growth and often associated with obesity.

Transient synovitis of the hip.description: A self-limited inflammatory hip effusion, often occurring after a viral illness, that causes acute hip pain and a limp in children.

Septic arthritis of the hip.description: A bacterial infection of the hip joint that can rapidly damage cartilage and bone; it is an orthopedic emergency and commonly causes severe pain, fever, and inability to bear weight.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving.normalized_text: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving the hip
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving.description: A chronic inflammatory arthritis beginning before age 16 that may cause joint pain, stiffness, reduced range of motion, and gait disturbance; isolated hip involvement is less common.

Gas-forming pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial abscess within the liver, sometimes caused by gas-producing organisms such as Klebsiella, Escherichia coli, or anaerobes. Gas within a hepatic abscess can mimic free intraperitoneal air on radiography.

Ruptured or perforated pyogenic liver ab.normalized_text: Ruptured or perforated pyogenic liver abscess with perihepatic gas
Ruptured or perforated pyogenic liver ab.description: A liver abscess may enlarge, rupture into the subcapsular or peritoneal space, and cause localized peritonitis, sepsis, and an apparent pneumoperitoneum.

Perforated peptic ulcer.description: A gastric or duodenal ulcer can perforate, releasing air and gastrointestinal contents into the peritoneal cavity and producing acute peritonitis with pneumoperitoneum.

Acute cholangitis due to biliary obstruc.normalized_text: Acute cholangitis due to biliary obstruction
Acute cholangitis due to biliary obstruc.description: Bacterial infection of an obstructed biliary system, commonly from choledocholithiasis or biliary stricture, causes fever, right upper-quadrant pain, and systemic inflammation.

Perforated hollow viscus from small-bowe.normalized_text: Perforated hollow viscus from small-bowel obstruction or adhesional complication
Perforated hollow viscus from small-bowe.description: Prior abdominal operations can cause adhesions leading to bowel obstruction; bowel ischemia or perforation can then produce vomiting, peritonitis, sepsis, and free intraperitoneal gas.

Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion syndro.description: A chromosomal disorder caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, classically associated with a high-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, characteristic facial features, and possible congenital heart defects. The documented 5p15.2 deletion is diagnostic.

Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome.description: A chromosomal deletion syndrome caused by loss of material from chromosome 4p. It commonly causes severe developmental delay, growth restriction, microcephaly, hypotonia, seizures, eye abnormalities, and congenital heart defects.

1p36 deletion syndrome.description: A chromosome deletion disorder involving the distal short arm of chromosome 1, associated with developmental delay or intellectual disability, hypotonia, microcephaly, visual problems, seizures, brain abnormalities, and congenital cardiac defects.

Phelan-McDermid syndrome (22q13 deletion.description: A neurodevelopmental disorder usually caused by deletion of chromosome 22q13 involving the SHANK3 gene. It is characterized by severe speech and developmental delay, neonatal hypotonia, reduced pain perception, autistic features, and sometimes minor dysmorphic or cardiac findings.

Congenital cytomegalovirus infection.description: A congenital viral infection that can cause microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia or motor impairment, intracranial abnormalities, hearing loss, visual abnormalities, and growth restriction.

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.icd11_title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of t.normalized_text: Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of the jejunum
Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of t.description: A malignant germ-cell tumor showing yolk-sac differentiation, typically associated with markedly elevated AFP and diverse histologic patterns including microcystic/reticular, papillary, solid, and glandular areas. Primary gastrointestinal involvement is exceptionally rare.

Embryonal carcinoma.description: An aggressive nonseminomatous germ-cell tumor that can produce AFP when associated with yolk-sac differentiation. Histology often shows primitive epithelial cells in solid, glandular, papillary, or tubular patterns.

Small intestinal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from intestinal mucosal glands, usually occurring in adults and capable of invading through the bowel wall and producing obstruction, pain, or peritoneal spread.

Desmoplastic small round cell tumor.description: A rare aggressive pediatric and young-adult malignancy that usually arises in the peritoneal cavity and commonly presents with abdominal masses, ascites, and peritoneal dissemination.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the small.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the small intestine
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the small.description: Pediatric non-Hodgkin lymphoma can involve the ileum or jejunum and cause abdominal pain, bowel-wall masses, ascites, and abdominal lymphadenopathy.

Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopi.normalized_text: Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa
Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopi.description: A congenital ileal diverticulum that may contain acid-secreting gastric mucosa, causing adjacent ileal ulceration and sometimes massive painless or painful lower gastrointestinal bleeding. The scan appearance is consistent with ectopic gastric mucosa in the right lower abdomen.

Intussusception.description: Telescoping of one segment of bowel into another, most often ileocolic in infants, causing episodic colicky pain, obstruction, ischemia, and bloody mucus-containing stool.

Enteric duplication cyst with ectopic ga.normalized_text: Enteric duplication cyst with ectopic gastric mucosa
Enteric duplication cyst with ectopic ga.description: A rare congenital duplication of the gastrointestinal tract that can contain ectopic gastric mucosa, resulting in ulceration, bleeding, abdominal pain, or obstruction.

Cow's milk protein allergic proctocoliti.description: A non-IgE-mediated food allergy in young infants that causes colonic inflammation and small amounts of rectal bleeding, often related to cow's milk protein exposure.

Acute infectious colitis.description: Inflammation of the intestine caused by bacterial or viral infection, which can produce abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, and bloody stools in infants.

diagnoses.name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

Multiple pulmonary arteriovenous malform.description: Abnormal direct connections between pulmonary arteries and veins that create right-to-left shunting; CT typically shows well-defined enhancing vascular nodules with feeding and draining vessels.

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (H.normalized_text: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (H.description: An inherited vascular disorder characterized by telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations, commonly involving the lungs, nose, gastrointestinal tract, liver, and brain.

Bronchiolitis obliterans.description: An obstructive small-airway disorder caused by inflammatory and fibrotic narrowing of bronchioles, producing progressive and often fixed airflow limitation; CT may show mosaic attenuation and air trapping.

Asthma with severe fixed airflow obstruc.normalized_text: Asthma with severe fixed airflow obstruction
Asthma with severe fixed airflow obstruc.description: A chronic inflammatory airway disease causing episodic or persistent airflow obstruction, breathlessness, wheeze, and cough; longstanding disease can produce partially fixed small-airway obstruction.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease du.normalized_text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease due to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency or other nonsmoking cause
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease du.description: COPD is persistent airflow obstruction, usually caused by smoking but occasionally occurring in nonsmokers because of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, environmental exposures, or chronic airway disease.

Pulmonary sarcoidosis with concomitant u.normalized_text: Pulmonary sarcoidosis with concomitant unicentric Castleman disease
Pulmonary sarcoidosis with concomitant u.description: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, often involving the lungs and lymph nodes. Unicentric Castleman disease is a localized benign lymphoproliferative disorder that can cause a chronic enlarged lymph node with characteristic hyaline-vascular histology.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Pulmonary tuberculosis is infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, commonly causing upper-lobe pulmonary infiltrates, cavitation, granulomatous inflammation, fever, cough, hemoptysis, and lymph node enlargement.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is an ANCA-associated necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis that can cause granulomatous lung lesions, pulmonary nodules or cavitation, hemoptysis, and systemic inflammation.

Chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis or anot.normalized_text: Chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis or another endemic fungal granulomatous infection
Chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis or anot.description: Endemic fungal infections, including histoplasmosis, can produce granulomatous pulmonary inflammation, upper-lobe infiltrates or cavities, fever, cough, hemoptysis, and lymphadenopathy.

Hodgkin lymphoma with a sarcoid-like gra.normalized_text: Hodgkin lymphoma with a sarcoid-like granulomatous reaction
Hodgkin lymphoma with a sarcoid-like gra.description: Hodgkin lymphoma can present with painless rubbery supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor. Granulomas may occasionally occur in lymph nodes or adjacent pulmonary lesions and can obscure the underlying malignancy.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.normalized_text: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) due to JC polyomavirus
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.description: A severe opportunistic demyelinating brain infection caused by reactivation of JC virus in immunosuppressed patients, particularly those exposed to natalizumab or fingolimod.

Multiple sclerosis relapse.description: An acute inflammatory demyelinating episode causing new or worsening neurologic deficits in a person with multiple sclerosis.

JC virus granule cell neuronopathy.description: A JC virus-associated infection that primarily affects cerebellar granule neurons and causes progressive cerebellar dysfunction; it can coexist with PML.

Herpes simplex virus encephalitis.description: An acute viral encephalitis, usually caused by HSV-1, which commonly involves the temporal lobes and can produce seizures and focal neurologic deficits.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: A clinicoradiologic syndrome of vasogenic edema, often involving posterior brain regions, that may cause seizures and visual disturbances; it is associated with hypertension, renal disease, cytotoxic therapies, and some immunomodulatory treatments.

Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-ga.normalized_text: Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency)
Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-ga.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic GLA variants, resulting in globotriaosylceramide accumulation in vascular, renal, neural, skin, ocular, and cardiac cells.

Fabry cardiomyopathy.description: Cardiac involvement from Fabry disease caused by glycosphingolipid storage in cardiomyocytes, often producing concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, repolarization abnormalities, arrhythmias, and chest pain.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: A myocardial disorder characterized by unexplained ventricular hypertrophy, commonly due to sarcomeric gene variants, which can cause chest pain, arrhythmias, dyspnea, and sudden cardiac death risk.

Fabry nephropathy.description: Renal involvement in Fabry disease due to glycosphingolipid deposition in podocytes, glomerular endothelial cells, tubular cells, and vascular cells, initially causing proteinuria and potentially progressing to chronic kidney disease.

Anderson-Fabry disease with small-fiber.description: A neurologic manifestation of Fabry disease in which glycolipid accumulation and small-fiber dysfunction produce episodic burning pain, dysesthesia, and pain crises, often beginning in childhood.

Infected intrahepatic hematoma.description: A traumatic hepatic hematoma can become secondarily infected, producing an abscess-like collection and systemic inflammatory signs.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A localized bacterial infection of the liver causing a pus-filled collection; it may occur after trauma, hematoma, biliary disease, or bloodstream infection.

Infected biloma.description: A biloma is a localized collection of bile caused by biliary tract injury; after liver trauma it may become infected and cause sepsis-like findings.

Acute cholangitis.description: Bacterial infection of the biliary tree, usually due to impaired bile drainage or obstruction, causing fever and abnormal liver biochemical tests.

Hepatic infarction or ischemic hepatic i.normalized_text: Hepatic infarction or ischemic hepatic injury after trauma
Hepatic infarction or ischemic hepatic i.description: Compromised hepatic blood flow after severe trauma, vascular injury, shock, or embolization can cause liver tissue necrosis, elevated liver enzymes, fever, and inflammatory laboratory findings.

Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.normalized_text: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) induced by iodinated contrast
Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.description: A severe sterile pustular drug eruption characterized by abrupt onset of numerous small nonfollicular pustules, neutrophilic inflammation, and frequent neutrophilia. Iodinated contrast media can rarely trigger it within hours to days.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or AGEP.normalized_text: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or AGEP-TEN overlap syndrome
Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or AGEP.description: TEN is a life-threatening, usually medication-induced epidermal necrolysis causing widespread blistering and skin detachment. Drug eruptions may occasionally show overlapping pustular AGEP and TEN-like necrosis.

Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption.normalized_text: Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption due to iodinated contrast
Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption.description: A drug reaction in which sharply demarcated erythematous or violaceous plaques recur after re-exposure and may develop vesicles, bullae, and epidermal necrosis. Iodinated contrast can cause fixed drug eruptions.

Generalized pustular psoriasis.description: A severe inflammatory psoriasis variant with widespread sterile pustules on erythematous skin, often accompanied by systemic illness and neutrophilia. It may be triggered by medications, infection, or withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids.

Drug-induced linear IgA bullous dermatos.description: An autoimmune blistering disease, often drug-induced, that produces tense vesicles and bullae and can occasionally mimic toxic epidermal necrolysis. Diagnosis requires direct immunofluorescence showing linear IgA deposition along the basement membrane.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis with pu.normalized_text: Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis with purpura fulminans
Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis with pu.description: A rapidly progressive gram-negative septicemia acquired from dog saliva or bites, particularly severe in people with heavy alcohol use, liver disease, or absent spleen. It can cause disseminated intravascular coagulation, shock, necrotic purpura, and limb ischemia.

Pasteurella multocida bite-wound infecti.normalized_text: Pasteurella multocida bite-wound infection with septic shock
Pasteurella multocida bite-wound infecti.description: Pasteurella multocida is a gram-negative bacterium commonly transmitted by dog or cat bites. It usually causes rapidly developing cellulitis but can occasionally produce bacteremia and severe sepsis in medically vulnerable patients.

Necrotizing soft-tissue infection (necro.normalized_text: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection (necrotizing fasciitis) following dog bites
Necrotizing soft-tissue infection (necro.description: A rapidly destructive infection of fascia and subcutaneous tissue, caused by organisms such as streptococci, staphylococci, anaerobes, or mixed bite-wound flora. It can cause skin necrosis, septic shock, and multiorgan failure.

Meningococcal septicemia with purpura fu.description: Invasive Neisseria meningitidis bloodstream infection can rapidly cause septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and a widespread petechial or purpuric rash that may progress to tissue necrosis.

Clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene) o.normalized_text: Clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene) or clostridial sepsis
Clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene) o.description: Clostridial infection can follow contaminated penetrating trauma and may cause rapidly progressive muscle necrosis, systemic toxicity, shock, and skin discoloration. It is classically associated with severe local pain, swelling, gas formation, and foul drainage.

diagnoses.name: MELAS syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: MELAS - [Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes] syndrome

MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalom.normalized_text: MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes)
MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalom.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder characterized by mitochondrial myopathy, elevated lactate, and recurrent neurologic stroke-like episodes, commonly associated with pathogenic MT-TL1 mitochondrial tRNA leucine mutations.

Mitochondrial myopathy due to MT-TL1 mut.normalized_text: Mitochondrial myopathy due to MT-TL1 mutation
Mitochondrial myopathy due to MT-TL1 mut.description: A mitochondrial cytopathy caused by impaired oxidative phosphorylation, producing chronic skeletal-muscle weakness, exercise intolerance, muscle wasting, and lactic acidosis; neurologic and cardiac involvement can occur.

Cardioembolic ischemic stroke due to lef.normalized_text: Cardioembolic ischemic stroke due to left ventricular noncompaction cardiomyopathy with ventricular thrombus
Cardioembolic ischemic stroke due to lef.description: Left ventricular noncompaction is a cardiomyopathy with prominent ventricular trabeculations and deep recesses. Reduced contractility and thrombus formation may lead to systemic embolism, including embolic ischemic stroke in young adults.

Mitochondrial arteriopathy causing cereb.description: Mitochondrial disease can involve vascular smooth muscle and endothelial energy metabolism, potentially causing intracranial arterial stenosis or impaired vascular reactivity and contributing to ischemic cerebral events.

Moyamoya disease or moyamoya syndrome.description: A progressive steno-occlusive cerebrovascular disorder involving the terminal internal carotid and proximal cerebral arteries, causing recurrent ischemic strokes or transient ischemic attacks in young individuals.

Extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (bile du.description: A malignant tumor arising from the bile duct lining that can obstruct bile flow, causing progressive cholestatic jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and biliary dilation. Imaging and pathology are concerning for an infiltrative biliary adenocarcinoma.

Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma.description: Cancer of the pancreatic head can compress or invade the distal common bile duct, producing painless or mildly painful obstructive jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, anorexia, and elevated CA 19-9.

Choledocholithiasis with obstructive jau.description: A gallstone lodged in the common bile duct causes impaired bile drainage, resulting in jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, elevated bilirubin and liver enzymes, and right upper quadrant pain.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis.description: A chronic inflammatory and fibrosing disease of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts that causes multifocal strictures, cholestasis, pruritus, fatigue, jaundice, and increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma.

IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis.description: An immune-mediated fibroinflammatory disorder causing bile duct wall thickening and strictures, often associated with autoimmune pancreatitis. It can mimic cholangiocarcinoma and produce obstructive jaundice.

Gallstone ileus with rectal gallstone im.normalized_text: Gallstone ileus with rectal gallstone impaction due to cholecystoenteric fistula
Gallstone ileus with rectal gallstone im.description: A gallstone enters the gastrointestinal tract through an abnormal fistula between the gallbladder and bowel, then migrates distally and may become impacted in the rectum, causing obstructive symptoms.

Crohn's disease with anorectal stricture.description: Crohn's disease can cause chronic inflammation and scarring of the anus or rectum, resulting in narrowing of the bowel lumen and obstructed defecation.

Rectal fecal impaction.description: Fecal impaction is accumulation of hardened stool in the rectum that can cause obstructed defecation, pressure, and minor mucosal bleeding.

Rectal foreign body.description: A retained object in the rectum can produce rectal pressure, impaired stool passage, mucosal trauma, and bleeding. In this case, the gallstone functioned as an intraluminal foreign body.

Rectal or colorectal malignancy causing.normalized_text: Rectal or colorectal malignancy causing partial obstruction
Rectal or colorectal malignancy causing.description: A rectal or colorectal tumor can narrow the bowel lumen and cause altered stool passage, rectal pressure, and bleeding.

Acute lateral patellar dislocation.description: Displacement of the patella to the outside of the knee, commonly occurring in adolescents with ligamentous laxity and often causing injury to the medial patellofemoral ligament.

Osteochondral fracture following patella.description: A fracture involving articular cartilage and underlying bone, often from the medial patellar facet or lateral femoral condyle after a lateral patellar dislocation; the fragment may detach and become a loose body.

Intra-articular loose body of the knee.normalized_text: Intra-articular loose body of the knee
Intra-articular loose body of the knee.description: A free fragment of cartilage, bone, or osteochondral tissue within the knee joint, commonly resulting from trauma such as patellar dislocation and capable of causing mechanical locking.

Medial patellofemoral ligament injury or.normalized_text: Medial patellofemoral ligament injury or tear
Medial patellofemoral ligament injury or.description: Sprain or tearing of the main ligament that restrains lateral patellar movement, typically occurring during an acute lateral patellar dislocation.

Meniscal tear.description: A tear of the medial or lateral meniscus, usually from a twisting knee injury, which may cause pain, swelling, catching, and mechanical locking.

Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome.description: A rare follicular variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by cicatricial scalp alopecia, non-scarring loss of axillary and pubic hair, and widespread keratotic follicular papules (lichen spinulosus-like lesions).

Lichen planopilaris.description: A lymphocyte-mediated inflammatory disorder that destroys hair follicles and causes permanent scarring alopecia; follicular keratotic papules and perifollicular scale may occur.

Lichen spinulosus.description: An uncommon follicular keratosis producing groups of rough, spiny keratotic papules, often on the trunk and extremities; it can resemble keratosis pilaris.

Keratosis pilaris.description: A common benign disorder of follicular keratinization causing rough, small keratotic papules, usually on the upper arms, thighs, buttocks, or cheeks.

Pityriasis rubra pilaris.description: A papulosquamous keratinization disorder that may cause follicular hyperkeratotic papules, reddish-orange scaling plaques, palmoplantar keratoderma, and sometimes alopecia.

Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic u.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy caused by dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, often triggered by pregnancy or the postpartum period and characterized by hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and prominent kidney injury.

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: Severe uncontrolled hypertension can damage small vessels, producing endothelial injury, renal failure, thrombocytopenia, and mechanical hemolytic anemia; it may also cause ischemic skin lesions.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: A severe thrombotic microangiopathy, usually due to marked ADAMTS13 deficiency, causing thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with variable kidney, neurologic, and systemic involvement.

Pregnancy-associated thrombotic microang.normalized_text: Pregnancy-associated thrombotic microangiopathy related to preeclampsia/HELLP-spectrum disease
Pregnancy-associated thrombotic microang.description: Preeclampsia and related pregnancy-associated endothelial injury can cause hypertension, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, and renal injury; persistent or delayed disease may reveal an underlying complement-mediated TMA.

Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (.normalized_text: Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS) or antiphospholipid-associated thrombotic vasculopathy
Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (.description: An autoimmune hypercoagulable disorder causing widespread small-vessel thrombosis, which may lead to renal thrombotic microangiopathy, thrombocytopenia, hypertension, skin necrosis, and pregnancy complications.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of.normalized_text: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of the ileum
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract arising from interstitial cells of Cajal or related precursors. Most GISTs express KIT (CD117), and activating KIT exon 11 mutations are characteristic and support this diagnosis.

Small-bowel neuroendocrine tumor (ileal.description: A neuroendocrine neoplasm that commonly arises in the distal ileum and may present as an enhancing small-bowel mass, sometimes with bleeding, obstruction, or metastatic mesenteric and liver disease.

Small-bowel adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the small intestine that can cause gastrointestinal bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, abdominal pain, obstruction, or weight loss.

Small-bowel lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the small intestine that may produce bowel-wall thickening or a mass and can present with bleeding, anemia, pain, obstruction, or systemic symptoms.

Leiomyosarcoma of the small intestine.description: A rare malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can arise from the intestinal wall and may cause bleeding, anemia, abdominal pain, or a mass. It can resemble GIST morphologically but generally lacks the characteristic KIT molecular alterations of GIST.

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

Solid serous adenoma of the pancreas.normalized_text: Solid serous adenoma of the pancreas
Solid serous adenoma of the pancreas.description: A rare solid variant of pancreatic serous cystadenoma, a generally benign epithelial neoplasm composed of glycogen-rich clear cells and a prominent capillary network. It can mimic hypervascular solid pancreatic tumors on imaging.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.description: A neoplasm arising from pancreatic endocrine cells. Nonfunctioning tumors may become large before detection and can present with abdominal mass effect, whereas functioning tumors produce hormone-related syndromes.

Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma.description: A rare malignant pancreatic epithelial tumor with acinar differentiation. It often forms a large, well-circumscribed solid mass and may cause nonspecific abdominal symptoms or pancreatic exocrine dysfunction.

Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.normalized_text: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.description: A low-grade malignant pancreatic neoplasm that is typically encapsulated and contains solid and degenerative or hemorrhagic areas. It occurs predominantly in young women but can rarely occur in older men.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: The most common primary pancreatic malignancy, usually arising from pancreatic ducts. It often causes obstructive jaundice, weight loss, abdominal or back pain, and progressive decline, especially when located in the pancreatic head.

Hailey-Hailey disease (benign familial p.description: An autosomal dominant acantholytic skin disorder caused by impaired keratinocyte adhesion, producing recurrent painful, erosive, crusted plaques in flexural areas that worsen with heat, sweating, and friction.

Pemphigus vegetans.description: A rare vegetating variant of pemphigus vulgaris characterized by flaccid blisters that evolve into painful, eroded, verrucous plaques, often in axillae, groin, and other intertriginous sites.
