Darier disease (keratosis follicularis).description: An inherited disorder of keratinization and epidermal adhesion causing greasy, crusted keratotic papules in seborrheic and flexural areas; heat, sweating, and friction commonly exacerbate it.

Inverse psoriasis.description: Psoriasis affecting skin folds, where lesions are often smooth, red or hyperpigmented, painful, and prone to maceration because of moisture and friction.

Acanthosis nigricans with superimposed i.description: Acanthosis nigricans causes velvety hyperpigmented thickening of flexural skin, commonly associated with obesity and insulin resistance; moisture and friction can lead to secondary intertrigo with odor, maceration, and erosion.

Myositis ossificans circumscripta.description: A benign reactive process in which bone forms within soft tissue or muscle, often after trauma but sometimes without a recognized injury. Imaging commonly shows a well-circumscribed mass with peripheral mature ossification (zonal pattern).

Extraskeletal osteosarcoma.description: A rare malignant mesenchymal tumor that produces osteoid or bone in soft tissues without originating from bone. It usually presents as an enlarging calcified soft-tissue mass.

Parosteal osteosarcoma.description: A low-grade bone-forming osteosarcoma arising from the outer cortical surface of bone, often producing a densely ossified mass adjacent to the pelvis or long bones.

Synovial sarcoma.description: A malignant soft-tissue sarcoma that commonly occurs in adolescents and young adults and may contain punctate or peripheral calcifications. It can arise near joints, including the hip and pelvic region.

Soft-tissue chondroma or extraskeletal c.description: A benign cartilaginous tumor arising in soft tissues, sometimes with calcification or ossification. It is usually slow growing and may be painful because of local mass effect.

Stiff-person syndrome (SPS).description: A rare autoimmune neurologic disorder characterized by progressive axial and limb muscle rigidity, painful stimulus-sensitive spasms, and continuous motor-unit activity on electromyography; commonly associated with anti-GAD65 or amphiphysin antibodies.

Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.normalized_text: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.description: A severe autoimmune stiff-person-spectrum disorder, often associated with glycine-receptor antibodies, producing rigidity, painful spasms, exaggerated reflexes, myoclonus, and potentially brainstem or respiratory involvement.

Anti-GAD65 autoimmune stiff-person spect.description: An autoimmune form of stiff-person spectrum disease caused by antibodies targeting glutamic acid decarboxylase 65, resulting in impaired inhibitory GABAergic signaling and severe muscle hyperexcitability.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia.description: A group of inherited upper-motor-neuron disorders causing slowly progressive bilateral leg spasticity, weakness, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses, sometimes with additional neurologic features.

Tetanus.description: An acute toxin-mediated neurologic illness caused by Clostridium tetani, producing painful generalized muscle rigidity, stimulus-induced spasms, and potentially life-threatening respiratory muscle involvement.

Takayasu arteritis.description: A chronic large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, typically in younger women, causing arterial stenosis, occlusion, cerebral hypoperfusion, and ischemic complications.

Premature atherosclerotic carotid and gr.normalized_text: Premature atherosclerotic carotid and great-vessel disease
Premature atherosclerotic carotid and gr.description: Atherosclerotic plaque formation can cause narrowing or occlusion of the carotid and subclavian arteries, producing transient cerebral hypoperfusion, ischemic stroke, and rarely scalp ischemia.

Giant cell arteritis with large-vessel i.normalized_text: Giant cell arteritis with large-vessel involvement
Giant cell arteritis with large-vessel i.description: A granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large arteries that can cause scalp ischemia or necrosis, stroke, and stenosis of the carotid or subclavian arteries.

Subclavian steal syndrome.description: Hemodynamically significant subclavian artery stenosis can reverse vertebral artery flow, reducing posterior cerebral circulation and causing presyncope, syncope, or neurologic symptoms.

Fibromuscular dysplasia of the cervical.normalized_text: Fibromuscular dysplasia of the cervical arteries
Fibromuscular dysplasia of the cervical.description: A non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory arterial disorder, more common in women, that may affect carotid and vertebral arteries and predispose to stenosis, dissection, transient ischemic attacks, and stroke.

Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).description: A systemic infection caused by Leishmania parasites, transmitted by sandflies and associated with dog reservoirs in Mediterranean regions. Immunosuppression from anti-TNF therapy can predispose to severe or atypical disease. The blood/bone-marrow image is compatible with intracellular Leishmania amastigotes within macrophages.

Felty syndrome.description: A complication of longstanding seropositive rheumatoid arthritis characterized by neutropenia, splenomegaly, and increased susceptibility to infection; anemia and thrombocytopenia may also occur.

T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukem.normalized_text: T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia associated with rheumatoid arthritis
T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukem.description: An indolent clonal lymphoproliferative disorder often associated with rheumatoid arthritis and characterized by chronic neutropenia, anemia, splenomegaly, and sometimes thrombocytopenia.

Systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumato.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid arthritis-systemic lupus overlap syndrome
Systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumato.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause inflammatory arthritis, fever, cytopenias, hypocomplementemia, autoantibodies, and immune-complex skin vasculitis. Anti-TNF therapy can also induce lupus-like autoimmunity.

Mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis caused by circulating cryoglobulins, commonly associated with hepatitis C, autoimmune disease, lymphoproliferative disorders, or chronic infections. It often causes purpura, arthralgia, low complement, and elevated rheumatoid factor.

Necrobiosis lipoidica.description: A chronic granulomatous inflammatory skin disorder, strongly associated with diabetes mellitus, that typically forms yellow-brown, atrophic, indurated plaques with violaceous or erythematous borders on the pretibial shins.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign granulomatous skin condition that usually causes firm papules arranged in annular plaques, often on the hands, feet, elbows, or ankles. Generalized forms may be associated with diabetes.

Diabetic dermopathy.description: A common diabetes-associated microvascular skin manifestation characterized by multiple small, round or oval, light-brown, slightly atrophic macules on the shins, often called diabetic shin spots.

Stasis dermatitis.description: An inflammatory dermatitis caused by chronic venous insufficiency, usually affecting the lower legs and causing edema, erythema, scaling, pruritus, and brown hemosiderin pigmentation.

Cutaneous sarcoidosis.description: A granulomatous inflammatory disease that can cause papules, plaques, nodules, or scars in the skin; histology typically shows noncaseating granulomas. Skin disease may occur with or without systemic sarcoidosis.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (PHP1B).description: A disorder of parathyroid hormone resistance, usually caused by abnormal methylation at the GNAS locus. It leads to hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia despite elevated parathyroid hormone levels. The abnormal GNAS methylation pattern in the patient strongly supports this diagnosis.

Hypocalcemia with tetany and laryngospas.description: Low serum calcium can cause increased neuromuscular excitability, including muscle stiffness, tetany, dysphagia, laryngospasm, stridor, and positive Chvostek's sign. In this case, it may be caused by parathyroid hormone resistance.

Acute hypoparathyroidism.description: Deficient parathyroid hormone secretion causes hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, producing tetany, paresthesias, muscle cramps, dysphagia, and laryngospasm. It is a key alternative cause of hypocalcemic symptoms, although the abnormal GNAS methylation favors pseudohypoparathyroidism rather than primary hypoparathyroidism.

Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorde.normalized_text: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), fear of aversive consequences subtype
Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorde.description: ARFID can develop after a frightening choking or vomiting event, leading to avoidance of eating or drinking because of fear of choking, vomiting, or other harmful consequences. It can rapidly cause dehydration and weight or nutritional compromise.

Eosinophilic esophagitis.description: A chronic allergic inflammatory disease of the esophagus that commonly occurs in children with atopic conditions and can cause dysphagia, food impaction, vomiting, and avoidance of eating.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, which can involve the lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, and reticuloendothelial system. Tissue may show granulomatous inflammation with small intracellular yeasts highlighted by fungal stains.

Dabrafenib-trametinib-associated pyrexia.description: A common adverse effect of combined BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy, characterized by recurrent high fever, chills, dehydration, hypotension, nausea, and sometimes renal or hepatic dysfunction. Symptoms often improve after temporary drug interruption.

Disseminated tuberculosis.description: Hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis can cause fever, constitutional illness, granulomatous hepatitis, hepatosplenic lesions, and diffuse pulmonary disease; acid-fast organisms may be demonstrable in tissue.

Bacterial sepsis from hepatobiliary infe.description: Severe bacterial infection, such as acute cholangitis, hepatic abscess, or another intra-abdominal source, can produce fever, hypotension, tachycardia, diaphoresis, nausea, and right upper quadrant abdominal discomfort.

Metastatic melanoma with hepatic, spleni.normalized_text: Metastatic melanoma with hepatic, splenic, and pulmonary involvement
Metastatic melanoma with hepatic, spleni.description: Melanoma can recur or disseminate to the lungs, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, bone, brain, and other organs. Extensive tumor burden can cause constitutional symptoms and abdominal discomfort.

Metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma invol.normalized_text: Metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma involving the gallbladder
Metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma invol.description: Rare metastatic spread of prostate cancer to the gallbladder, potentially causing gallbladder enlargement, biliary-type pain, and cholecystitis-like symptoms. The histologic and immunohistochemical appearance is consistent with metastatic prostatic carcinoma.

Acute cholecystitis.description: Acute inflammation of the gallbladder, most commonly caused by cystic-duct obstruction from gallstones, although malignant obstruction or infiltration can also produce cholecystitis.

Gallbladder adenocarcinoma.description: A primary malignant epithelial tumor of the gallbladder that may cause abdominal pain, gallbladder distention, cholestatic liver-test abnormalities, and local invasion or biliary obstruction.

Malignant biliary obstruction from metas.normalized_text: Malignant biliary obstruction from metastatic lymphadenopathy or periportal metastatic disease
Malignant biliary obstruction from metas.description: Compression or invasion of the biliary tract by metastatic lymph nodes or tumor deposits can cause cholestatic enzyme elevation, abdominal pain, gallbladder distention, and sometimes pancreatitis.

Acute pancreatitis due to transient panc.normalized_text: Acute pancreatitis due to transient pancreatobiliary obstruction
Acute pancreatitis due to transient panc.description: Inflammation of the pancreas, often caused by transient obstruction at the ampulla from gallstones, sludge, tumor, or metastatic compression of the biliary-pancreatic outflow tract.

Allgrove syndrome (Triple A syndrome; AA.normalized_text: Allgrove syndrome (Triple A syndrome; AAAS-related disorder)
Allgrove syndrome (Triple A syndrome; AA.description: A rare autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by alacrima, achalasia/dysphagia, ACTH-resistant isolated glucocorticoid deficiency, and progressive neurologic/autonomic dysfunction; the neurologic form is often called 4A syndrome.

Familial glucocorticoid deficiency.description: An inherited ACTH-resistance disorder causing isolated cortisol deficiency, elevated ACTH, hyperpigmentation, hypoglycemia, and recurrent adrenal crises while mineralocorticoid function is generally preserved.

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.description: A peroxisomal disorder caused by ABCD1 variants that can produce primary adrenal insufficiency and progressive neurologic disease, including spasticity, ataxia, cognitive decline, and peripheral neuropathy.

Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1.description: An autosomal-recessive autoimmune disease caused by AIRE variants, classically featuring chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and primary adrenal insufficiency, with possible ectodermal and neurologic complications.

X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita (N.normalized_text: X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita (NR0B1/DAX1-related adrenal insufficiency)
X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita (N.description: An X-linked developmental disorder of the adrenal cortex causing childhood primary adrenal insufficiency; affected males may later develop hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and reproductive abnormalities.

Cerebral fat embolism syndrome.description: Neurologic injury from fat or marrow emboli entering the cerebral circulation, causing multifocal microinfarcts and petechial hemorrhages. It may occur with extensive bone disease or marrow necrosis even without a recent fracture.

Cancer-associated multifocal embolic isc.description: Multiple acute ischemic strokes caused by malignancy-related hypercoagulability, nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, or tumor-associated embolic disease.

Cerebral intravascular tumor embolism fr.normalized_text: Cerebral intravascular tumor embolism from metastatic breast carcinoma
Cerebral intravascular tumor embolism fr.description: Tumor cells or tumor emboli occlude small cerebral vessels in disseminated cancer, producing multifocal ischemic lesions, hemorrhagic microvascular injury, and rapidly progressive encephalopathy.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: A vasogenic edema syndrome causing seizures, altered mental status, headache, or visual symptoms, often associated with hypertension, renal dysfunction, cytotoxic therapy, or endothelial injury from malignancy.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.description: A JC-virus demyelinating infection of the central nervous system occurring in immunosuppressed patients, typically causing progressive cognitive, motor, and visual deficits with multifocal white-matter MRI lesions.

Isolated intramedullary spinal neurosarc.description: Sarcoidosis involving the spinal cord without detectable systemic disease. It commonly produces an enhancing intramedullary cervical lesion and noncaseating granulomas on biopsy.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune inflammatory demyelinating disorder that can cause longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, often with severe motor, sensory, and autonomic deficits.

Multiple sclerosis with cervical myeliti.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that may cause focal spinal cord lesions with weakness, sensory deficits, and bladder dysfunction.

Intramedullary spinal cord tumor (ependy.normalized_text: Intramedullary spinal cord tumor (ependymoma or astrocytoma)
Intramedullary spinal cord tumor (ependy.description: A primary tumor arising within the spinal cord that can enlarge the cord and progressively disrupt corticospinal, spinothalamic, and dorsal-column pathways.

Tuberculous intramedullary granuloma (sp.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can form granulomatous inflammatory lesions within the spinal cord, causing subacute compressive or inflammatory myelopathy.

Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lun.normalized_text: Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lung abscess
Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lun.description: A severe bacterial infection causing consolidation and tissue necrosis, sometimes forming cavitary lesions or abscesses in the lung.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: A chronic lung infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that may produce cough, sputum, chest discomfort, consolidation, and cavitary lung lesions.

Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia.description: An inflammatory lung disorder in which granulation tissue plugs fill small airways and alveoli, often causing persistent cough and consolidative opacities that do not respond to antibiotics.

Pulmonary actinomycosis.description: A chronic bacterial infection caused by Actinomyces species that can cause mass-like consolidation, abscess formation, cavitation, and chest pain; it may mimic cancer or tuberculosis.

Endobronchial obstruction with post-obst.normalized_text: Endobronchial obstruction with post-obstructive pneumonia, including bronchial carcinoid or other lung tumor
Endobronchial obstruction with post-obst.description: A lesion obstructing a bronchus can impair drainage and cause recurrent or persistent localized pneumonia, mucus retention, collapse, or abscess-like changes distal to the obstruction.

Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirof.normalized_text: Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirofilaria repens
Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirof.description: A zoonotic filarial nematode infection transmitted by mosquitoes, commonly affecting dogs and occasionally causing solitary or migrating subcutaneous nodules in humans in Mediterranean Europe. Histology typically shows a thick-cuticled nematode within an inflammatory nodule.

Subcutaneous cysticercosis.description: Infection with larval Taenia solium cysts, which can form painless mobile subcutaneous or intramuscular nodules. It is usually acquired through ingestion of parasite eggs and may occur with or without neurologic disease.

Gnathostomiasis.description: A tissue-invasive nematode infection caused by Gnathostoma species. Larval migration can cause intermittent or migratory subcutaneous swellings, often after eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish, amphibians, or other intermediate hosts.

Sparganosis.description: A larval tapeworm infection caused by Spirometra species. It may produce slowly growing or migrating subcutaneous nodules after ingestion of contaminated water or raw intermediate-host meat.

Onchocerciasis.description: A filarial infection caused by Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by blackflies. Adult worms may reside in subcutaneous nodules, while microfilariae cause pruritic dermatitis and ocular disease.

Progressive supranuclear palsy, Richards.description: A rapidly progressive tauopathy causing early falls, axial-predominant parkinsonism, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, dysarthria, dysphagia, and frontal-subcortical dysfunction. Midbrain atrophy may produce the "hummingbird" sign on sagittal MRI.

Multiple system atrophy, parkinsonian ty.description: A synucleinopathy characterized by poorly levodopa-responsive parkinsonism with autonomic failure; cerebellar dysfunction, dysarthria, dysphagia, and dystonia may occur.

Corticobasal syndrome (often due to cort.normalized_text: Corticobasal syndrome (often due to corticobasal degeneration)
Corticobasal syndrome (often due to cort.description: A progressive neurodegenerative syndrome, frequently caused by a tauopathy, that produces asymmetric parkinsonism, limb apraxia, cortical sensory deficits, dystonia, myoclonus, and sometimes supranuclear gaze impairment.

Adult-onset Niemann-Pick disease type C.description: A lysosomal lipid-trafficking disorder that can present in adulthood with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia, and neuropsychiatric or cognitive symptoms.

Whipple disease with central nervous sys.normalized_text: Whipple disease with central nervous system involvement
Whipple disease with central nervous sys.description: A rare infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that can involve the brainstem and cause supranuclear gaze palsy, oculomasticatory myorhythmia, cognitive changes, ataxia, and systemic gastrointestinal or joint symptoms.

Cryptococcal meningitis.description: Subacute fungal meningitis caused most often by Cryptococcus neoformans in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS. The images show encapsulated budding yeasts with prominent clear halos, characteristic of Cryptococcus on India ink preparation.

Tuberculous meningitis.description: A subacute or chronic meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, commonly producing lymphocytic CSF inflammation, elevated protein, reduced glucose, and raised intracranial pressure; risk is increased in advanced HIV.

Viral meningitis or meningoencephalitis.description: Inflammation of the meninges, sometimes with brain involvement, caused by viruses such as HSV, VZV, enteroviruses, or HIV itself. CSF usually shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose.

Neurosyphilis with syphilitic meningitis.description: Central nervous system infection with Treponema pallidum that can cause chronic or subacute meningitis, headache, cranial neuropathies, and lymphocytic CSF inflammation. Coinfection is common among people with HIV.

Acute bacterial meningitis.description: Rapid-onset infection of the meninges caused by bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae or Neisseria meningitidis. It generally produces fever, severe headache, meningismus, altered mental status, neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis, high protein, and low glucose.

Acute left medial longitudinal fasciculu.normalized_text: Acute left medial longitudinal fasciculus infarction causing internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Acute left medial longitudinal fasciculu.description: A small acute ischemic stroke affecting the left medial longitudinal fasciculus in the pons, disrupting coordination between the left medial rectus and right lateral rectus muscles. This produces left internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

Posterior circulation ischemic stroke.description: An acute ischemic stroke involving the vertebrobasilar circulation, affecting a small area of the dorsal pons or midbrain responsible for horizontal eye movement coordination.

Multiple sclerosis causing internuclear.description: Multiple sclerosis can cause demyelinating plaques in the medial longitudinal fasciculus, producing internuclear ophthalmoplegia with impaired adduction of one eye and abducting nystagmus of the other.

Left oculomotor nerve palsy.description: A third cranial nerve palsy causes impaired eye adduction and may produce diplopia, often with additional deficits in elevation, depression, eyelid elevation, or pupillary function depending on the cause.

Myasthenia gravis with ocular involvemen.description: Ocular myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that can cause fluctuating diplopia and variable ocular muscle weakness, sometimes mimicking cranial nerve palsies or internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

Congenital Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: Malaria acquired transplacentally or around delivery, causing febrile hemolytic illness in the first weeks of life. P. falciparum commonly produces multiple delicate ring forms within erythrocytes and can cause severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, hemoglobinuria, and shock.

Congenital babesiosis.description: Babesiosis is a protozoal infection of red blood cells that can rarely be transmitted congenitally. It causes hemolytic anemia, fever, thrombocytopenia, and intraerythrocytic ring forms; some species may form tetrads known as Maltese crosses.

Neonatal bacterial sepsis with dissemina.normalized_text: Neonatal bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation
Neonatal bacterial sepsis with dissemina.description: Serious bacterial infection in a young infant can cause fever, shock, respiratory distress, thrombocytopenia, anemia, organ injury, and abnormal urine findings. Disseminated intravascular coagulation may contribute to thrombocytopenia and bleeding or hematuria.

Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection.normalized_text: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection with hepatitis
Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection.description: Disseminated neonatal HSV can present during the first weeks of life with fever, irritability, respiratory compromise, hepatitis, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, and shock; skin vesicles may be absent.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase defici.normalized_text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency with acute hemolytic crisis
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase defici.description: G6PD deficiency is an inherited red-cell enzymatic disorder in which oxidative stress, including infection or medication exposure, can precipitate acute intravascular hemolysis with anemia, jaundice, elevated LDH, and dark urine.

Recurrent metastatic prostate adenocarci.normalized_text: Recurrent metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma with pelvic/rectal involvement
Recurrent metastatic prostate adenocarci.description: Late recurrence of high-grade prostate cancer after radical prostatectomy, with local pelvic recurrence and distant metastases such as lung and liver lesions.

Neuroendocrine/small-cell transformation.normalized_text: Neuroendocrine/small-cell transformation of recurrent prostate cancer
Neuroendocrine/small-cell transformation.description: An aggressive, poorly differentiated prostate cancer phenotype that may develop after prior prostate adenocarcinoma and can spread rapidly to visceral organs such as the liver and lungs.

Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with metas.normalized_text: Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with metastatic disease
Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with metas.description: Cancer arising from the rectum that commonly causes tenesmus and rectal pain and may metastasize to the liver and lungs.

Metastatic urothelial carcinoma of the b.normalized_text: Metastatic urothelial carcinoma of the bladder or prostatic urethra
Metastatic urothelial carcinoma of the b.description: An aggressive urinary tract malignancy that can invade pelvic structures and metastasize to lymph nodes, liver, lungs, and bone.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma with extranodal pel.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma with extranodal pelvic and visceral involvement
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma with extranodal pel.description: A lymphoid malignancy that can involve abdominal or pelvic tissues and may produce systemic symptoms with liver and lung involvement.

Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis due to Gra.normalized_text: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis due to Graves disease
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis due to Gra.description: An acute hypokalemic paralysis caused by intracellular potassium shift during thyrotoxicosis, most commonly from Graves disease. Graves disease is an autoimmune hyperthyroid disorder with diffuse thyroid enlargement and increased vascularity.

Familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis.description: A genetic skeletal-muscle ion-channel disorder causing recurrent episodes of weakness due to potassium shifting into cells, often triggered by carbohydrate intake, rest after exercise, stress, or medications.

Toxic multinodular goiter with thyrotoxi.normalized_text: Toxic multinodular goiter with thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
Toxic multinodular goiter with thyrotoxi.description: Autonomously functioning thyroid nodules can cause hyperthyroidism and, rarely, hypokalemic periodic paralysis. It is more common in older adults and usually has a nodular rather than diffuse thyroid pattern.

Thyroiditis-associated thyrotoxicosis wi.description: Inflammatory thyroid disorders can release preformed thyroid hormone and produce transient thyrotoxicosis. Hypokalemic periodic paralysis is much less common than with Graves disease.

Guillain-Barre syndrome.description: An acute immune-mediated peripheral neuropathy that typically causes progressive symmetric weakness, often beginning in the legs and potentially involving the arms and respiratory muscles.

Torus palatinus.description: A benign, slow-growing bony exostosis of the midline hard palate, often nodular or lobulated and usually asymptomatic.

Palatal exostosis.description: A benign localized overgrowth of mature bone on the palate; it may resemble a torus but can be less classically midline or more focal.

Osteoma of the palate.description: A benign tumor composed of mature bone that usually presents as a slow-growing, firm, painless mass; oral osteomas are uncommon.

Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary.normalized_text: Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary gland
Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary.description: A benign salivary-gland tumor that commonly occurs on the palate as a painless, slowly enlarging, firm submucosal mass.

Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the palate.description: A malignant salivary-gland tumor that may present as a painless palatal swelling, sometimes with a bluish or ulcerated surface and gradual enlargement.

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.icd11_title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

Lumbar disc herniation with left-sided r.normalized_text: Lumbar disc herniation with left-sided radiculopathy
Lumbar disc herniation with left-sided r.description: Protrusion or extrusion of lumbar disc material can compress a lumbar nerve root, causing acute radiating leg pain and motor weakness. The MRI appearance is compatible with degenerative lower-lumbar disc disease and possible canal/nerve-root compression.

Thrombosed lumbar epidural venous varix.description: An enlarged or thrombosed epidural vein can form a mass-like lesion in the spinal canal and compress a nerve root, often mimicking a lumbar disc prolapse on MRI. It may produce abrupt radicular pain and weakness.

Lumbar facet synovial cyst.description: A synovial cyst is a fluid-containing outpouching from a degenerated facet joint. In the lower lumbar spine, particularly at L4-L5, it can narrow the canal or neural foramen and compress nerve roots.

Spinal epidural hematoma.description: Bleeding into the epidural space can rapidly compress the cauda equina or lumbar nerve roots, causing acute back pain, radicular symptoms, and motor weakness. MRI signal varies with the age of blood products.

Lumbar epidural cavernous hemangioma.description: An epidural cavernous hemangioma is a vascular malformation that can appear as an extradural spinal canal mass and cause radiculopathy or neurological weakness through compression of lumbar nerve roots.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.normalized_text: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with eosinophilic cardiac involvement and cerebral embolic infarctions
Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.description: A disorder characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia causing organ damage, commonly involving the heart, nervous system, skin, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract. Cardiac endomyocardial injury and mural thrombi can cause systemic embolic strokes.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.normalized_text: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, Churg-Strauss syndrome)
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: A systemic small- and medium-vessel necrotizing vasculitis associated with eosinophilia, asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis, pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy, cardiac disease, and occasional central nervous system ischemia.

Eosinophilic myocarditis with Loeffler e.normalized_text: Eosinophilic myocarditis with Loeffler endocarditis and cardioembolic stroke
Eosinophilic myocarditis with Loeffler e.description: Eosinophil-mediated myocardial and endocardial inflammation can progress to mural thrombosis and fibrosis. Ventricular thrombi may embolize to the brain and produce multifocal ischemic strokes.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia or other c.normalized_text: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia or other clonal myeloid neoplasm with eosinophilia
Chronic eosinophilic leukemia or other c.description: A clonal bone-marrow disorder can cause sustained marked eosinophilia and eosinophil-mediated organ damage, including cardiac disease, thrombosis, pulmonary lesions, and neurologic ischemic events.

Parasitic helminth infection with second.normalized_text: Parasitic helminth infection with secondary hypereosinophilia and eosinophil-mediated organ injury
Parasitic helminth infection with second.description: Helminthic infections can produce prominent eosinophilia and may cause pulmonary infiltrates or nodules, systemic symptoms, and rarely cardiac or neurologic complications depending on the organism.

Sarcoidosis.description: A multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly affecting hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and lungs.

Metastatic breast cancer with mediastina.normalized_text: Metastatic breast cancer with mediastinal and hilar lymph-node metastases
Metastatic breast cancer with mediastina.description: Recurrent breast cancer may spread to mediastinal lymph nodes, lungs, bone, liver, or other organs and can be strongly FDG-avid on PET imaging.

Tuberculous lymphadenitis with pulmonary.description: Tuberculosis is an infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can cause granulomatous lymphadenitis and pulmonary nodules or infiltrates; granulomas are often necrotizing but may occasionally be non-necrotizing.

Lymphoma.description: Lymphoma is a malignancy of lymphocytes that may present with FDG-avid mediastinal lymphadenopathy, pulmonary involvement, cytopenias, and systemic symptoms.

Pulmonary fungal infection with granulom.normalized_text: Pulmonary fungal infection with granulomatous lymphadenitis, such as histoplasmosis
Pulmonary fungal infection with granulom.description: Endemic fungal infections can produce pulmonary nodules and mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy with granulomatous inflammation, sometimes mimicking sarcoidosis or malignancy on FDG-PET.

Multiple myeloma (IgG kappa plasma-cell.description: A malignant clonal proliferation of plasma cells in bone marrow that produces a monoclonal immunoglobulin and/or free light chains, causing anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, and bone disease.

Smoldering multiple myeloma.description: An asymptomatic plasma-cell disorder with a substantial monoclonal protein and/or marrow plasma-cell burden but without definite myeloma-related organ damage attributable to the plasma-cell clone.

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined si.description: A premalignant clonal plasma-cell condition characterized by a low-level monoclonal protein without significant marrow involvement, end-organ damage, or myeloma-defining events.

Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia / lymphopl.description: An indolent B-cell lymphoma with lymphoplasmacytic marrow infiltration and monoclonal immunoglobulin production, classically IgM, which can cause anemia, fatigue, hyperviscosity, neuropathy, and lymphadenopathy.

Metastatic bone malignancy with secondar.normalized_text: Metastatic bone malignancy with secondary anemia and hypercalcemia
Metastatic bone malignancy with secondar.description: Disseminated solid-organ cancer, such as breast, lung, renal, thyroid, or prostate cancer, can infiltrate bone marrow or involve bone, producing fatigue, anemia, elevated inflammatory markers, bone lesions, and hypercalcemia.

Intracranial germinoma (multifocal/bifoc.normalized_text: Intracranial germinoma (multifocal/bifocal pineal and suprasellar germinoma)
Intracranial germinoma (multifocal/bifoc.description: A malignant central nervous system germ-cell tumor that commonly affects adolescent and young adult males and often involves the pineal and suprasellar regions. It can cause diabetes insipidus, pituitary hormone deficiency, visual disturbance, and multifocal brain lesions.

Craniopharyngioma.description: A benign but locally aggressive tumor arising near the pituitary stalk and suprasellar region. It can impair pituitary function, cause diabetes insipidus, visual deficits, and headaches, although it is less likely to explain multiple intracranial lesions.

Pituitary macroadenoma with hypopituitar.description: A large pituitary adenoma can compress the optic pathways and normal pituitary tissue, causing headache, visual deficits, hypogonadism, and occasionally gynecomastia. Diabetes insipidus is uncommon in a typical pituitary adenoma.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypot.normalized_text: Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypothalamic-pituitary involvement
Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypot.description: A histiocytic inflammatory disorder that can infiltrate the pituitary stalk and hypothalamus, commonly causing central diabetes insipidus and anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies. Central nervous system involvement can occasionally produce additional brain lesions.

Neurosarcoidosis involving the hypothala.description: Sarcoidosis can cause granulomatous inflammation of the pituitary stalk, hypothalamus, optic pathways, and meninges. This may result in diabetes insipidus, hypopituitarism, visual symptoms, headaches, and occasionally seizures.

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aur.normalized_text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus native aortic valve infective endocarditis
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aur.description: A severe bacterial infection of the native aortic valve caused by MRSA, producing valvular vegetations, systemic inflammation, and embolic complications.

Aortic root abscess complicating infecti.normalized_text: Aortic root abscess complicating infective endocarditis
Aortic root abscess complicating infecti.description: A periannular extension of infective endocarditis in which infection destroys tissue around the aortic valve root; it can cause conduction abnormalities, worsening aortic regurgitation, and persistent bacteremia.

Septic embolic ischemic stroke due to in.normalized_text: Septic embolic ischemic stroke due to infective endocarditis
Septic embolic ischemic stroke due to in.description: An ischemic stroke caused by embolization of infected material from a cardiac valve vegetation into the cerebral circulation.

Acute severe aortic regurgitation second.normalized_text: Acute severe aortic regurgitation secondary to infective endocarditis
Acute severe aortic regurgitation second.description: Valve leaflet destruction or perforation from infection can produce acute aortic regurgitation, classically causing an early diastolic decrescendo murmur and potentially progressing to heart failure.

Recurrent or persistent disseminated MRS.normalized_text: Recurrent or persistent disseminated MRSA infection with metastatic foci
Recurrent or persistent disseminated MRS.description: Hematogenous MRSA infection can seed multiple sites, causing endocarditis, vertebral discitis, psoas abscess, septic emboli, and central nervous system complications.

Infantile-onset Pompe disease (acid alph.normalized_text: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, GAA deficiency)
Infantile-onset Pompe disease (acid alph.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal glycogen-storage disorder caused by deficient acid alpha-glucosidase activity, resulting in glycogen accumulation in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Classic infantile-onset disease commonly causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, elevated muscle enzymes, hypotonia, and later respiratory failure.

Danon disease.description: An X-linked lysosomal/autophagy disorder caused by LAMP2 deficiency. It can produce severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and elevated CK, often accompanied by skeletal myopathy and intellectual or developmental impairment; it is much more typical in males.

PRKAG2-related glycogen-storage cardiomy.description: A dominantly inherited cardiac glycogen-storage disorder caused by PRKAG2 variants. It typically causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with ventricular pre-excitation and conduction-system disease, usually presenting later in childhood or adulthood.

Very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (.description: A fatty-acid oxidation disorder caused by ACADVL deficiency. Severe neonatal VLCAD deficiency may present with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, hepatopathy, hypoglycemia, and elevated CK.

Neonatal myocarditis.description: Inflammation of the myocardium, often viral, that can cause cardiomegaly, ventricular dysfunction, heart-failure biomarkers, arrhythmias, poor feeding, respiratory distress, and elevated CK or liver enzymes.

Precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leu.description: A childhood hematologic malignancy caused by proliferation of immature B-lymphoblasts in bone marrow and sometimes extramedullary tissues. The marrow morphology and CD19/CD10-positive blast immunophenotype in the provided images strongly support this diagnosis.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML).description: A malignancy of immature myeloid blood cells that can cause marrow failure, bone pain, fever, bruising, and extramedullary leukemic infiltrates. It is an important leukemia differential, although the illustrated B-cell marker pattern favors B-ALL instead.

Neuroblastoma.description: A pediatric embryonal tumor of sympathetic nervous system tissue, commonly arising in the adrenal gland or abdomen. It can metastasize to bone and bone marrow, causing bone pain, limping, fever, abdominal enlargement, and periorbital ecchymoses.

Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia.description: A highly aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that may involve the abdomen, bone marrow, and occasionally the orbit. Marrow involvement can produce leukemia-like symptoms, fever, bruising, and bone pain.

Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (.description: A childhood inflammatory rheumatic disease characterized by recurrent high fever and arthritis, often with systemic inflammation. It can cause limping, hip pain, and migratory musculoskeletal symptoms, but it does not explain leukemic marrow findings.

Necrotizing fasciitis.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection of fascia and subcutaneous tissue, often causing severe pain, swelling, skin discoloration, and sometimes soft-tissue gas. The ultrasound appearance of subcutaneous edema with possible gas/fascial involvement raises concern for this diagnosis.

Bacterial cellulitis.description: Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissues, usually caused by streptococci or staphylococci. Ultrasound may show diffuse subcutaneous edema with a cobblestoning appearance.

Gluteal soft-tissue abscess.description: A soft-tissue abscess is a localized collection of pus, often occurring as a complication of cellulitis. It typically produces focal tenderness, swelling, erythema, and may require drainage.

Gluteal hematoma.description: A hematoma is a collection of blood in soft tissue, usually caused by trauma, anticoagulation, injection, or a bleeding disorder. It can cause painful swelling and bruiselike discoloration.

Pyomyositis of the gluteal muscles.description: Pyomyositis is a bacterial infection of skeletal muscle that can progress from muscle inflammation to intramuscular abscess formation. It commonly causes focal muscle pain, swelling, and fever, although fever may be absent early.

Chronic graft-versus-host disease (scler.normalized_text: Chronic graft-versus-host disease (sclerodermatous cutaneous chronic GVHD)
Chronic graft-versus-host disease (scler.description: A late complication of allogeneic stem-cell transplantation in which donor immune cells attack recipient tissues. Cutaneous chronic GVHD may cause lichenoid or sclerotic skin changes, reduced joint mobility, and autoimmune-like laboratory findings.

Dermatomyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and distinctive photosensitive cutaneous eruptions, including facial erythema, Gottron papules, and shawl-sign rash.

Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), includ.normalized_text: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), including scleroderma-like chronic GVHD
Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), includ.description: An autoimmune connective-tissue disease causing progressive skin thickening and fibrosis, joint contractures, and possible internal-organ involvement. A very similar scleroderma-like syndrome may occur with chronic GVHD after transplantation.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lu.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lupus-like autoimmune syndrome
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lu.description: A systemic autoimmune disorder that can cause photosensitive skin eruptions, constitutional symptoms, musculoskeletal complaints, cytopenias, renal disease, and positive antinuclear antibodies.

Drug-induced photosensitive eruption or.normalized_text: Drug-induced photosensitive eruption or subacute cutaneous lupus-like reaction
Drug-induced photosensitive eruption or.description: A medication-associated immune or phototoxic skin reaction that develops on sun-exposed areas and may occasionally be associated with positive ANA and systemic symptoms. Acyclovir is an uncommon cause, but medication-related photosensitivity remains a consideration.

Multiple eruptive keratoacanthomas (gene.normalized_text: Multiple eruptive keratoacanthomas (generalized eruptive keratoacanthoma of Grzybowski type)
Multiple eruptive keratoacanthomas (gene.description: A rare disorder characterized by the repeated eruption of numerous keratoacanthomas, which are rapidly growing crateriform keratinizing tumors considered to lie on the squamous-cell-carcinoma spectrum. Lesions may be intensely pruritic and occur on sun-exposed skin.

Acquired perforating dermatosis (Kyrle d.normalized_text: Acquired perforating dermatosis (Kyrle disease or acquired reactive perforating collagenosis)
Acquired perforating dermatosis (Kyrle d.description: An intensely pruritic perforating skin disorder strongly associated with diabetes and chronic kidney disease/dialysis. It causes umbilicated hyperkeratotic papules and excoriations, usually on the extremities.

Multiple cutaneous squamous cell carcino.normalized_text: Multiple cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas, keratoacanthoma type
Multiple cutaneous squamous cell carcino.description: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is a keratinocyte malignancy that may present as hyperkeratotic papules, nodules, ulcers, or crateriform keratoacanthoma-like lesions. Risk is increased by prior immunosuppression, transplantation, ultraviolet exposure, and chronic skin injury.

Prurigo nodularis.description: A chronic itch-scratch disorder causing multiple intensely pruritic, firm, excoriated papules or nodules, commonly on accessible areas of the arms and legs. Chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus can contribute to this condition.

Verruca vulgaris (multiple common warts).description: Common warts are benign human-papillomavirus-associated epidermal proliferations that appear as rough hyperkeratotic papules. They may be numerous in people with impaired immune function.

Acute transverse myelitis.description: An inflammatory disorder of the spinal cord causing acute or subacute motor weakness, sensory-level deficits, pain, and autonomic dysfunction. MRI commonly shows intramedullary T2 hyperintensity.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune astrocytopathy, often associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies, that can cause severe longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis and optic neuritis. Spinal attacks may produce weakness, sensory loss, pain, and bladder dysfunction.

Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein anti.normalized_text: Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) with myelitis
Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein anti.description: An immune-mediated demyelinating disease that can cause acute transverse myelitis, often in children and adolescents, with motor, sensory, and autonomic spinal cord dysfunction.

Spinal cord infarction.description: Ischemic injury to the spinal cord, usually with sudden severe back or limb pain followed by weakness, loss of pain and temperature sensation, and bladder dysfunction. Cerebrospinal fluid is often normal early in the illness.

Multiple sclerosis presenting with parti.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis presenting with partial transverse myelitis
Multiple sclerosis presenting with parti.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can initially present with a spinal cord lesion causing asymmetric weakness, sensory symptoms, and bladder dysfunction.

T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: An aggressive neoplasm of immature T-cell precursors that commonly presents with circulating blasts, marrow involvement, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and high LDH. The immunophenotype is typically positive for T-cell markers such as cytoplasmic/surface CD3, CD2, CD5, and CD7.

Early T-cell precursor acute lymphoblast.normalized_text: Early T-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ETP-ALL)
Early T-cell precursor acute lymphoblast.description: A high-risk subtype of T-ALL arising from very early thymic progenitors. It often has an immature phenotype with weak or absent CD5, expression of stem-cell or myeloid markers, and frequent CD34 and TdT positivity.

T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL).description: A mature post-thymic T-cell leukemia characterized by marked lymphocytosis and expression of mature T-cell markers, usually CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7. It is often associated with chromosome 14 rearrangements involving T-cell receptor loci.

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL).description: A mature peripheral T-cell neoplasm caused by human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1). Leukemic ATLL typically expresses CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, and CD25, often with hypercalcemia, lymphadenopathy, skin disease, and characteristic multilobated 'flower' cells.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), including.normalized_text: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), including minimally differentiated AML
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), including.description: An acute leukemia caused by clonal proliferation of myeloid blasts in bone marrow and blood. AML commonly presents with leukocytosis or leukopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, high LDH, and symptoms related to leukostasis.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T cells, producing fever, cytopenias, hypofibrinogenemia, extreme hyperferritinemia, and hemophagocytosis in bone marrow or other tissues.

Disseminated tuberculosis with tuberculo.description: Widespread Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can involve the lungs, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and bone marrow. In severe cases it triggers secondary HLH, with hemophagocytosis, pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, and multiorgan failure.

Severe viral infection with secondary HL.normalized_text: Severe viral infection with secondary HLH, such as Epstein-Barr virus-associated HLH
Severe viral infection with secondary HL.description: EBV and other viruses can provoke secondary HLH, particularly with persistent fever, cytopenias, hemophagocytosis, coagulopathy, and markedly elevated ferritin.

Disseminated histoplasmosis with seconda.description: Disseminated Histoplasma infection can involve the reticuloendothelial system and bone marrow, causing prolonged fever, cytopenias, pulmonary infiltrates, very high ferritin, and secondary HLH.

Hematologic malignancy-associated HLH, e.normalized_text: Hematologic malignancy-associated HLH, especially lymphoma-associated HLH
Hematologic malignancy-associated HLH, e.description: Lymphoma, leukemia, and other hematologic malignancies can trigger HLH through immune dysregulation and marrow involvement, resulting in fever, cytopenias, coagulopathy, hyperferritinemia, and organ failure.

West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease wi.normalized_text: West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease with cerebral vasculitis
West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease wi.description: Mosquito-borne flaviviral encephalitis that can cause fever, rash, coma, acute flaccid or asymmetric weakness, and occasionally cerebral vasculitis with ischemic brain lesions.

Japanese encephalitis.description: A mosquito-borne flavivirus infection causing severe encephalitis, often with altered consciousness, movement abnormalities, focal neurologic deficits, and inflammatory CSF findings.

Varicella-zoster virus meningoencephalit.normalized_text: Varicella-zoster virus meningoencephalitis with cerebral vasculopathy
Varicella-zoster virus meningoencephalit.description: Reactivation or primary infection with varicella-zoster virus can cause encephalitis and granulomatous vasculopathy, resulting in multifocal cerebral infarctions and focal neurologic deficits.

Dengue encephalitis or dengue-associated.normalized_text: Dengue encephalitis or dengue-associated cerebral vasculopathy
Dengue encephalitis or dengue-associated.description: Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral infection that may rarely cause encephalitis, encephalopathy, rash, and cerebrovascular complications including ischemic or hemorrhagic lesions.

Rickettsial meningoencephalitis with cer.description: Tick-, mite-, or flea-borne rickettsial infections can cause fever, rash, meningoencephalitis, small-vessel vasculitis, cerebral infarction, and severe neurologic dysfunction.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis characterized by palpable purpura, arthritis or arthralgia, gastrointestinal involvement, and possible kidney disease. Skin biopsy typically shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA and C3 deposition.

Adalimumab-associated IgA vasculitis.description: A drug-associated immune-complex vasculitis in which anti-TNF therapy, including adalimumab, can rarely trigger IgA-mediated leukocytoclastic vasculitis. It may present with palpable purpura and joint symptoms.

Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis.description: An inflammatory small-vessel vasculitis of the skin that produces palpable purpura, usually on dependent areas of the legs. It may be triggered by infections, medications, autoimmune disease, or inflammatory bowel disease.

Crohn's disease-associated extraintestin.description: Inflammatory bowel disease can be associated with immune-mediated skin and joint manifestations, including leukocytoclastic vasculitis, peripheral arthritis, erythema nodosum, and pyoderma gangrenosum.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: A systemic necrotizing small- and medium-vessel vasculitis that commonly affects the upper airways, lungs, kidneys, skin, and joints. It can cause purpura and arthralgia or arthritis, but usually has more destructive sinonasal, pulmonary, or renal features.

HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous ce.normalized_text: HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil with cervical lymph-node metastasis
HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous ce.description: A malignant tumor arising in the palatine tonsil or adjacent oropharynx, commonly associated with high-risk human papillomavirus in nonsmokers and often presenting with metastatic upper-neck lymphadenopathy.

Non-HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamou.description: Squamous cell cancer of the tonsil, base of tongue, or other oropharyngeal mucosa, traditionally associated with tobacco and heavy alcohol exposure and capable of spreading to cervical lymph nodes.

Tonsillar lymphoma.description: A lymphoma involving Waldeyer's ring, including the palatine tonsil, which may cause tonsillar enlargement and cervical lymphadenopathy.

Metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma.description: A carcinoma arising in the nasopharynx that can present with painless cervical lymph-node metastases and may cause referred ear symptoms through Eustachian-tube dysfunction or local nerve irritation.

Deep neck infection or suppurative cervi.normalized_text: Deep neck infection or suppurative cervical lymphadenitis
Deep neck infection or suppurative cervi.description: Bacterial infection of the pharynx or deep neck spaces that can produce painful sore throat, enlarged cervical lymph nodes, and occasionally a neck abscess.

Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell.normalized_text: Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma) of the urinary bladder
Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell.description: An indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, rarely involving the bladder. It is often associated with chronic cystitis and may show an API2-MALT1 rearrangement such as t(11;18).

Chronic follicular cystitis.description: A benign chronic inflammatory bladder condition characterized by lymphoid follicle formation, usually caused by recurrent bacterial urinary tract infections or chronic bladder irritation.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the uri.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the urinary bladder
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the uri.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that can rarely arise primarily in the bladder or occur through secondary involvement. It generally consists of large atypical lymphoid cells and may cause a bladder mass.

Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder with.normalized_text: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder with prominent inflammatory infiltrate
Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder with.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the bladder that can present as a mucosal lesion and may be accompanied by chronic inflammation. It is more commonly associated with hematuria than recurrent infection alone.

Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma involving the.normalized_text: Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma involving the urinary bladder
Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma involving the.description: A usually bone-marrow-based indolent B-cell lymphoma composed of small lymphocytes, plasmacytoid lymphocytes, and plasma cells; extranodal bladder involvement is uncommon and usually occurs with systemic disease.

Emphysematous cystitis.description: A complicated urinary tract infection caused by gas-forming organisms, producing gas within the bladder wall and/or lumen. It occurs most often in older patients with diabetes and can be caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae.

Complicated acute bacterial cystitis due.normalized_text: Complicated acute bacterial cystitis due to Klebsiella pneumoniae
Complicated acute bacterial cystitis due.description: Infection of the urinary bladder caused by bacteria; diabetes, advanced age, and impaired functional status increase the likelihood of complicated infection.

Emphysematous pyelonephritis.description: A severe gas-forming infection of the renal parenchyma and surrounding tissues, usually occurring in patients with diabetes and often caused by gram-negative organisms such as Klebsiella.

Acute pyelonephritis.description: An upper urinary tract infection involving the kidney, commonly caused by gram-negative urinary pathogens and associated with systemic inflammatory-marker elevation.

Colovesical fistula.description: An abnormal communication between the colon and urinary bladder that can introduce gas and enteric bacteria into the bladder, leading to recurrent urinary infections and intravesical gas.

Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral.normalized_text: Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral condyle with a detached osteochondral loose body
Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral.description: A focal area of subchondral bone and cartilage injury, usually involving a femoral condyle, that may become unstable and detach into the joint as an osteochondral fragment. Detached fragments can cause intermittent locking and effusions.

Osteochondral fracture with retained int.normalized_text: Osteochondral fracture with retained intra-articular loose body
Osteochondral fracture with retained int.description: A cartilage-and-bone fragment may separate after prior knee trauma, often following patellar dislocation, twisting injury, or direct impact. A chronic retained fragment can produce recurrent pain, swelling, and locking.

Synovial chondromatosis.description: A benign proliferative synovial disorder in which cartilage nodules form within the joint and may detach, calcify, or ossify into loose bodies. It commonly causes recurrent effusion, pain, restricted motion, and locking.

Meniscal tear, especially a bucket-handl.normalized_text: Meniscal tear, especially a bucket-handle tear
Meniscal tear, especially a bucket-handl.description: A displaced meniscal tear can mechanically block knee motion and cause true locking, joint-line pain, and recurrent effusion. Chronic tears may arise after remote athletic twisting injuries.

Para-articular osteochondroma or solitar.normalized_text: Para-articular osteochondroma or solitary intra-articular osteocartilaginous loose body
Para-articular osteochondroma or solitar.description: A benign ossified/cartilaginous mass adjacent to or within the knee joint can impinge on joint movement and produce recurrent swelling and mechanical symptoms. It may be primary or represent an old detached osteochondral fragment.

diagnoses.name: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma

Primary pancreatic lymphoma (diffuse lar.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic lymphoma (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma)
Primary pancreatic lymphoma (diffuse lar.description: A rare extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising predominantly in the pancreas, often presenting as a pancreatic head mass with biliary obstruction. Histology commonly shows diffuse sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells with B-cell immunophenotypic markers.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: The most common pancreatic malignancy, usually originating from ductal epithelium in the pancreatic head and causing obstruction of the common bile duct.

Primary pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.description: A tumor arising from pancreatic neuroendocrine cells that may be functioning or nonfunctioning. Larger nonfunctioning tumors can compress the bile duct and produce obstructive jaundice.

Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.normalized_text: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.description: A rare, usually low-grade pancreatic tumor with solid and pseudopapillary microscopic areas. It occurs predominantly in young women but can rarely occur in middle-aged men.

Autoimmune pancreatitis (IgG4-related di.description: An inflammatory fibroimmune pancreatic disorder that can form a mass-like pancreatic lesion and mimic pancreatic cancer, often causing obstructive jaundice.

Secondary tumoral calcinosis (uremic tum.description: Massive periarticular or subcutaneous calcium-phosphate deposition occurring in patients with chronic renal failure, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Calcinosis cutis due to metastatic calci.normalized_text: Calcinosis cutis due to metastatic calcification
Calcinosis cutis due to metastatic calci.description: Deposition of insoluble calcium salts in otherwise normal skin and subcutaneous tissues due to systemic calcium-phosphate imbalance, often from renal failure.

Calciphylaxis (calcific uremic arteriolo.description: A severe dialysis-associated disorder involving calcification and thrombosis of small dermal and subcutaneous vessels, usually causing painful ischemic skin lesions and necrosis.

Tophaceous gout with calcification.description: Chronic deposition of monosodium urate crystals forming firm nodules (tophi), which can occasionally calcify and is more common in patients with renal dysfunction.

Myositis ossificans / heterotopic ossifi.description: Abnormal bone formation in soft tissues, usually after trauma, surgery, neurologic injury, or prolonged immobilization; it may present as a firm calcified mass.

Lateral tibial plateau fracture (split-d.description: An intra-articular fracture of the lateral upper tibia, often caused by valgus force or axial loading, with fracture splitting and depression of the joint surface.

Bicondylar tibial plateau fracture.description: A more extensive intra-articular fracture involving both medial and lateral tibial plateaus, usually due to high-energy trauma and associated with substantial swelling and instability.

Tibial spine (intercondylar eminence) fr.description: An avulsion fracture of the tibial intercondylar eminence, often related to anterior cruciate ligament traction during twisting or high-energy knee trauma.

Anterior cruciate ligament rupture with.normalized_text: Anterior cruciate ligament rupture with hemarthrosis
Anterior cruciate ligament rupture with.description: Tearing of the anterior cruciate ligament, commonly caused by pivoting, hyperextension, or high-energy trauma, producing rapid swelling from bleeding into the joint and instability.

Patellar dislocation with osteochondral.description: Displacement of the patella, usually laterally, which can cause acute pain, swelling, inability to bear weight, and occasionally an associated osteochondral fracture.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Rectal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (G.description: A mesenchymal tumor arising from the gastrointestinal tract wall, usually composed of spindle cells and often presenting as a submucosal rectal mass. Larger tumors can infiltrate the muscular wall and produce obstructive symptoms.

Rectal leiomyosarcoma.description: A rare malignant smooth-muscle tumor of the rectum that can form a deep intramural or submucosal mass. It may cause pain, bowel obstruction, and local invasion.

Rectal leiomyoma.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor arising from the muscularis mucosae or muscularis propria of the rectum. Large lesions may produce obstructive symptoms despite benign histology.

Rectal schwannoma.description: A rare nerve-sheath tumor that may arise in the rectal wall and appear as a slowly growing, well-defined submucosal mass. Most gastrointestinal schwannomas are benign.

Rectal adenocarcinoma with submucosal or.normalized_text: Rectal adenocarcinoma with submucosal or intramural growth
Rectal adenocarcinoma with submucosal or.description: The most common malignant rectal tumor, usually originating from mucosal glandular epithelium. It commonly causes altered bowel habits, tenesmus, obstruction, and local invasion, although it typically appears as a mucosal lesion rather than a smooth submucosal mass.

SHORT syndrome.description: A rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic PIK3R1 variants, characterized by intrauterine growth restriction, postnatal short stature, partial lipodystrophy, characteristic facial appearance, delayed dentition, and often insulin resistance later in life.

Berardinelli-Seip congenital lipodystrop.description: A genetic disorder with near-complete lack of subcutaneous fat from birth, resulting in a muscular appearance, prominent veins, metabolic complications, and often enlarged liver or heart.

Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome.description: A premature-aging disorder, usually caused by a de novo LMNA variant, characterized by postnatal growth failure, loss of subcutaneous fat, thin skin, prominent veins, and an aged facial appearance.

Russell-Silver syndrome.description: A growth-restriction syndrome most often related to abnormal methylation at 11p15 or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7, featuring prenatal and postnatal growth failure, relative macrocephaly, triangular face, and feeding difficulties.

Donohue syndrome (leprechaunism).description: A severe autosomal recessive insulin-receptor disorder caused by biallelic INSR variants, characterized by profound fetal and postnatal growth restriction, loss of fat, distinctive facial features, and severe insulin-resistance-related metabolic disease.

Good syndrome (thymoma-associated immuno.description: A rare acquired immunodeficiency associated with thymoma, characterized by hypogammaglobulinemia, marked B-cell depletion, impaired T-cell function, and recurrent bacterial and opportunistic infections.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP).description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia occurring primarily in patients with impaired cellular immunity, especially reduced CD4 T-cell function.

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID).description: A primary antibody deficiency characterized by impaired antibody production, recurrent respiratory infections, and sometimes gastrointestinal disease and chronic lung damage.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: A chronic mycobacterial pulmonary infection that can cause constitutional symptoms and cavitary lung disease, particularly in patients with impaired cellular immunity.

Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infec.normalized_text: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection with advanced immunosuppression
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infec.description: HIV causes progressive CD4 T-cell depletion and predisposes to opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia, chronic diarrhea, constitutional symptoms, and recurrent infections.

Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease (histiocytic ne.description: A benign, self-limited inflammatory lymph-node disorder characterized by patchy necrosis with abundant histiocytes and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, most commonly affecting cervical lymph nodes in young adults.

Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A malignant lymphoid neoplasm that commonly presents with persistent painless cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy; diagnosis requires identification of Reed-Sternberg cells in an appropriate inflammatory background.

Tuberculous lymphadenitis.description: Mycobacterial infection of lymph nodes, usually causing chronic cervical lymph-node enlargement with granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis; mediastinal nodal disease may coexist.

Systemic lupus erythematosus-associated.description: Autoimmune lymph-node inflammation that can resemble Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease histologically, sometimes with necrosis, hematoxylin bodies, and vascular immune-complex changes.

Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytos.normalized_text: Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy)
Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytos.description: A nonmalignant histiocytic disorder that typically produces painless cervical lymphadenopathy and may involve mediastinal or other extranodal sites; lymph-node histology classically shows S100-positive histiocytes with emperipolesis.

Fulminant viral myocarditis.description: Acute inflammatory injury of the heart muscle, often following a viral respiratory illness, which can rapidly cause severe ventricular dysfunction, malignant ventricular arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, and cardiac arrest.

Peripartum cardiomyopathy.description: Pregnancy-associated systolic heart failure occurring late in pregnancy or in the months after delivery, characterized by reduced left-ventricular function, fluid overload, arrhythmias, and possible cardiogenic shock.

Massive pulmonary embolism.description: Acute obstruction of the pulmonary arterial circulation by thrombus, commonly arising from deep venous thrombosis; pregnancy, obesity, and immobility are important risk factors.

Acute coronary syndrome due to spontaneo.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome due to spontaneous coronary artery dissection
Acute coronary syndrome due to spontaneo.description: A nontraumatic tear or intramural hematoma in a coronary artery that can cause myocardial infarction; it occurs disproportionately in pregnant and postpartum women and may provoke ventricular arrhythmias.

Acute myopericarditis.description: Inflammation involving both the myocardium and pericardium, usually viral, which may cause chest pain, electrocardiographic changes, impaired ventricular function, arrhythmia, and occasionally fulminant shock.

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (H.description: An autosomal-dominant vascular disorder characterized by recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias, and arteriovenous malformations in organs such as the liver, lungs, brain, and gastrointestinal tract. The imaging is compatible with hepatic vascular malformations/shunting.

Hepatic arteriovenous malformations due.normalized_text: Hepatic arteriovenous malformations due to HHT
Hepatic arteriovenous malformations due.description: Abnormal direct connections between hepatic arteries, portal veins, and hepatic veins that can cause high-output heart failure, portal hypertension, biliary ischemia, or portosystemic shunting. Doppler findings of turbulent high-flow vascular channels support this diagnosis.

Hepatic encephalopathy from portosystemi.description: A neuropsychiatric syndrome caused by impaired clearance of neurotoxins, commonly ammonia, when portal venous blood bypasses the liver through cirrhosis-related or congenital/acquired portosystemic shunts. Hepatic vascular malformations can produce clinically significant shunting even without classic cirrhosis.

Delirium due to dehydration and acute in.normalized_text: Delirium due to dehydration and acute infectious gastroenteritis
Delirium due to dehydration and acute in.description: Acute delirium in an older adult can be precipitated by volume depletion, poor oral intake, electrolyte abnormalities, or infection. Diarrhea, chills, lethargy, and dry mucous membranes suggest an acute systemic illness with dehydration.

High-output heart failure secondary to h.normalized_text: High-output heart failure secondary to hepatic arteriovenous shunting
High-output heart failure secondary to h.description: Large hepatic arteriovenous shunts can substantially increase cardiac output and eventually cause heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, atrial arrhythmias, hepatic congestion, and fatigue. This complication is particularly associated with hepatic involvement in HHT.

Macular juvenile xanthogranuloma.description: A benign non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis of infancy that can rarely present as flat orange-brown macules rather than the more typical yellow-red papules or nodules.

Maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (ur.description: A mast-cell proliferation in the skin, usually presenting during infancy or childhood with multiple tan, brown, or red-brown macules and papules that may urticate after rubbing.

Café-au-lait macules.description: Benign, flat, uniformly light-brown pigmented patches that may be isolated or, when numerous, associated with genetic disorders such as neurofibromatosis type 1.

Benign cephalic histiocytosis.description: A self-limited non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis of infancy characterized by asymptomatic red-yellow to red-brown papules, usually beginning on the head and spreading to the upper body.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis, cutaneous.description: A clonal proliferation of Langerhans cells that can affect infants and may produce papules, crusted lesions, seborrheic-like eruptions, or purpuric lesions; systemic involvement must be assessed.

Superior mesenteric artery syndrome (Wil.description: Compression of the third portion of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta, usually after substantial loss of retroperitoneal fat from weight loss. The imaging demonstrates a markedly narrowed aortomesenteric angle and distance with gastric/duodenal dilatation.

Anorexia nervosa or severe malnutrition-.normalized_text: Anorexia nervosa or severe malnutrition-related eating disorder
Anorexia nervosa or severe malnutrition-.description: An eating disorder characterized by inadequate caloric intake and very low body weight, often causing amenorrhea, constipation, fatigue, delayed gastric emptying, and risk of secondary superior mesenteric artery syndrome.

Gastroparesis.description: Delayed gastric emptying due to impaired stomach motility, producing nausea, vomiting after meals, early satiety, poor nutritional intake, and weight loss.

Peptic ulcer disease with gastric outlet.normalized_text: Peptic ulcer disease with gastric outlet obstruction
Peptic ulcer disease with gastric outlet.description: Inflammation or ulcer-related scarring at the pylorus or proximal duodenum can obstruct gastric emptying, causing postprandial vomiting, dehydration, and weight loss.

Mechanical small-bowel obstruction (ileu.description: A partial or complete blockage of intestinal transit can cause vomiting, constipation, abdominal distension, and inability to tolerate oral intake. In this case, duodenal obstruction from superior mesenteric artery compression is a more specific mechanical cause.

Gastrocolic fistula involving the gastri.normalized_text: Gastrocolic fistula involving the gastric pouch and transverse colon
Gastrocolic fistula involving the gastri.description: An abnormal connection between the stomach/gastric pouch and colon, allowing recently ingested food to pass directly into the colon. This can occur as a rare late complication after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and causes severe diarrhea, malnutrition, and feculent belching. The contrast study demonstrates communication between the gastric pouch and transverse/descending colon.

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (S.description: Excessive growth of bacteria in the small intestine, often related to altered anatomy after gastrointestinal surgery. It can cause malabsorption, bloating, foul gas, diarrhea, and nutritional deficiencies.

Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.description: Insufficient secretion of pancreatic digestive enzymes, resulting in fat malabsorption and steatorrhea. It may cause pale, greasy, floating, foul-smelling stools, weight loss, and nutritional deficiency.

Dumping syndrome after Roux-en-Y gastric.normalized_text: Dumping syndrome after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
Dumping syndrome after Roux-en-Y gastric.description: Rapid delivery of hyperosmolar gastric contents into the small bowel after gastric surgery, causing postprandial cramping, diarrhea, bloating, and sometimes vasomotor symptoms. Chronic symptoms can contribute to weight loss.

Clostridioides difficile infection or ot.normalized_text: Clostridioides difficile infection or other infectious enterocolitis
Clostridioides difficile infection or ot.description: An infection of the colon that commonly causes frequent watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, dehydration, and systemic illness. C. difficile is especially associated with recent antibiotic exposure or healthcare contact.

Spontaneous pneumomediastinum.description: Air in the mediastinum, often caused by alveolar rupture during coughing or an asthma exacerbation; it can produce chest pain radiating to the neck and may be visible as mediastinal air on chest radiography.
