Acute asthma exacerbation.description: Acute worsening of reversible lower-airway obstruction causing wheeze, cough, chest tightness, and breathlessness, often precipitated by poor adherence to inhaled treatment or respiratory infection.

Acute bronchitis or viral lower respirat.normalized_text: Acute bronchitis or viral lower respiratory tract infection
Acute bronchitis or viral lower respirat.description: Inflammation of the bronchi, usually viral, causing cough, sputum production, wheeze, and chest discomfort; it can trigger an asthma exacerbation.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries by thrombus, commonly presenting with acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and sometimes cough or hemoptysis.

Community-acquired pneumonia.description: Infection of the lung parenchyma that may cause cough, sputum production, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, fever, and raised inflammatory markers.

Pellagra (niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency).description: A nutritional deficiency disorder causing photosensitive dermatitis, gastrointestinal symptoms, and neurologic manifestations including cognitive changes and peripheral neuropathy. The images are suggestive of photosensitive dermatitis with a Casal necklace pattern on the neck.

Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency neuro.description: Pyridoxine deficiency can occur with poor nutrition, substance use, or certain medications and may cause a painful length-dependent sensory polyneuropathy; dermatitis may also occur.

Dry beriberi (thiamine/vitamin B1 defici.description: Thiamine deficiency can produce painful symmetric peripheral neuropathy, sensory loss, weakness, and gait difficulty, particularly in people with malnutrition or substance-use disorders.

Hepatitis C-associated mixed cryoglobuli.description: Chronic hepatitis C can cause immune-complex cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, which may produce painful peripheral neuropathy, purpura, arthralgias, renal disease, and skin lesions.

HIV-associated distal symmetric polyneur.description: HIV infection, especially in advanced disease or with certain antiretroviral therapies, can cause a painful distal symmetric sensory polyneuropathy. Intravenous drug use increases HIV exposure risk.

X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton agam.normalized_text: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton agammaglobulinemia) due to BTK mutation
X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton agam.description: A primary immunodeficiency caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked BTK gene, resulting in arrested B-cell maturation, profoundly reduced or absent mature B cells, and very low levels of all immunoglobulin classes. The displayed BTK c.494G>A (p.Cys165Tyr) variant and absent/reduced BTK expression strongly support this diagnosis.

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID).description: A heterogeneous antibody-deficiency disorder characterized by low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM, impaired antibody responses, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. It usually presents later in childhood or adulthood and typically has circulating B cells.

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).description: A group of severe inherited immunodeficiencies with major T-cell dysfunction, often accompanied by B-cell and/or NK-cell abnormalities, causing severe recurrent bacterial, viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections in infancy.

Hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40 ligand deficien.normalized_text: Hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40 ligand deficiency or related disorder)
Hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40 ligand deficien.description: A primary immunodeficiency in which defective immunoglobulin class-switch recombination causes low IgG and IgA with normal or elevated IgM. Patients may have recurrent respiratory and opportunistic infections.

Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infan.description: A temporary prolongation of the physiologic decline in maternally acquired IgG, causing low IgG and sometimes recurrent respiratory infections in infancy; endogenous immunoglobulin production generally normalizes with time.

Penile fracture with rupture of the righ.normalized_text: Penile fracture with rupture of the right corpus cavernosum
Penile fracture with rupture of the righ.description: Acute tear of the tunica albuginea surrounding an erect corpus cavernosum, usually during sexual intercourse, causing bleeding and soft-tissue hematoma. The MRI demonstrates a defect in the tunica albuginea near the penile base with adjacent hematoma extending into the scrotum.

Isolated scrotal hematoma secondary to g.normalized_text: Isolated scrotal hematoma secondary to genital trauma
Isolated scrotal hematoma secondary to g.description: A collection of blood within scrotal soft tissues after trauma, which may result from direct scrotal injury or blood tracking from a more proximal penile or perineal injury.

Penile dorsal vein rupture.description: Tear of the superficial or deep dorsal penile vein during intercourse, producing penile or scrotal bruising and hematoma; it can clinically resemble penile fracture but generally lacks a tunica albuginea tear.

Testicular torsion.description: Twisting of the spermatic cord that compromises testicular blood flow and causes an acute scrotum; it is a time-critical urologic emergency.

Acute epididymo-orchitis.description: Inflammation or infection of the epididymis and sometimes the testis, usually producing gradually progressive unilateral scrotal pain, tenderness, and swelling.

Muscle-eye-brain disease (POMGNT1-relate.description: An autosomal-recessive congenital muscular dystrophy caused by abnormal alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation, characterized by severe developmental delay, hypotonia, elevated CK, eye abnormalities, and structural brain malformations.

Walker-Warburg syndrome.description: A severe congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy with congenital brain malformations, eye abnormalities, profound developmental impairment, hypotonia, and elevated muscle enzymes.

Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy.description: An alpha-dystroglycan-related congenital muscular dystrophy causing early hypotonia, weakness, intellectual disability, elevated CK, contractures, and brain developmental abnormalities.

MDC1C / FKRP-related congenital muscular.description: A dystroglycanopathy due to FKRP variants that can cause congenital muscular dystrophy with weakness, high CK, contractures, and, in severe cases, brain and eye involvement.

LAMA2-related congenital muscular dystro.normalized_text: LAMA2-related congenital muscular dystrophy (merosin-deficient congenital muscular dystrophy)
LAMA2-related congenital muscular dystro.description: An autosomal-recessive congenital muscular dystrophy characterized by severe neonatal or infantile hypotonia, profound weakness, absent reflexes, contractures, elevated CK, and characteristic diffuse cerebral white-matter abnormalities.

Primary seminal vesicle adenocarcinoma.description: A rare malignant gland-forming tumor arising from a seminal vesicle, usually in older men. It may form a pelvic mass and cause nonspecific lower abdominal or pelvic symptoms.

Urachal adenocarcinoma.description: A mucin-producing adenocarcinoma arising from remnants of the urachus, most often near the bladder dome or midline anterior pelvis. It can present as a lower abdominal mass and pain.

Colorectal adenocarcinoma, especially si.normalized_text: Colorectal adenocarcinoma, especially sigmoid colon cancer
Colorectal adenocarcinoma, especially si.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the colon that may produce a left lower abdominal mass, abdominal pain, and local tenderness, particularly when locally advanced.

Primary bladder adenocarcinoma.description: A rare gland-forming carcinoma originating in the urinary bladder. Advanced tumors can form a pelvic mass and cause lower abdominal discomfort or tenderness.

Prostate adenocarcinoma with locally adv.normalized_text: Prostate adenocarcinoma with locally advanced pelvic extension
Prostate adenocarcinoma with locally adv.description: A common malignancy in older men that can extend beyond the prostate into adjacent pelvic structures and occasionally produce a palpable pelvic mass or lower abdominal discomfort.

Ethylene glycol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion, commonly from antifreeze, causing high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, elevated osmolality gap, and increased lactate or falsely elevated lactate on some analyzers. Early neurologic depression may occur.

Methanol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol poisoning that produces formic acid accumulation, resulting in severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and an elevated osmolality gap; central nervous system depression can occur early.

Propylene glycol poisoning.description: Propylene glycol toxicity may occur after ingestion or excessive exposure to medications containing propylene glycol as a solvent. It can cause central nervous system depression, hyperosmolality, an increased osmolality gap, lactic acidosis, and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

Diethylene glycol poisoning.description: Diethylene glycol is a toxic solvent or contaminant that can cause early intoxication with metabolic acidosis and an elevated osmolality gap, followed by delayed kidney injury and neurologic complications.

Cyanide poisoning.description: Cyanide toxicity blocks cellular oxygen utilization and can rapidly produce profound lactic acidosis, altered mental status, cardiovascular collapse, and sometimes high venous oxygen saturation.

diagnoses.name: Juvenile granulosa-cell tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumour unknown behaviour of unspecified site

Primary ovarian Burkitt lymphoma.description: An aggressive high-grade B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that can rarely present as a rapidly enlarging ovarian or pelvic mass in children and adolescents. Histology often shows a 'starry-sky' pattern due to numerous macrophages among rapidly proliferating tumor cells.

Ovarian dysgerminoma.description: A malignant ovarian germ-cell tumor that most often affects adolescents and young women. It commonly presents as a unilateral solid pelvic mass with abdominal pain or distension and may have hemorrhage or necrosis.

Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ova.normalized_text: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ovary
Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ova.description: A sex cord-stromal ovarian tumor occurring predominantly in children and young women. These tumors are often unilateral, can become large, and may produce estrogen, causing precocious puberty or abnormal uterine bleeding.

Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hyper.normalized_text: Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type
Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hyper.description: A rare, highly aggressive ovarian malignancy that occurs mainly in adolescents and young women. It usually presents as a large unilateral ovarian mass with abdominal pain and distension; hypercalcemia may occur but is not universal.

Ovarian torsion with hemorrhagic infarct.normalized_text: Ovarian torsion with hemorrhagic infarction of a large ovarian neoplasm or cyst
Ovarian torsion with hemorrhagic infarct.description: Twisting of the ovarian vascular pedicle can cause venous obstruction, edema, hemorrhage, ischemia, and necrosis. Torsion may occur with an ovarian cyst or tumor and can produce a painful enlarging adnexal mass with inflammatory laboratory abnormalities.

diagnoses.name: X-linked alpha-thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: X-linked alpha thalassaemia with mental retardation

Alpha-thalassemia X-linked intellectual.normalized_text: Alpha-thalassemia X-linked intellectual disability syndrome (ATR-X syndrome)
Alpha-thalassemia X-linked intellectual.description: An X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in ATRX. It is characterized by severe developmental delay, infantile hypotonia, distinctive facial features, seizures, skeletal/hand abnormalities, and sometimes hemoglobin H inclusion bodies on supravital-stained blood smears.

Angelman syndrome.description: A neurogenetic disorder, usually caused by loss of maternal UBE3A expression, producing severe developmental delay, absent or limited speech, seizures, hypotonia in infancy, gait impairment, and frequent stereotyped movements or excitable behavior.

Christianson syndrome.description: An X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder caused by SLC9A6 variants. Affected boys commonly have severe intellectual disability, infantile hypotonia, seizures, delayed walking or absent ambulation, stereotypic behaviors, and a recognizable facial appearance that may include a long/narrow face and prominent jaw.

Coffin-Siris syndrome.description: A chromatin-remodeling disorder characterized by developmental delay, infantile hypotonia, feeding difficulties, seizures in some patients, coarse or distinctive facial features, and digital abnormalities. Hypoplasia of the fifth fingernails or distal phalanges is particularly characteristic.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type II (Hunter sy.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency. It can cause developmental delay, progressive coarse facial features, joint contractures, skeletal abnormalities, behavioral problems, and seizures in more severe disease.

Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis/spondyl.normalized_text: Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis/spondylodiscitis with secondary iliopsoas abscess
Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis/spondyl.description: Bacterial infection of an intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral bodies that can extend into the psoas muscle, forming an abscess. It commonly presents with fever, severe back pain, and marked inflammatory markers.

Iliopsoas abscess.description: A collection of pus within the iliopsoas muscle, either primary from hematogenous bacterial spread or secondary to spinal, gastrointestinal, urinary, or pelvic infection. It often causes fever, back, flank, hip, or groin pain.

Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with me.normalized_text: Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with metastatic infection
Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with me.description: Bloodstream infection with Staphylococcus aureus can seed distant sites, particularly the spine, psoas muscle, lungs, joints, and heart valves. It may cause vertebral osteomyelitis, abscesses, and septic thrombosis.

Infective endocarditis with septic embol.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis with septic embolic or metastatic infection
Infective endocarditis with septic embol.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve, can produce persistent fever and systemic inflammation and may cause metastatic infections such as vertebral osteomyelitis, psoas abscess, pulmonary lesions, or venous thromboembolic complications.

Tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott disea.normalized_text: Tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott disease) with psoas abscess
Tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott disea.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can infect the spine, causing gradual vertebral destruction and paraspinal or psoas abscesses. It is usually more indolent than pyogenic spinal infection and is often accompanied by constitutional symptoms.

Re-expansion pulmonary edema.description: Acute noncardiogenic pulmonary edema that develops after rapid re-expansion of a chronically collapsed lung following drainage of a large pleural effusion or pneumothorax.

Cardiogenic pulmonary edema.description: Fluid accumulation in the lungs caused by elevated pulmonary venous pressure, usually due to acute or chronic left-sided heart failure.

Aspiration pneumonitis.description: Chemical lung injury caused by aspiration of gastric contents, often producing acute hypoxemia and infiltrates in dependent lung regions.

Community-acquired or hospital-acquired.description: Infection of the lung parenchyma that causes alveolar inflammation and consolidation, commonly presenting with cough, hypoxemia, crackles, and infiltrates.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial blood flow by thrombus, which can cause acute dyspnea, hypoxemia, tachycardia, and occasionally pleural-based pulmonary infarction.

Iliac artery fibromuscular dysplasia.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disease causing alternating stenosis and dilation ('string-of-beads' appearance). It commonly affects middle-aged women and may involve renal and iliac arteries.

Aortoiliac peripheral artery disease cau.normalized_text: Aortoiliac peripheral artery disease causing buttock claudication
Aortoiliac peripheral artery disease cau.description: Obstructive disease of the distal aorta or iliac arteries reduces blood flow during exercise and causes buttock, hip, thigh, or calf claudication.

External iliac artery endofibrosis.description: A flow-limiting fibrotic narrowing of the external iliac artery, classically associated with endurance athletes and producing exertional unilateral leg or buttock symptoms with normal findings at rest.

Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia wit.normalized_text: Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia with associated iliac artery involvement
Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia wit.description: Fibromuscular dysplasia can involve multiple arterial beds. Renal artery involvement may cause hypertension and an abdominal bruit, while iliac involvement can cause exercise-induced claudication.

Lumbar spinal stenosis causing neurogeni.normalized_text: Lumbar spinal stenosis causing neurogenic claudication
Lumbar spinal stenosis causing neurogeni.description: Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal can produce exertional buttock and thigh discomfort, usually worsened by standing or walking and relieved by sitting or spinal flexion.

Torsades de pointes (drug-induced polymo.normalized_text: Torsades de pointes (drug-induced polymorphic ventricular tachycardia)
Torsades de pointes (drug-induced polymo.description: A potentially life-threatening polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with QT-interval prolongation, often triggered by QT-prolonging medications such as sotalol. The ECG appearance is consistent with a twisting, polymorphic wide-complex tachycardia.

Acquired long QT syndrome due to sotalol.normalized_text: Acquired long QT syndrome due to sotalol
Acquired long QT syndrome due to sotalol.description: QT prolongation caused by medication, especially class III antiarrhythmic drugs such as sotalol. It predisposes patients to torsades de pointes and syncope-like symptoms.

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.description: A rapid ventricular rhythm with beat-to-beat variation in QRS morphology. When associated with QT prolongation, it is termed torsades de pointes; it can cause hypotension, presyncope, syncope, or sudden cardiac arrest.

Sotalol-associated proarrhythmia.description: A medication-induced worsening or creation of an arrhythmia caused by antiarrhythmic therapy. Sotalol can prolong repolarization and provoke severe ventricular arrhythmias, particularly shortly after initiation or dose escalation.

Recurrent atrial tachycardia.description: A supraventricular tachycardia arising from the atria, causing a rapid regular or irregular pulse and symptoms such as palpitations and lightheadedness. This patient has a known history of recurrent atrial tachycardia.

Systemic sarcoidosis with Löfgren-like p.description: A multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, often involving hilar lymph nodes, skin, joints, liver, and lungs. Acute sarcoidosis may present with fever, erythema nodosum, and arthritis.

Tuberculosis with erythema nodosum and r.normalized_text: Tuberculosis with erythema nodosum and reactive polyarthritis
Tuberculosis with erythema nodosum and r.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause constitutional symptoms, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, granulomatous inflammation, erythema nodosum, and a sterile reactive arthritis known as Poncet disease.

Lymphoma, particularly Hodgkin lymphoma.description: Hodgkin lymphoma can present in young adults with fever, lymphadenopathy, mediastinal or hilar adenopathy, hepatomegaly, fatigue, and occasionally paraneoplastic inflammatory skin or joint manifestations.

Reactive arthritis secondary to an occul.normalized_text: Reactive arthritis secondary to an occult infection
Reactive arthritis secondary to an occul.description: Reactive arthritis is a sterile inflammatory arthritis that occurs after gastrointestinal, genitourinary, or occasionally respiratory infections. It most commonly affects large lower-extremity joints and may include skin manifestations.

Adult-onset Still disease.description: Adult-onset Still disease is a systemic autoinflammatory disorder characterized by high spiking fever, inflammatory arthritis, an evanescent salmon-colored rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers.

Osteonecrosis of the distal radius (trea.normalized_text: Osteonecrosis of the distal radius (treatment-associated avascular necrosis)
Osteonecrosis of the distal radius (trea.description: Death of bone marrow and trabecular bone from impaired blood supply, potentially associated with antiangiogenic cancer therapy and sometimes occurring without corticosteroid exposure. The MRI appearance of a subchondral/epiphyseal low-signal band is compatible with osteonecrosis.

Distal radial stress fracture or insuffi.normalized_text: Distal radial stress fracture or insufficiency fracture
Distal radial stress fracture or insuffi.description: A microscopic or nondisplaced fracture caused by repetitive loading or weakened bone, which can produce wrist pain and marrow signal abnormalities before a fracture is visible on radiographs.

Kienböck disease (avascular necrosis of.normalized_text: Kienböck disease (avascular necrosis of the lunate)
Kienböck disease (avascular necrosis of.description: Avascular necrosis of the lunate carpal bone causing progressive dorsal wrist pain, stiffness, and reduced grip or wrist motion.

Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of the.normalized_text: Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of the wrist
Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of the.description: Bacterial infection of the wrist joint or adjacent bone that can cause acute pain, tenderness, restricted motion, and destructive marrow or joint changes.

Osseous metastasis involving the distal.normalized_text: Osseous metastasis involving the distal radius or wrist
Osseous metastasis involving the distal.description: Spread of malignancy to bone can cause focal pain, tenderness, reduced motion, and abnormal marrow signal; however, distal extremity metastasis is uncommon for pilocytic astrocytoma.

Menkes disease (ATP7A-related copper tra.description: An X-linked disorder of intestinal copper transport causing systemic copper deficiency, low ceruloplasmin, neurodegeneration, connective-tissue abnormalities, characteristic sparse kinky hair, and tortuous cerebral vessels.

Nutritional or acquired copper deficienc.description: Copper deficiency caused by inadequate intake, malabsorption, prolonged parenteral nutrition, excess zinc exposure, or severe gastrointestinal disease; it can produce low copper and ceruloplasmin with anemia and neurologic dysfunction.

Occipital horn syndrome (milder ATP7A-re.description: A milder allelic ATP7A disorder causing impaired copper transport and connective-tissue abnormalities, classically with occipital bone horns, joint laxity, bladder diverticula, vascular tortuosity, and sometimes mild neurologic impairment.

Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome / m.normalized_text: Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome / mitochondrial encephalopathy
Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome / m.description: A group of inherited energy-metabolism disorders that may present in infancy with failure to thrive, hypotonia, developmental regression, recurrent illness, and brain injury, often with lactic acidosis or liver/muscle involvement.

Wilson disease.description: An ATP7B-related disorder of impaired biliary copper excretion causing copper accumulation, usually presenting later in childhood or adulthood with liver disease, psychiatric symptoms, movement disorders, and low ceruloplasmin.

Adrenocortical oncocytoma.description: A rare adrenal cortical tumor composed of eosinophilic, mitochondria-rich oncocytic cells. Most are nonfunctioning, incidentally discovered, and benign, although large size or growth can raise concern for uncertain malignant potential.

Adrenocortical carcinoma.description: A rare aggressive malignant tumor of the adrenal cortex that may be hormonally active or nonfunctioning. Large size, heterogeneous imaging appearance, and interval growth are concerning features.

Pheochromocytoma.description: A catecholamine-producing tumor arising from adrenal medullary chromaffin cells. Some pheochromocytomas are clinically silent and are identified as enlarging adrenal masses on imaging.

Nonfunctioning adrenocortical adenoma.description: A common benign adrenal cortical tumor, often found incidentally during imaging performed for unrelated reasons. Most nonfunctioning adenomas cause no clinical symptoms, although marked growth and a size near 6 cm are less typical.

Adrenal ganglioneuroma.description: A rare, usually benign and nonfunctioning tumor derived from sympathetic neural crest tissue. It is often discovered incidentally and may become large before producing symptoms.

Linear morphea (linear localized sclerod.normalized_text: Linear morphea (linear localized scleroderma, "en coup de sabre")
Linear morphea (linear localized sclerod.description: A localized autoimmune fibrosing disorder causing a linear indurated plaque, classically affecting the forehead and scalp and sometimes producing alopecia and facial asymmetry.

Parry-Romberg syndrome (progressive hemi.description: A rare condition characterized by progressive unilateral loss of facial skin, subcutaneous tissue, muscle, and sometimes bone; it may overlap clinically with linear scleroderma en coup de sabre.

Lupus erythematosus profundus (lupus pan.description: A form of chronic cutaneous lupus in which inflammation affects subcutaneous fat, producing firm plaques or nodules that may heal with depressed scars and alopecia when the scalp is involved.

Discoid lupus erythematosus of the scalp.normalized_text: Discoid lupus erythematosus of the scalp
Discoid lupus erythematosus of the scalp.description: A chronic cutaneous lupus variant that causes well-demarcated inflammatory, scaly plaques with scarring alopecia, pigment alteration, and follicular plugging, commonly on sun-exposed scalp and face.

Eosinophilic fasciitis.description: An uncommon scleroderma-like inflammatory disorder involving fascia and deep soft tissue, usually causing symmetric painful swelling and subsequent induration of the extremities.

ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosu.normalized_text: ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus enteritis
ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosu.description: A rare form of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in which ANA is negative but other lupus-specific antibodies and complement consumption are present. Lupus enteritis results from immune-mediated small-bowel vasculitis and edema.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with mesent.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with mesenteric vasculitis
Systemic lupus erythematosus with mesent.description: SLE-associated mesenteric vasculitis is immune-complex inflammation of mesenteric vessels that can cause bowel ischemia, intestinal wall thickening, abdominal pain, vomiting, and paralytic ileus.

Behcet disease with gastrointestinal inv.description: Behcet disease is a multisystem inflammatory vasculitis characterized by recurrent oral aphthous ulcers and, in some patients, gastrointestinal ulceration causing abdominal pain and vomiting.

Polyarteritis nodosa or another medium-v.normalized_text: Polyarteritis nodosa or another medium-vessel systemic vasculitis
Polyarteritis nodosa or another medium-v.description: Medium-vessel vasculitis can involve mesenteric arteries, causing abdominal pain, vomiting, bowel ischemia, and intestinal edema. Polyarteritis nodosa usually does not cause glomerulonephritis.

Crohn disease or other inflammatory bowe.normalized_text: Crohn disease or other inflammatory bowel disease
Crohn disease or other inflammatory bowe.description: Inflammatory bowel disease can cause abdominal pain, vomiting, anemia, elevated inflammatory markers, and bowel-wall thickening, particularly when there is small-bowel inflammation or obstruction.

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (.description: A nontraumatic separation of layers within a coronary artery wall that creates an intramural hematoma or false lumen, obstructing coronary blood flow and causing acute coronary syndrome. It commonly affects younger women and is associated with fibromuscular dysplasia and pregnancy-related hormonal changes.

Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD).description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disease causing stenosis, aneurysm, dissection, or arterial tortuosity, most often involving renal and carotid arteries. It is strongly associated with SCAD.

Pregnancy-associated spontaneous coronar.description: SCAD occurring during pregnancy or in the postpartum period, likely related to hormonal and hemodynamic effects on vulnerable arterial walls. It can also occur after pregnancy loss.

Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS).description: A hereditary connective-tissue disorder, usually due to pathogenic COL3A1 variants, characterized by fragile arteries and organs, arterial aneurysm or dissection, and risk of spontaneous rupture. Coronary and renal arterial dissections can occur.

Acute coronary syndrome due to atheroscl.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome due to atherosclerotic coronary artery disease
Acute coronary syndrome due to atheroscl.description: Myocardial ischemia caused by coronary plaque rupture, erosion, or progressive atherosclerotic narrowing, producing unstable angina or myocardial infarction.

Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.description: Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle causes progressive gastric outlet obstruction in early infancy; upper gastrointestinal contrast studies may show an elongated, narrowed pyloric channel.

Pyloric stenosis due to pyloric/antral w.normalized_text: Pyloric stenosis due to pyloric/antral web
Pyloric stenosis due to pyloric/antral w.description: A congenital mucosal diaphragm or web at the gastric antrum or pylorus can partially obstruct gastric emptying and cause chronic feeding intolerance and poor growth.

Intestinal malrotation with intermittent.normalized_text: Intestinal malrotation with intermittent midgut volvulus
Intestinal malrotation with intermittent.description: Congenital abnormal rotation and fixation of the intestine can lead to intermittent or acute duodenal obstruction and may be evaluated with an upper gastrointestinal contrast study.

Congenital duodenal stenosis or duodenal.normalized_text: Congenital duodenal stenosis or duodenal web
Congenital duodenal stenosis or duodenal.description: Partial congenital obstruction of the duodenum from narrowing or an intraluminal web can produce chronic impaired feeding, vomiting, and poor weight gain; incomplete obstruction may present after birth rather than immediately.

Annular pancreas.description: A congenital ring of pancreatic tissue surrounding the duodenum may cause partial duodenal obstruction, resulting in feeding intolerance and poor growth in infancy.

Edematous dermatomyositis.description: An inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness, markedly elevated muscle enzymes, characteristic cutaneous findings, and sometimes prominent generalized or localized subcutaneous edema. Bulbar, pharyngeal, and laryngeal muscle involvement can cause dysphagia and dysphonia.

Polymyositis.description: A systemic autoimmune inflammatory myopathy that causes symmetric proximal muscle weakness, elevated CK, and possible involvement of swallowing and respiratory muscles; unlike dermatomyositis, it does not usually produce characteristic skin findings.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: A severe autoimmune myopathy causing rapidly progressive proximal weakness and very high CK levels, often associated with statin exposure, anti-SRP antibodies, anti-HMGCR antibodies, or malignancy. Biopsy usually shows myofiber necrosis with relatively limited inflammation.

Bradykinin-mediated angioedema, includin.description: Nonpruritic swelling of the lips, tongue, face, and upper airway caused by increased bradykinin activity. It may occur in patients taking ACE inhibitors for hypertension and can cause hoarseness, throat tightness, and dysphagia without urticaria.

Systemic lupus erythematosus-associated.description: An inflammatory myopathy occurring as a manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus or an autoimmune overlap syndrome. It can cause proximal weakness, myalgia, elevated CK, dysphagia, positive ANA, and inflammatory muscle biopsy findings.

Allergic contact dermatitis due to para-.normalized_text: Allergic contact dermatitis due to para-phenylenediamine (PPD) in black henna
Allergic contact dermatitis due to para-.description: A delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction to PPD, a common additive in black henna tattoos. The eruption often precisely follows the tattoo pattern and can be severe with vesicles or bullae.

Bullous impetigo.description: A superficial Staphylococcus aureus skin infection that produces fragile bullae, erosions, yellow fluid, and honey-colored or golden crusts.

Impetiginized allergic contact dermatiti.description: Allergic contact dermatitis complicated by secondary bacterial infection, commonly with Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. This can cause oozing, pustules, and honey-colored crusting over an allergic rash.

Irritant contact dermatitis from tattoo.normalized_text: Irritant contact dermatitis from tattoo dye or application chemicals
Irritant contact dermatitis from tattoo.description: Inflammation caused by direct chemical injury to the skin from tattoo additives, solvents, or prolonged exposure to dye. It can cause erythema, burning, itching, blistering, and oozing.

Cellulitis or erysipelas complicating a.normalized_text: Cellulitis or erysipelas complicating a skin reaction
Cellulitis or erysipelas complicating a.description: A bacterial infection of the deeper skin and subcutaneous tissue, usually causing expanding warmth, erythema, swelling, tenderness, and sometimes fever. It may occur after disruption of the skin barrier from dermatitis or blistering.

Chronic tophaceous gout.description: Advanced gout caused by long-term deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and soft tissues, producing tophi, erosive arthritis, and deformity.

Rheumatoid arthritis with rheumatoid nod.description: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory polyarthritis that usually affects small joints symmetrically and may produce subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules and hand deformities.

Calcinosis cutis / tumoral calcinosis.description: Deposition of calcium salts in skin and periarticular soft tissues, sometimes forming large lobulated masses near major joints and causing restricted movement.

Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis.description: A rare systemic histiocytic disorder causing destructive polyarthritis and multiple reddish-brown or yellowish papulonodular skin lesions, often affecting the hands and face.

Synovial chondromatosis.description: A proliferative disorder in which cartilaginous nodules form within synovium, usually affecting one large joint and causing swelling, pain, restricted motion, and loose bodies.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.normalized_text: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis subtype
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.description: A common subtype of classical Hodgkin lymphoma in young adults, frequently presenting with mediastinal and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. It is characterized by Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells that are typically CD15-positive, CD30-positive, and CD45-negative, often with fibrosis and an inflammatory background containing eosinophils.

Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphom.description: An aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that commonly arises as a bulky anterior mediastinal mass in young adults and can cause dyspnea or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma.description: A CD30-positive T-cell lymphoma that may present with lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms. It can occasionally involve the mediastinum but usually has a different immunophenotype and morphology from classical Hodgkin lymphoma.

T-lymphoblastic lymphoma.description: An aggressive immature T-cell neoplasm that often affects adolescent or young adult males and commonly presents with a large anterior mediastinal mass, respiratory symptoms, and lymphadenopathy.

Primary mediastinal germ cell tumor.description: A germ cell tumor arising in the anterior mediastinum, most often in young men. It may cause mediastinal widening, dyspnea, chest symptoms, and occasionally constitutional symptoms.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP/PC.description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia in people with advanced HIV infection, typically causing diffuse bilateral interstitial or perihilar lung infiltrates and progressive hypoxemic respiratory symptoms.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection involving the lungs; HIV increases the risk of both typical and atypical radiographic presentations, including diffuse infiltrates.

Cytomegalovirus pneumonitis.description: A viral opportunistic pneumonia that can occur in severely immunocompromised people with HIV, producing dyspnea, cough, and diffuse interstitial or patchy lung opacities.

Kaposi sarcoma with pulmonary involvemen.description: A vascular tumor associated with human herpesvirus 8 that may involve the lungs in advanced HIV, causing cough, dyspnea, and bilateral perihilar or interstitial infiltrates.

Atypical community-acquired pneumonia.description: Pneumonia caused by organisms such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, or respiratory viruses, often producing a dry cough and diffuse or patchy interstitial radiographic infiltrates.

Pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis.description: Diffuse infiltration of pulmonary lymphatic vessels by metastatic carcinoma, producing interlobular septal and peribronchovascular thickening; it may be asymmetric and can present with rapidly progressive dyspnea.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial blood flow by thrombus, commonly causing acute or subacute dyspnea, pleuritic or nonspecific chest pain, syncope, and an elevated D-dimer.

Pulmonary tumor thrombotic microangiopat.description: A rare cancer-related condition in which microscopic tumor emboli and secondary small-vessel remodeling cause rapidly progressive pulmonary hypertension, hypoxemia, and dyspnea; D-dimer may be elevated.

Congestive heart failure with pulmonary.normalized_text: Congestive heart failure with pulmonary interstitial edema
Congestive heart failure with pulmonary.description: Elevated left-sided cardiac filling pressures can cause exertional dyspnea and interstitial pulmonary edema, visible as septal thickening and increased lung markings on imaging.

Primary lung cancer with associated inte.normalized_text: Primary lung cancer with associated interstitial or lymphatic spread
Primary lung cancer with associated inte.description: Lung cancer is strongly associated with tobacco exposure and may cause progressive dyspnea through airway obstruction, pleural disease, lymphangitic spread, or cancer-associated thrombosis.

Right hemidiaphragm eventration.description: Congenital or acquired thinning and abnormal elevation of an intact hemidiaphragm, causing reduced lung expansion and basal compressive atelectasis. The imaging shows marked elevation of the right hemidiaphragm.

Right phrenic nerve palsy causing unilat.normalized_text: Right phrenic nerve palsy causing unilateral diaphragmatic paralysis
Right phrenic nerve palsy causing unilat.description: Loss of phrenic nerve function causes elevation and reduced movement of one hemidiaphragm, producing restrictive ventilatory impairment and basal atelectasis. It can be especially symptomatic in patients with obesity or underlying lung disease.

Right basal compressive atelectasis seco.normalized_text: Right basal compressive atelectasis secondary to elevated hemidiaphragm
Right basal compressive atelectasis seco.description: Partial collapse of the lower lung due to external compression or inadequate ventilation, in this case likely related to the markedly elevated right hemidiaphragm. It can impair gas exchange and cause abnormal basal chest findings.

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome.description: Chronic hypoventilation related to severe obesity, often associated with sleep-disordered breathing, hypercapnia, and resting or exertional hypoxemia. An elevated hemidiaphragm can further reduce respiratory reserve.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease wi.normalized_text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with acute exacerbation
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease wi.description: COPD is an obstructive lung disease commonly caused by smoking and may present with dyspnea, wheeze, and hypoxemia. A viral upper respiratory illness can precipitate an exacerbation.

diagnoses.name: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not other.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (DLBCL-NOS) of the maxilla
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not other.description: An aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma that commonly presents as a rapidly enlarging extranodal mass. In the oral cavity it can mimic dental infection, cause nonhealing extraction sockets, and produce maxillary bone destruction.

Plasmablastic lymphoma.description: A highly aggressive lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation that often arises in the oral cavity, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. It may present as a rapidly enlarging gingival, palatal, or maxillary mass after dental procedures.

Burkitt lymphoma.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma characterized by extremely rapid growth and a high proliferation rate. It can involve the jaws and produce dental loosening, swelling, and nonhealing extraction sites, although it is much less common in older adults.

Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.normalized_text: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to the maxilla/oral cavity
Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.description: Metastatic spread of colorectal cancer to the oral cavity or jaw is uncommon but can present as a painful or painless gingival/maxillary mass, swelling, delayed healing after extraction, and bone destruction.

Odontogenic infection with maxillary ost.normalized_text: Odontogenic infection with maxillary osteomyelitis or post-extraction abscess
Odontogenic infection with maxillary ost.description: Bacterial infection of an extraction site can lead to delayed healing, facial swelling, elevated inflammatory markers, abscess formation, and osteomyelitis of the maxilla. It is an important initial clinical differential diagnosis for this presentation.

Tinea incognito (steroid-modified tinea.description: A dermatophyte fungal infection whose typical scaly, raised ring-like border has been altered and allowed to spread by topical corticosteroid use. It commonly affects the groin, thighs, and trunk.

Tinea corporis with tinea cruris.description: A superficial dermatophyte infection of glabrous skin and the groin, classically producing pruritic expanding annular plaques with a more active scaly border and central clearing.

Erythema annulare centrifugum.description: A reactive inflammatory eruption characterized by slowly enlarging annular plaques, often with trailing scale inside the advancing edge. It can be itchy and may be triggered by infections, medications, or other inflammatory conditions.

Nummular dermatitis.description: A chronic eczematous dermatitis causing pruritic coin-shaped erythematous, scaly plaques, usually on the limbs. Lesions may become extensive and excoriated.

Plaque psoriasis.description: A chronic immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease producing well-demarcated erythematous plaques with scale. Inverse psoriasis may involve the groin, although scale is often reduced in moist folds.

Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma (lin.normalized_text: Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma (linitis plastica/signet-ring cell carcinoma) causing gastric outlet obstruction
Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma (lin.description: An infiltrative gastric cancer that spreads diffusely through the stomach wall, producing marked wall thickening, rigid folds, impaired gastric emptying, and sometimes no obvious intraluminal mass. The imaging, endoscopic appearance, and deep-wall histology are highly suggestive of this diagnosis.

Gastric outlet obstruction due to peptic.normalized_text: Gastric outlet obstruction due to peptic ulcer-related pyloric or duodenal stricture
Gastric outlet obstruction due to peptic.description: Chronic peptic ulcer disease can cause inflammation and fibrosis at the pylorus or proximal duodenum, narrowing the gastric outlet and resulting in retention of food, nausea, and vomiting or inability to tolerate oral intake.

Primary gastric lymphoma.description: Lymphoma involving the stomach can cause diffuse gastric wall thickening, enlarged folds, early satiety, nausea, and occasionally gastric outlet obstruction. It may appear as an infiltrative rather than discrete mass lesion.

Gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor (.description: A GIST is a mesenchymal tumor arising from the gastric wall. Large tumors can compress or obstruct the gastric outlet and cause early satiety, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and poor oral intake.

Severe gastroparesis.description: Gastroparesis is delayed gastric emptying caused by impaired gastric motility, often related to diabetes, medications, neurologic disease, or idiopathic dysfunction. It causes nausea, early satiety, and retained food without a mechanical obstruction.

Fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocyt.description: Maternal antibodies against fetal platelet antigens cross the placenta and destroy fetal platelets, causing severe thrombocytopenia with petechiae, purpura, and bleeding shortly after birth.

Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytope.description: A rare inherited bone-marrow failure disorder, often caused by MPL gene variants, characterized by severe thrombocytopenia beginning at birth due to markedly reduced or absent megakaryocytes; it may later progress to pancytopenia.

Bernard-Soulier syndrome.description: An inherited platelet adhesion disorder caused by defects of the platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex. It produces thrombocytopenia with giant platelets and mucocutaneous bleeding manifestations.

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.description: An X-linked disorder in boys characterized by thrombocytopenia, classically with small platelets, eczema, immunodeficiency, and bleeding that can begin in infancy or the neonatal period.

Hemophilia A or hemophilia B.description: X-linked deficiencies of coagulation factor VIII or IX that cause impaired clot formation and bleeding, especially after trauma, procedures, or injections; affected newborn boys may have bruising after delivery.

Chronic subdural hematoma.description: A slowly accumulating collection of old blood beneath the dura, often occurring weeks after minor or repetitive head trauma and commonly presenting with progressive headache.

Acute-on-chronic subdural hematoma.description: A chronic subdural blood collection with more recent rebleeding, which can cause worsening headache and imaging with mixed-density subdural collections.

Subdural hygroma.description: A collection of cerebrospinal fluid in the subdural space, often following minor trauma; it may produce headache and can resemble a chronic subdural hematoma on CT.

Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage.description: Bleeding into the subarachnoid space after trauma, typically causing sudden severe headache and sometimes neurological symptoms depending on the amount and location of bleeding.

Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.description: Thrombosis of intracranial venous sinuses that can cause persistent progressive headache, intracranial hypertension, venous infarction, or hemorrhage.

Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma / peripheral.normalized_text: Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma / peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor (pPNET)
Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma / peripheral.description: A malignant small round-cell sarcoma arising in soft tissue rather than bone. It commonly shows neuroectodermal differentiation and an EWSR1 gene rearrangement, most often involving an EWSR1-FLI1 fusion.

Desmoplastic small round cell tumor.description: An aggressive small round-cell sarcoma that typically arises in the abdominal or pelvic peritoneum of young people. It is usually driven by an EWSR1-WT1 fusion and often presents as an intra-abdominal mass or peritoneal disease.

Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue.normalized_text: Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue
Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue.description: A rare malignant soft-tissue tumor, sometimes called melanoma of soft parts, often associated with EWSR1-ATF1 or EWSR1-CREB1 rearrangements. It usually occurs in tendons or aponeuroses of the extremities and commonly expresses melanocytic markers.

EWSR1-rearranged myoepithelial carcinoma.normalized_text: EWSR1-rearranged myoepithelial carcinoma of soft tissue
EWSR1-rearranged myoepithelial carcinoma.description: A malignant myoepithelial neoplasm that can arise in soft tissue, including the trunk and abdominal wall. A subset has EWSR1 rearrangements, but tumors generally show epithelial and myoepithelial marker expression rather than a purely neuroendocrine phenotype.

Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine car.normalized_text: Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma metastatic to the abdominal wall or omentum
Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine car.description: A high-grade epithelial malignancy with neuroendocrine differentiation that can involve the peritoneum, omentum, or abdominal wall, usually as metastasis from a gastrointestinal, pancreatic, pulmonary, or gynecologic primary tumor.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T lymphocytes, often associated with malignancy, infection, or medications. It commonly causes fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, liver dysfunction, coagulopathy, and markedly elevated ferritin.

Dabrafenib/trametinib-induced hemophagoc.description: Drug-induced HLH is a severe immune-mediated adverse reaction in which a medication triggers excessive macrophage activation and systemic inflammation. BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy can rarely precipitate this syndrome.

Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated h.description: HLH can occur as a rare immune-related adverse event after immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment, including pembrolizumab. It may develop during therapy or, less commonly, after treatment has been discontinued, and can be difficult to distinguish from malignancy- or drug-triggered HLH.

Drug reaction with eosinophilia and syst.normalized_text: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome
Drug reaction with eosinophilia and syst.description: DRESS is a severe delayed drug hypersensitivity reaction characterized by fever, widespread rash, internal-organ involvement, and hematologic abnormalities. Liver involvement is common, although eosinophilia and lymphadenopathy are often expected.

Sepsis with disseminated intravascular c.description: Severe infection can produce systemic inflammation, fever, thrombocytopenia, liver injury, and coagulation abnormalities. Sepsis may also trigger secondary HLH, particularly in patients with advanced cancer or immunomodulatory treatment exposure.

Traumatic panhypopituitarism from sellar.normalized_text: Traumatic panhypopituitarism from sellar/pituitary stalk injury
Traumatic panhypopituitarism from sellar.description: Deficiency of multiple anterior pituitary hormones caused by penetrating craniofacial trauma, likely involving the sella turcica or pituitary stalk; the retained bullet is located near the sellar region.

Central adrenal insufficiency (secondary.description: Inadequate ACTH stimulation of the adrenal glands due to pituitary or hypothalamic damage, resulting in deficient cortisol production.

Central hypothyroidism.description: Hypothyroidism caused by insufficient pituitary TSH secretion or hypothalamic TRH stimulation, rather than primary thyroid gland disease.

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism due to pit.normalized_text: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism due to pituitary injury
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism due to pit.description: Failure of hypothalamic-pituitary gonadotropin production causing low LH and testosterone and impaired pubertal development.

Growth hormone deficiency secondary to t.normalized_text: Growth hormone deficiency secondary to traumatic hypopituitarism
Growth hormone deficiency secondary to t.description: Reduced growth hormone secretion from pituitary injury, often reflected by low IGF-1 and potentially accompanied by other anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies.

Congenital aqueductal stenosis causing o.normalized_text: Congenital aqueductal stenosis causing obstructive hydrocephalus
Congenital aqueductal stenosis causing o.description: Narrowing or obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct blocks cerebrospinal-fluid flow from the third to fourth ventricle, producing triventricular hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure. Imaging is consistent with marked enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles with obstruction at the aqueduct.

Tectal plate glioma with aqueductal obst.normalized_text: Tectal plate glioma with aqueductal obstruction
Tectal plate glioma with aqueductal obst.description: A low-grade tumor of the tectal region can compress the cerebral aqueduct and cause slowly progressive obstructive hydrocephalus. Such lesions often present primarily with symptoms of raised intracranial pressure rather than focal neurologic deficits.

Obstructive hydrocephalus due to an aque.normalized_text: Obstructive hydrocephalus due to an aqueductal web or membranous aqueductal obstruction
Obstructive hydrocephalus due to an aque.description: A thin congenital membrane or web within the cerebral aqueduct may cause partial obstruction that becomes clinically apparent during infancy as cerebrospinal-fluid production exceeds drainage capacity.

Postinfectious obstructive hydrocephalus.description: Prior meningitis or ventriculitis can produce scarring of the aqueduct or other cerebrospinal-fluid pathways, resulting in progressive hydrocephalus and increased intracranial pressure.

Dandy-Walker spectrum malformation with.description: Dandy-Walker spectrum disorders are congenital posterior-fossa developmental abnormalities that can impair cerebrospinal-fluid circulation and cause hydrocephalus, macrocephaly, vomiting, and developmental delay.

Primary (essential) hypertension.description: Chronic high blood pressure without a single identifiable secondary cause; it is common in people with obesity, smoking exposure, and family or lifestyle risk factors.

Obstructive sleep apnea-associated hyper.description: Obstructive sleep apnea causes recurrent nighttime airway obstruction, intermittent low oxygen levels, and sympathetic activation, contributing to resistant or severe hypertension.

Pheochromocytoma.description: A catecholamine-secreting tumor, usually arising from the adrenal glands, that can cause severe or episodic hypertension with headaches, palpitations, sweating, and tachycardia.

Primary aldosteronism.description: Excess aldosterone production, commonly from an adrenal adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, causing hypertension and often low potassium levels.

Cushing syndrome.description: A disorder of excess cortisol production that may cause hypertension, weight gain, glucose intolerance, muscle weakness, mood changes, and characteristic physical features.

Coronary vasospasm (vasospastic/Prinzmet.normalized_text: Coronary vasospasm (vasospastic/Prinzmetal angina) causing acute myocardial infarction
Coronary vasospasm (vasospastic/Prinzmet.description: Transient intense constriction of an epicardial coronary artery can cause severe ischemia, ST-segment elevation, myocardial infarction, and malignant ventricular arrhythmias despite otherwise normal coronary arteries.

Sumatriptan-associated coronary vasospas.description: Triptans can cause coronary vasoconstriction through serotonin receptor activity and may rarely trigger coronary spasm, ST-elevation myocardial infarction, ventricular arrhythmia, or cardiac arrest.

Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.normalized_text: Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (anterior STEMI)
Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.description: An anterior STEMI is acute myocardial necrosis from severe reduction or interruption of blood flow in the left anterior descending coronary artery territory; it may result from thrombosis, spasm, embolism, or dissection.

Myocardial infarction with non-obstructi.normalized_text: Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA)
Myocardial infarction with non-obstructi.description: MINOCA refers to myocardial infarction occurring without obstructive coronary artery disease on angiography. Potential causes include coronary vasospasm, plaque erosion, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, coronary embolism, and microvascular dysfunction.

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (.description: SCAD is a nontraumatic tear or intramural hematoma within a coronary artery that causes acute coronary obstruction. It is an important cause of myocardial infarction in younger and middle-aged women with few traditional atherosclerotic risk factors.

Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvi.description: Functional obstruction of the colon causing marked colonic dilatation without a mechanical blockage, often occurring in patients with neurologic disease, severe illness, or impaired autonomic bowel control.

Stercoral colitis with impending or actu.normalized_text: Stercoral colitis with impending or actual colonic perforation
Stercoral colitis with impending or actu.description: Inflammation, pressure necrosis, ischemia, and possible perforation of the colon caused by severe fecal impaction, usually in patients with chronic constipation or neurologic impairment.

Acute megacolon due to severe neurogenic.normalized_text: Acute megacolon due to severe neurogenic constipation
Acute megacolon due to severe neurogenic.description: Massive dilation of the colon resulting from longstanding impaired colonic motility and fecal evacuation, which can occur in multiple sclerosis, cerebral palsy, and other neurologic disorders.

Large-bowel obstruction from fecal impac.description: Mechanical obstruction of the distal colon caused by a large mass of impacted stool, producing proximal colonic dilatation, pain, vomiting, and risk of ischemia or perforation.

Ischemic colitis with colonic pneumatosi.normalized_text: Ischemic colitis with colonic pneumatosis and perforation secondary to massive distension
Ischemic colitis with colonic pneumatosi.description: Compromised blood flow to an overdistended colon can cause bowel-wall ischemia, pneumatosis intestinalis, necrosis, and perforation, particularly when severe constipation or pseudo-obstruction produces high intraluminal pressure.

Disseminated cryptococcosis with pulmona.normalized_text: Disseminated cryptococcosis with pulmonary cryptococcosis and cryptococcal meningitis
Disseminated cryptococcosis with pulmona.description: Infection with Cryptococcus species that can cause subacute pulmonary disease and spread to the central nervous system, producing meningitis, particularly in immunocompromised individuals but occasionally in apparently immunocompetent hosts.

Pulmonary tuberculosis with tuberculous.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause chronic pulmonary symptoms with constitutional features and, when disseminated, meningeal inflammation causing headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia.

Disseminated histoplasmosis with central.normalized_text: Disseminated histoplasmosis with central nervous system involvement
Disseminated histoplasmosis with central.description: Histoplasma capsulatum is an endemic fungal infection acquired by inhalation; it may cause pulmonary nodules or diffuse infiltrates and can rarely disseminate to the meninges.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.description: Pneumocystis jirovecii causes an opportunistic pneumonia characterized by subacute cough, progressive hypoxemic dyspnea, fever, and diffuse bilateral ground-glass or interstitial lung abnormalities; fluorescent respiratory staining can identify the organism.

Legionnaires' disease due to Legionella.normalized_text: Legionnaires' disease due to Legionella pneumonia with neurologic involvement
Legionnaires' disease due to Legionella.description: Legionella infection produces an atypical pneumonia with fever, cough, dyspnea, myalgias, headache, and sometimes altered mental status or meningeal symptoms; exposure can occur during travel or through water systems.

Renal-limited thrombotic microangiopathy.description: A microvascular occlusive disorder causing endothelial injury, arteriolar/arterial intimal thickening, glomerular ischemia, and thrombosis; it may occur without the full systemic hemolytic uremic syndrome picture.

Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic u.description: A complement dysregulation disorder causing thrombotic microangiopathy, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and kidney injury; some cases are predominantly renal.

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: Severe hypertension can injure renal arterioles and glomeruli, producing fibrinoid vascular injury, onion-skin arteriolar thickening, ischemic glomeruli, hematuria, and anemia.

Antiphospholipid syndrome nephropathy.description: Renal small-vessel thrombosis and chronic vascular lesions caused by antiphospholipid antibodies, often manifesting with hypertension, hematuria, proteinuria, and impaired kidney function.

Renal infarction due to renal arterial t.normalized_text: Renal infarction due to renal arterial thrombosis or embolism
Renal infarction due to renal arterial t.description: Acute interruption of renal arterial blood flow causes flank pain, hematuria, and ischemic renal injury; segmental or small-vessel infarction may result from thrombotic disease.

Uterine arteriovenous malformation (uter.description: An abnormal high-flow connection between uterine arteries and veins, which may be acquired after pregnancy loss, curettage, or other uterine trauma and can cause life-threatening uterine bleeding.

Retained products of conception.description: Persistence of placental or fetal tissue in the uterus following miscarriage, often causing prolonged or heavy vaginal bleeding and sometimes infection.

Gestational trophoblastic disease.description: Abnormal proliferation of placental trophoblastic tissue, including molar pregnancy or persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which can present with abnormal bleeding after a pregnancy event.

Subinvolution of the placental implantat.normalized_text: Subinvolution of the placental implantation site
Subinvolution of the placental implantat.description: Failure of the uteroplacental vessels at a previous implantation site to regress normally after pregnancy termination, causing delayed and sometimes severe uterine bleeding.

Uterine leiomyoma (fibroid), especially.normalized_text: Uterine leiomyoma (fibroid), especially a submucosal fibroid
Uterine leiomyoma (fibroid), especially.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor of the uterus; submucosal fibroids can distort the endometrial cavity and cause marked heavy menstrual bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia.

Recurrent Clostridioides difficile infec.description: A recurrence of toxin-producing C. difficile colitis after an initial episode, often occurring within weeks after apparent clinical resolution and commonly associated with recent antibiotic exposure.

Post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome.description: A functional bowel disorder that can develop after infectious gastroenteritis or colitis, causing recurrent abdominal discomfort associated with bowel movements and altered stool frequency or consistency.

Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic Cl.normalized_text: Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic Clostridioides difficile colonization with another cause of diarrhea
Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic Cl.description: C. difficile can be present in the colon without causing active toxin-mediated colitis; PCR detects the organism's genetic material but does not by itself prove active infection.

Antibiotic-associated diarrhea not cause.normalized_text: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea not caused by Clostridioides difficile
Antibiotic-associated diarrhea not cause.description: Diarrhea resulting from disruption of normal intestinal flora during or after antibiotic therapy, usually mild and self-limited and not necessarily due to C. difficile toxin-mediated disease.

Inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulce.normalized_text: Inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease
Inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulce.description: Chronic immune-mediated inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract that can cause recurrent diarrhea and abdominal pain, although objective inflammatory findings are often present during active disease.

Disseminated tuberculosis with miliary p.normalized_text: Disseminated tuberculosis with miliary pulmonary and abdominal involvement
Disseminated tuberculosis with miliary p.description: Widespread Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can produce diffuse micronodular lung disease, fever, profound weight loss, lymphadenopathy, and gastrointestinal or abdominal involvement, particularly in an immunocompromised person.

Advanced HIV infection/AIDS with opportu.normalized_text: Advanced HIV infection/AIDS with opportunistic infections
Advanced HIV infection/AIDS with opportu.description: Advanced HIV infection causes severe weight loss, generalized lymphadenopathy, oral candidiasis, recurrent or unusual infections, and susceptibility to disseminated fungal or mycobacterial disease.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: Disseminated Histoplasma capsulatum infection, especially in people with advanced HIV, can cause fever, wasting, diffuse pulmonary nodules, lymphadenopathy, mucosal lesions, and gastrointestinal disease.

Disseminated talaromycosis (Talaromyces.description: Talaromycosis is an opportunistic fungal infection, classically associated with advanced HIV in Southeast Asia, that causes fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, and skin or gastrointestinal manifestations.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including HIV-asso.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including HIV-associated lymphoma with gastrointestinal involvement
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including HIV-asso.description: Aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma can cause constitutional symptoms, enlarged lymph nodes, abdominal pain from gastrointestinal or abdominal disease, and occasionally pulmonary nodules; risk is increased in advanced HIV infection.

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma with cuta.normalized_text: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma with cutaneous involvement
Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma with cuta.description: An aggressive mature CD4-positive T-cell neoplasm caused by HTLV-1 infection that can involve skin, lymph nodes, blood, and other organs.

Mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymp.description: The most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, typically causing slowly progressive pruritic patches, plaques, and sometimes tumors with epidermotropic atypical T cells.

Sézary syndrome.description: A leukemic variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma characterized by generalized itchy erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and malignant T cells in the blood.

Secondary syphilis.description: The disseminated stage of Treponema pallidum infection, often producing a diffuse papulosquamous rash that may involve the palms and soles with generalized lymphadenopathy.

Crusted scabies.description: A severe infestation with Sarcoptes scabiei, often occurring in immunocompromised or chronically ill patients and causing widespread pruritic scaling and crusting.

Giant cell myocarditis.description: A rare, rapidly progressive inflammatory myocarditis characterized by myocardial destruction, lymphocytic inflammation, and multinucleated giant cells on biopsy. It commonly causes ventricular arrhythmias, conduction disease, heart failure, and sudden cardiac death.

Cardiac sarcoidosis.description: Inflammatory cardiac involvement by sarcoidosis, typically producing noncaseating granulomas that may lead to conduction block, ventricular tachycardia, cardiomyopathy, and heart failure.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: An inherited myocardial disease characterized by left ventricular hypertrophy, often asymmetric, which can cause exertional dyspnea, angina, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death.

Acute coronary syndrome due to obstructi.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome due to obstructive coronary artery disease
Acute coronary syndrome due to obstructi.description: Myocardial ischemia caused by coronary atherosclerotic plaque rupture or severe fixed coronary stenosis. Diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and obesity substantially increase risk.

Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.description: A genetic myocardial disorder, usually involving the right ventricle but sometimes the left ventricle, that predisposes to ventricular tachycardia, sudden death, and progressive ventricular dysfunction due to fibrofatty myocardial replacement.

Postoperative pyoderma gangrenosum.description: A rare neutrophilic inflammatory skin disease causing rapidly progressive painful ulceration, often triggered by surgical trauma (pathergy). It can mimic wound infection but worsens despite antibiotics and debridement.

Post-cesarean surgical-site infection wi.normalized_text: Post-cesarean surgical-site infection with wound dehiscence
Post-cesarean surgical-site infection wi.description: A bacterial infection involving the cesarean incision that may cause cellulitis, purulent drainage, separation of wound edges, fever, and delayed healing.

Necrotizing fasciitis.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening deep soft-tissue infection that can occur after surgery and causes systemic toxicity, severe pain, tissue necrosis, and wound breakdown.

Clinical chorioamnionitis (intra-amnioti.description: Infection and inflammation of the amniotic fluid, placenta, membranes, or uterus, usually presenting in pregnancy with maternal fever, uterine tenderness or contractions, maternal leukocytosis, and fetal tachycardia.

Preeclampsia with fetal growth restricti.description: A hypertensive disorder of pregnancy that can impair placental function, leading to fetal growth restriction, oligohydramnios, and nonreassuring fetal testing. It may coexist with infection or another inflammatory condition.

Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH, Forestier disease) with large anterior cervical osteophytes
Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis.description: A noninflammatory disorder characterized by flowing calcification and ossification along spinal ligaments, often producing large anterior cervical osteophytes that can compress the pharynx or esophagus.

Cervical spondylosis with anterior cervi.normalized_text: Cervical spondylosis with anterior cervical osteophyte formation
Cervical spondylosis with anterior cervi.description: Age-related degeneration of the cervical spine can cause osteophytes; very large anterior osteophytes may mechanically obstruct the hypopharynx or cervical esophagus and cause swallowing impairment.

Ossification of the anterior longitudina.normalized_text: Ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament
Ossification of the anterior longitudina.description: Pathologic calcification or ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament can create a prominent anterior cervical mass effect, sometimes overlapping with DISH and causing dysphagia.

Retropharyngeal or hypopharyngeal tumor.description: A mass in the retropharyngeal space or hypopharynx can externally compress the larynx, pharynx, or esophagus and lead to progressive dysphagia and aspiration.

Zenker diverticulum.description: A pharyngoesophageal pouch that can retain food and secretions, causing dysphagia, regurgitation, coughing, choking, and aspiration, particularly in older adults.

NUT carcinoma (NUT midline carcinoma) of.normalized_text: NUT carcinoma (NUT midline carcinoma) of the mediastinum
NUT carcinoma (NUT midline carcinoma) of.description: A rare, highly aggressive poorly differentiated carcinoma driven by rearrangement of the NUTM1 gene, often arising in the mediastinum of adolescents and young adults and frequently initially mistaken for thymic carcinoma.

Thymic carcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from the thymus in the anterior mediastinum. It can cause cough, dyspnea, chest symptoms, and weight loss due to local compression or invasion.

Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphom.description: An aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that commonly affects young women and presents as a bulky anterior mediastinal mass causing respiratory symptoms.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma with mediasti.normalized_text: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma with mediastinal involvement
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma with mediasti.description: A lymphoid malignancy frequently affecting adolescents and young adults; nodular sclerosis classical Hodgkin lymphoma often presents with a bulky anterior mediastinal mass in young women.

Primary mediastinal germ cell tumor.description: A germ cell tumor arising in the anterior mediastinum, including seminomatous and nonseminomatous tumors, which can produce a large mass causing cough, dyspnea, and chest radiographic widening.

Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal h.normalized_text: Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia (PBMAH) causing ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome
Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal h.description: A bilateral adrenal disorder with nodular enlargement of both adrenal glands that can autonomously produce cortisol, often presenting subtly in older adults. The CT appearance of bilateral adrenal nodularity/enlargement and abnormal cortisol testing strongly support this diagnosis.

Adrenal cortisol-producing adenoma.description: A benign adrenal cortical tumor that autonomously secretes cortisol and causes ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome. Bilateral adrenal nodules can occasionally represent adenomas, although a single unilateral lesion is more typical.

Cushing disease due to an ACTH-secreting.normalized_text: Cushing disease due to an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma
Cushing disease due to an ACTH-secreting.description: Pituitary overproduction of ACTH stimulates both adrenal glands to produce excess cortisol. It is the most common endogenous cause of Cushing syndrome but does not usually cause discrete bilateral adrenal masses.

Ectopic ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome.description: Excess ACTH produced by a non-pituitary tumor, such as a small-cell lung cancer or neuroendocrine tumor, causes marked cortisol excess and bilateral adrenal stimulation. It often develops more rapidly and can be clinically severe.

Adrenocortical carcinoma with cortisol e.description: A malignant adrenal cortical tumor that may produce cortisol and cause Cushing syndrome. It typically appears as a large, irregular, unilateral adrenal mass and may cause rapid onset of severe cortisol-excess manifestations.

diagnoses.name: Membranous nephropathy
diagnoses.icd11_title: Glomerular disease associated with thin basement membrane nephropathy

Nephrotic syndrome, likely due to membra.normalized_text: Nephrotic syndrome, likely due to membranous nephropathy
Nephrotic syndrome, likely due to membra.description: A glomerular kidney disorder causing heavy urinary protein loss, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and increased risk of venous thrombosis. Membranous nephropathy is particularly associated with renal-vein and inferior-vena-cava thrombosis.

Extensive inferior vena cava thrombosis.normalized_text: Extensive inferior vena cava thrombosis with renal and iliac venous involvement
Extensive inferior vena cava thrombosis.description: Thrombosis of the inferior vena cava, often extending into renal and iliac veins, obstructs venous return from the legs and abdomen. It can produce marked bilateral leg edema, abdominal wall collateral vessels, flank pain, and renal dysfunction or hematuria.

Renal vein thrombosis secondary to nephr.normalized_text: Renal vein thrombosis secondary to nephrotic syndrome
Renal vein thrombosis secondary to nephr.description: A clot in a renal vein, commonly associated with nephrotic syndrome and especially membranous nephropathy. It may extend into the inferior vena cava and cause flank pain, hematuria, worsening proteinuria, and lower-extremity edema.

Lupus nephritis with nephrotic-range pro.description: Kidney involvement from systemic lupus erythematosus can cause proteinuria, hematuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and nephrotic syndrome. Lupus may also increase thrombotic risk, particularly if antiphospholipid antibodies are present.

Antiphospholipid syndrome.description: An autoimmune hypercoagulable disorder characterized by arterial or venous thrombosis and/or characteristic pregnancy morbidity in the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies. It may be primary or associated with systemic lupus erythematosus.

Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleo.description: A systemic Epstein-Barr virus infection that commonly causes fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and sometimes hepatitis with splenic enlargement.

Epstein-Barr virus-associated cholestati.description: An uncommon hepatic manifestation of acute Epstein-Barr virus infection in which inflammation of the liver causes predominantly cholestatic jaundice, sometimes without viral hepatitis A, B, or C.

Acute acalculous cholecystitis associate.normalized_text: Acute acalculous cholecystitis associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection
Acute acalculous cholecystitis associate.description: Gallbladder inflammation without gallstones, which can occur during Epstein-Barr virus infection because of gallbladder wall edema and systemic inflammation. Imaging may show gallbladder wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid without stones.

Acute cholangitis.description: A bacterial infection of the biliary tree, usually caused by obstruction such as a bile duct stone or stricture. It classically presents with fever, jaundice, and right-upper-quadrant pain.

Choledocholithiasis with obstructive jau.description: Obstruction of the common bile duct by a gallstone, producing conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and cholestasis; it may precipitate cholecystitis or cholangitis.
