Polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis that can cause renal arterial microaneurysms, stenoses, thrombosis, and renal infarctions; angiography often shows multiple small aneurysms and irregular arterial narrowing.

Bilateral renal infarction.description: Acute ischemic necrosis of renal tissue caused by occlusion or severe narrowing of renal arterial branches, producing wedge-shaped renal perfusion defects, flank pain, hypertension, elevated LDH, and kidney dysfunction.

Segmental arterial mediolysis.description: A rare noninflammatory arteriopathy involving medium-sized abdominal arteries that can cause arterial dissections, stenoses, aneurysms, thrombosis, and renal or visceral infarction.

Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia.description: A nonatherosclerotic arterial disorder that causes alternating renal artery stenosis and aneurysmal dilation, often described as a string-of-beads appearance, and may lead to severe hypertension or renal ischemia.

ANCA-associated vasculitis with renal in.description: A group of small-vessel autoimmune vasculitides that can cause constitutional symptoms, elevated inflammatory markers, hypertension, acute kidney injury, and glomerulonephritis; renal disease usually produces an active urinary sediment.

Intestinal tuberculosis with disseminate.normalized_text: Intestinal tuberculosis with disseminated tuberculosis and tuberculous aortitis
Intestinal tuberculosis with disseminate.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection involving the ileocecal bowel, lungs, lymph nodes, and potentially the aortic wall, which can cause an infected inflammatory aneurysm.

Colorectal adenocarcinoma, particularly.normalized_text: Colorectal adenocarcinoma, particularly cecal or ascending-colon cancer
Colorectal adenocarcinoma, particularly.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the colon that may cause constitutional symptoms, abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, and an ulcerated colonic mass.

Primary gastrointestinal lymphoma.description: Lymphoid malignancy involving the gastrointestinal tract, often affecting the ileocecal region and causing abdominal pain, weight loss, diarrhea, bowel-wall thickening, or ulceration.

Chronic mesenteric ischemia with ischemi.normalized_text: Chronic mesenteric ischemia with ischemic colitis
Chronic mesenteric ischemia with ischemi.description: Insufficient intestinal blood flow from severe atherosclerotic mesenteric arterial disease, producing postprandial abdominal pain, food avoidance, weight loss, diarrhea, and sometimes colonic ulceration.

Infected abdominal aortic aneurysm (myco.normalized_text: Infected abdominal aortic aneurysm (mycotic aneurysm), such as Salmonella-associated aortitis
Infected abdominal aortic aneurysm (myco.description: Bacterial infection of the aortic wall causing rapid aneurysmal enlargement, periaortic inflammation, abdominal or back pain, and systemic illness; older patients with atherosclerosis are at increased risk.

Pancreatic panniculitis secondary to acu.normalized_text: Pancreatic panniculitis secondary to acute pancreatitis
Pancreatic panniculitis secondary to acu.description: A rare inflammatory skin manifestation caused by release of pancreatic enzymes into the bloodstream, leading to enzymatic fat necrosis in subcutaneous tissue. It classically produces tender erythematous nodules and histologic 'ghost adipocytes.'

Acute alcoholic pancreatitis.description: Acute inflammation of the pancreas, commonly caused by heavy alcohol use, characterized by abdominal pain, vomiting, and substantial elevation of pancreatic enzymes. Severe pancreatitis can cause pancreatic panniculitis.

Pancreatitis, panniculitis, and polyarth.description: A rare systemic syndrome caused by pancreatic enzyme release, most often from pancreatitis or pancreatic malignancy. It includes pancreatitis, painful panniculitic nodules from fat necrosis, and inflammatory arthritis caused by periarticular fat necrosis.

Erythema nodosum.description: An inflammatory panniculitis that produces painful red nodules, usually on the shins, and may be associated with infections, inflammatory bowel disease, medications, or systemic inflammatory disorders. Histology is typically septal panniculitis without vasculitis.

Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma with pa.normalized_text: Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma with pancreatic panniculitis
Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma with pa.description: A rare pancreatic tumor that can produce excessive lipase and other pancreatic enzymes, causing panniculitis with tender nodules and enzymatic fat necrosis; it may also cause pancreatitis-like abdominal symptoms.

Multiple myeloma with skull plasmacytoma.description: A malignant clonal plasma-cell disorder causing monoclonal light-chain production, bone lesions, anaemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcaemia, and focal plasmacytomas.

Macrofocal multiple myeloma.description: A less common variant of multiple myeloma characterized by multiple lytic bone or soft-tissue plasma-cell lesions with relatively low marrow plasma-cell involvement.

Multiple solitary plasmacytomas / multif.description: A plasma-cell neoplasm with more than one localized bone or extramedullary plasmacytoma, potentially representing an early or marrow-sparse form of systemic myeloma.

Solitary osseous plasmacytoma of the sku.normalized_text: Solitary osseous plasmacytoma of the skull
Solitary osseous plasmacytoma of the sku.description: A localized collection of neoplastic plasma cells arising in a single bone, commonly causing a painless enlarging mass; it can progress to multiple myeloma.

Metastatic plasma-cell neoplasm with ext.normalized_text: Metastatic plasma-cell neoplasm with extramedullary disease
Metastatic plasma-cell neoplasm with ext.description: Systemic plasma-cell myeloma may form destructive bone masses and extend into adjacent soft tissues, including the skull and thoracic skeleton.

Hepatic tuberculosis (multiple hepatic t.description: Tuberculous infection of the liver can produce single or multiple focal hypodense lesions (tuberculomas or microabscesses), particularly in patients with prior abdominal tuberculosis.

Pyogenic liver abscesses.description: Bacterial infection of the liver may cause one or multiple focal hepatic abscesses, usually associated with abdominal pain, systemic illness, fever, and inflammatory laboratory abnormalities.

Hepatic lymphoma.description: Lymphoma may involve the liver as solitary or multiple hypodense lesions and can cause abdominal pain, anorexia, hepatomegaly, and constitutional symptoms.

Multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma or h.description: Primary hepatic malignancies can present as focal or multifocal liver masses with abdominal pain, anorexia, and liver enlargement; hepatoblastoma is much more common in younger children, while hepatocellular carcinoma may occur in older children with chronic liver disease.

Hepatic inflammatory pseudotumor (inflam.description: An inflammatory pseudotumor is a benign but mass-forming inflammatory lesion of the liver that can mimic malignancy or infection and may occur in children and adolescents.

Cholesterol crystal embolization syndrom.normalized_text: Cholesterol crystal embolization syndrome (atheroembolic renal disease)
Cholesterol crystal embolization syndrom.description: Embolization of cholesterol crystals from disrupted aortic or arterial atherosclerotic plaques, often after angiography, vascular surgery, or anticoagulation. It commonly causes acute or subacute kidney failure, eosinophilia, and painful blue or purple distal digits with preserved large-vessel pulses.

Polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that can cause renal ischemia, hypertension, skin nodules, livedo reticularis, digital ischemia, neuropathy, and systemic inflammation.

ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatos.normalized_text: ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis or microscopic polyangiitis)
ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatos.description: A small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis that commonly produces rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and may cause purpura, systemic inflammation, pulmonary disease, and neurologic manifestations.

Acute interstitial nephritis.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory injury of the renal interstitium, commonly triggered by medications such as antibiotics, proton-pump inhibitors, NSAIDs, or other drugs. It can cause acute kidney injury, pyuria, mild proteinuria, hematuria, and eosinophilia.

Infective endocarditis with systemic emb.description: Infection of a cardiac valve or endocardial surface that may produce emboli to the brain, kidneys, and peripheral arteries, causing altered mental status, renal injury, and painful ischemic digits or other skin findings.

Severe accidental hypothermia.description: A life-threatening reduction in core body temperature, often causing depressed consciousness, bradycardia, hypotension, and characteristic J (Osborn) waves on ECG.

Myxedema coma.description: A severe, decompensated form of hypothyroidism characterized by altered mental status, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, and hypoventilation.

Septic shock with hypothermia.description: Severe infection causing circulatory failure and altered mental status; elderly patients may become hypothermic rather than febrile.

Adrenal crisis.description: Acute adrenal insufficiency causing severe hypotension, weakness, confusion or coma, and sometimes hypothermia, usually precipitated by illness or physiologic stress.

Beta-blocker or other rate-limiting medi.normalized_text: Beta-blocker or other rate-limiting medication toxicity
Beta-blocker or other rate-limiting medi.description: Toxicity from beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, digoxin, or similar agents can cause profound bradycardia, hypotension, and depressed consciousness.

Seronegative anti-glomerular basement me.normalized_text: Seronegative anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (seronegative Goodpasture syndrome)
Seronegative anti-glomerular basement me.description: An autoimmune pulmonary-renal syndrome caused by antibodies targeting basement-membrane components, sometimes with negative circulating anti-GBM testing. It commonly produces diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis; linear IgG staining along basement membranes is characteristic.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with diffus.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage
Systemic lupus erythematosus with diffus.description: A multisystem immune-complex autoimmune disease that can cause diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, lupus nephritis, seizures, and focal neurologic deficits. Renal immunofluorescence usually shows granular immune-complex deposition rather than isolated linear IgG staining.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: An ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis that may cause pulmonary capillaritis with hemoptysis and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Neurologic involvement can occur, but tissue immunofluorescence is usually pauci-immune rather than IgG-positive.

Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis.description: A rare disorder characterized by recurrent diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, iron-deficiency anemia, and pulmonary hemosiderin deposition, without an identifiable systemic vasculitis or anti-GBM antibody. Renal disease is generally absent.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system with pulmonary hemorrhage from systemic small-vessel vasculitis
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: Inflammatory vasculitis affecting small cerebral vessels can cause seizures and transient focal deficits. If part of an occult systemic vasculitic syndrome, pulmonary capillaritis and renal urinary abnormalities may also occur.

Metastatic mixed nonseminomatous testicu.normalized_text: Metastatic mixed nonseminomatous testicular germ cell tumor
Metastatic mixed nonseminomatous testicu.description: A testicular cancer containing one or more nonseminomatous components, commonly embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, or teratoma. It can metastasize through retroperitoneal lymph nodes to the gastrointestinal tract and cause ulceration and bleeding.

Testicular embryonal carcinoma with gast.normalized_text: Testicular embryonal carcinoma with gastrointestinal metastasis
Testicular embryonal carcinoma with gast.description: Embryonal carcinoma is an aggressive nonseminomatous germ cell tumor of the testis that commonly occurs in young adult men and may produce AFP and/or hCG. It frequently spreads early to retroperitoneal lymph nodes and can involve the gastrointestinal tract.

Testicular yolk sac tumor with metastati.normalized_text: Testicular yolk sac tumor with metastatic gastrointestinal involvement
Testicular yolk sac tumor with metastati.description: A yolk sac tumor is a nonseminomatous testicular germ cell tumor characterized by substantial AFP production. In adults it often occurs as part of a mixed germ cell tumor and may metastasize to retroperitoneal nodes and distant organs.

Testicular choriocarcinoma or a mixed ge.normalized_text: Testicular choriocarcinoma or a mixed germ cell tumor containing choriocarcinoma
Testicular choriocarcinoma or a mixed ge.description: Choriocarcinoma is a highly vascular nonseminomatous germ cell tumor that can metastasize hematogenously and cause prominent bleeding, including gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Pure choriocarcinoma usually produces markedly high hCG.

NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease with.normalized_text: NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease with upper gastrointestinal bleeding
NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease with.description: Frequent NSAID use can cause gastric or duodenal mucosal injury and peptic ulcers, leading to epigastric pain, melena, and iron-deficiency anemia. This may explain the initial gastrointestinal presentation but does not account for the tumor-marker pattern or testicular mass.

diagnoses.name: Poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma of gastric origin
diagnoses.normalized_text: Poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma of gastric origin

Phlegmasia cerulea dolens.description: A severe form of extensive deep venous thrombosis causing near-total venous outflow obstruction, massive edema, cyanosis, arterial compromise, and risk of venous gangrene.

Extensive acute iliofemoral deep vein th.normalized_text: Extensive acute iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis
Extensive acute iliofemoral deep vein th.description: Acute thrombus involving the deep veins of the thigh and pelvis, producing unilateral limb pain, swelling, venous congestion, and potentially progressing to phlegmasia cerulea dolens.

Acute arterial limb ischemia due to arte.normalized_text: Acute arterial limb ischemia due to arterial embolism
Acute arterial limb ischemia due to arte.description: Sudden interruption of arterial blood flow to a limb, often caused by embolization from atrial fibrillation, leading to pain, pallor or cyanosis, coldness, pulselessness, sensory loss, and possible tissue necrosis.

Acute compartment syndrome.description: A limb-threatening condition in which increased pressure within a fascial compartment compromises tissue perfusion, causing severe pain, swelling, neurologic deficits, and late pulselessness or cyanosis.

Occult gastric adenocarcinoma with cance.normalized_text: Occult gastric adenocarcinoma with cancer-associated thrombosis (Trousseau syndrome)
Occult gastric adenocarcinoma with cance.description: Gastric adenocarcinoma can produce a hypercoagulable state that predisposes to extensive venous thrombosis; the abdominal imaging, endoscopic mass, and histology are consistent with an underlying gastric malignancy.

Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma with.normalized_text: Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma with penile involvement
Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma with.description: A rare aggressive extranodal lymphoma in which malignant large B cells proliferate mainly within small blood vessels. It commonly causes fever and may lack lymphadenopathy or organ enlargement; penile vascular involvement can cause ischemic priapism.

Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of.normalized_text: Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the penis
Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of.description: An uncommon extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving penile erectile tissue. It can infiltrate the corpora cavernosa and impair venous drainage, producing painful priapism.

Chronic myeloid leukemia or other myelop.normalized_text: Chronic myeloid leukemia or other myeloproliferative neoplasm causing leukostasis
Chronic myeloid leukemia or other myelop.description: Myeloproliferative blood cancers can produce marked leukocytosis and hyperviscosity, leading to sludging in the corpora cavernosa and ischemic priapism.

Penile metastasis from prostate, bladder.normalized_text: Penile metastasis from prostate, bladder, colorectal, or other pelvic malignancy
Penile metastasis from prostate, bladder.description: Secondary spread of a pelvic or systemic cancer to the penis can obstruct venous or lymphatic drainage and cause malignant priapism, often with deep corporal infiltration.

Penile tuberculosis or granulomatous inf.normalized_text: Penile tuberculosis or granulomatous infection involving the corpora cavernosa
Penile tuberculosis or granulomatous inf.description: Tuberculosis and other granulomatous infections can involve genitourinary structures and produce fever and inflammatory penile disease, although priapism from corporal involvement is rare.

Struma ovarii with pseudo-Meigs syndrome.description: A rare monodermal ovarian teratoma composed predominantly of thyroid tissue. It can cause ascites, pleural effusion, and marked CA-125 elevation despite being benign; thyroid function is often normal.

Epithelial ovarian carcinoma.description: A malignant ovarian epithelial tumor, particularly high-grade serous carcinoma, commonly presents with an adnexal mass, ascites, abdominal symptoms, and elevated CA-125.

Ovarian fibroma or fibrothecoma with Mei.normalized_text: Ovarian fibroma or fibrothecoma with Meigs syndrome
Ovarian fibroma or fibrothecoma with Mei.description: A benign ovarian sex-cord stromal tumor that may be associated with ascites and pleural effusion, known as Meigs syndrome. CA-125 can rise substantially because of peritoneal and pleural irritation.

Granulosa cell tumor of the ovary.normalized_text: Granulosa cell tumor of the ovary
Granulosa cell tumor of the ovary.description: A sex-cord stromal ovarian tumor that may be solid and cystic and can occur around menopause. Some tumors produce estrogen and cause endometrial stimulation or postmenopausal bleeding.

Metastatic ovarian malignancy (Krukenber.normalized_text: Metastatic ovarian malignancy (Krukenberg tumor or other metastatic tumor)
Metastatic ovarian malignancy (Krukenber.description: Secondary ovarian involvement by a gastrointestinal, breast, or other primary cancer can produce complex ovarian masses, ascites, and elevated CA-125.

Primary osseous lymphoma of the cervical.normalized_text: Primary osseous lymphoma of the cervical spine
Primary osseous lymphoma of the cervical.description: A malignant lymphoid tumor arising in bone that may produce extensive marrow replacement and a large paraspinal or epidural soft-tissue component while early plain radiographs remain normal.

Cervical spinal tuberculosis (tuberculou.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the spine causing vertebral marrow destruction, paravertebral or prevertebral inflammatory soft tissue, and possible epidural extension; early radiographs can be unrevealing.

Pyogenic cervical discitis-osteomyelitis.normalized_text: Pyogenic cervical discitis-osteomyelitis with epidural or prevertebral phlegmon
Pyogenic cervical discitis-osteomyelitis.description: Bacterial infection involving vertebral endplates and intervertebral discs that can extend into prevertebral tissues or the epidural space, causing persistent focal spinal pain and potential cord compression.

Chordoma involving the clivus and upper.normalized_text: Chordoma involving the clivus and upper cervical spine
Chordoma involving the clivus and upper.description: A rare slow-growing malignant tumor derived from notochordal remnants, usually centered in the midline clivus or sacrum; skull-base lesions can extend into the upper cervical region and cause pain.

Metastatic malignancy involving the cerv.normalized_text: Metastatic malignancy involving the cervical spine
Metastatic malignancy involving the cerv.description: Secondary malignant involvement of vertebral marrow, which can cause persistent pain, pathologic fracture, epidural disease, or paraspinal soft-tissue extension; MRI is more sensitive than radiographs early in disease.

Congenital smooth muscle hamartoma.description: A benign developmental overgrowth of arrector pili smooth muscle in the skin, usually present at birth or early infancy and often occurring on the trunk or lumbosacral region. It may appear as a skin-colored or hyperpigmented plaque, sometimes with increased hair growth or sweating.

Eccrine nevus.description: A rare benign hamartoma characterized by increased or enlarged eccrine sweat glands. It usually presents in childhood as a localized skin-colored plaque or nodule with focal hyperhidrosis.

Eccrine angiomatous hamartoma.description: A benign congenital or childhood-onset hamartoma composed of eccrine sweat glands and vascular structures. It commonly presents as a slowly enlarging plaque or nodule and may cause localized hyperhidrosis, pain, or color change.

Fibrous hamartoma of infancy.description: A benign, poorly circumscribed fibrous and fatty soft-tissue tumor that develops during the first two years of life. It often presents as a painless, firm, progressively enlarging subcutaneous mass on the trunk or upper extremities.

Connective tissue nevus.description: A benign cutaneous hamartoma caused by excess collagen, elastin, or other dermal connective tissue. It presents as a firm skin-colored plaque, often on the trunk, and may become more noticeable as the child grows.

SAPHO syndrome (synovitis, acne, pustulo.normalized_text: SAPHO syndrome (synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, osteitis)
SAPHO syndrome (synovitis, acne, pustulo.description: An autoinflammatory osteoarticular syndrome characterized by sterile osteitis/hyperostosis, often involving the anterior chest wall, together with severe acne, pustulosis, or other inflammatory skin disease. Pulmonary inflammatory involvement and bronchiectasis are uncommon but reported.

Cystic fibrosis.description: An inherited CFTR-related disorder causing thick airway secretions, recurrent respiratory infection, upper-lobe-predominant bronchiectasis, nutritional problems, and possible liver disease.

Primary immunodeficiency with recurrent.normalized_text: Primary immunodeficiency with recurrent sinopulmonary infection (such as common variable immunodeficiency)
Primary immunodeficiency with recurrent.description: Antibody or combined immune deficiencies can cause recurrent bacterial respiratory infections leading to chronic bronchiectasis, systemic inflammation, fatigue, and weight loss.

Primary ciliary dyskinesia.description: A genetic disorder of impaired mucociliary clearance that causes recurrent airway infection and bronchiectasis, often beginning in childhood and frequently associated with chronic sinus or ear disease.

Pulmonary tuberculosis with postinfectio.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can produce constitutional symptoms and chronic upper-lung disease; longstanding infection can lead to bronchiectasis and fibrotic or cavitary lung destruction.

Invasive breast carcinoma of no special.normalized_text: Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (NST), grade 2
Invasive breast carcinoma of no special.description: The most common form of invasive breast cancer, arising from breast ducts and infiltrating surrounding breast tissue. This diagnosis was confirmed on biopsy.

Multifocal or multicentric invasive brea.normalized_text: Multifocal or multicentric invasive breast carcinoma
Multifocal or multicentric invasive brea.description: Breast cancer involving more than one distinct tumor focus in the same breast, which may be in the same quadrant or in different quadrants. MRI is particularly useful for defining the full extent of disease.

Invasive ductal carcinoma with possible.normalized_text: Invasive ductal carcinoma with possible internal mammary nodal metastasis
Invasive ductal carcinoma with possible.description: Invasive breast carcinoma can spread to regional lymph nodes, including axillary and internal mammary nodes. A suspicious enhancing parasternal/internal mammary focus on MRI can represent nodal involvement.

Breast fibroadenoma.description: A common benign fibroepithelial breast tumor that often presents as a palpable breast lump, particularly in younger women. It is usually circumscribed and noninvasive on imaging and pathology.

Phyllodes tumor.description: A fibroepithelial breast neoplasm that can be benign, borderline, or malignant and often presents as a rapidly enlarging palpable mass. It can be difficult to distinguish from fibroadenoma without tissue diagnosis.

Hydroxychloroquine retinopathy (bull's-e.description: A toxic maculopathy caused by cumulative hydroxychloroquine exposure, characterized by parafoveal photoreceptor and retinal pigment epithelium damage, often producing bilateral bull's-eye macular changes and paracentral ring scotomas.

Cone-rod dystrophy.description: An inherited retinal degeneration in which cone photoreceptors are affected first, causing reduced central vision, impaired color discrimination, photophobia, and sometimes bull's-eye macular atrophy; rod dysfunction may develop later.

Autoimmune retinopathy.description: A rare immune-mediated retinal disorder, sometimes associated with systemic autoimmune disease or malignancy, that causes progressive photoreceptor dysfunction with visual-field loss, photopsias, reduced color vision, and decreased visual acuity.

Age-related macular degeneration, partic.normalized_text: Age-related macular degeneration, particularly geographic atrophy
Age-related macular degeneration, partic.description: A degenerative macular disease in older adults involving retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptor loss, causing progressive central visual impairment and, in advanced atrophic disease, central scotomas.

Macular dystrophy, such as Stargardt-lik.normalized_text: Macular dystrophy, such as Stargardt-like or pattern dystrophy
Macular dystrophy, such as Stargardt-lik.description: A group of inherited disorders affecting the macula and retinal pigment epithelium that can cause bilateral reduction in central vision, color vision abnormalities, and pigmentary macular changes that may occasionally resemble a bull's-eye lesion.

Primary extranodal classic Hodgkin lymph.normalized_text: Primary extranodal classic Hodgkin lymphoma of the nasopharynx
Primary extranodal classic Hodgkin lymph.description: A rare localized form of classic Hodgkin lymphoma arising in nasopharyngeal lymphoid tissue, characterized by scattered Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells in an inflammatory background; these cells commonly express CD30 and CD15.

Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia of the nas.normalized_text: Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia of the nasopharynx
Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia of the nas.description: A benign enlargement of lymphoid tissue due to chronic inflammation, infection, irritation, or immune stimulation; it can resemble lymphoma on small biopsy specimens.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from the nasopharyngeal mucosa, often presenting with nasal obstruction, ear symptoms, or cervical lymph-node metastases; smoking is a risk factor for head and neck malignancies.

Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal typ.description: An aggressive Epstein-Barr virus-associated lymphoma that commonly involves the nasal cavity or nasopharynx and may cause obstructive, destructive, or ulcerative sinonasal disease.

Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin l.description: A distinct, usually indolent Hodgkin lymphoma composed of nodular B-cell-rich infiltrates containing LP cells; it more often presents with peripheral lymph-node enlargement than extranodal disease.

Ipilimumab-induced immune checkpoint inh.description: An immune-mediated inflammation of the heart muscle caused by ipilimumab, a CTLA-4 immune checkpoint inhibitor. It can produce chest pain, ECG abnormalities, troponin elevation, arrhythmias, and reduced cardiac function despite nonobstructive coronary arteries.

Acute myopericarditis.description: Inflammation involving the myocardium and sometimes the pericardium, which may be infectious, autoimmune, malignant-associated, or medication-induced. It can mimic acute myocardial infarction with chest pain, ST elevation, and elevated troponin.

Acute coronary syndrome with nonobstruct.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome with nonobstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA)
Acute coronary syndrome with nonobstruct.description: Myocardial infarction or ischemic myocardial injury with elevated troponin and ischemic ECG changes but without obstructive epicardial coronary artery disease. Possible mechanisms include coronary vasospasm, microvascular dysfunction, embolism, or transient plaque disruption.

Stress-induced cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo.normalized_text: Stress-induced cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo syndrome), possibly with dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction
Stress-induced cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo.description: A transient stress-related myocardial dysfunction, most often affecting older women, that can cause chest pain, dyspnea, ST elevation, modest troponin elevation, and dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction in some cases. Severe illness, cancer, and immunotherapy-related stress can act as triggers.

Cardiac metastasis from melanoma.description: Melanoma can metastasize to the heart, including the myocardium or pericardium, and may cause chest pain, dyspnea, arrhythmia, myocardial injury, or inflammatory imaging abnormalities. PET avidity can identify metabolically active metastatic disease.

Syphilitic proctitis (anorectal syphilis.description: Rectal involvement by Treponema pallidum, usually sexually acquired. It can cause proctitis, anal fissures, ulcers, bleeding, and a plasma-cell-rich inflammatory infiltrate; spirochetes may be demonstrated by immunohistochemical staining.

Lymphogranuloma venereum proctitis.description: A sexually transmitted infection caused by invasive Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3. In men who have sex with men, it can cause painful inflammatory proctitis, rectal bleeding, ulceration, and anorectal symptoms that can mimic inflammatory bowel disease.

Herpes simplex virus proctitis.description: HSV-1 or HSV-2 infection of the rectum and anus, commonly sexually acquired, which may produce severe anorectal pain, painful defecation, ulcers, bleeding, and distal proctitis.

Ulcerative proctitis (ulcerative colitis.normalized_text: Ulcerative proctitis (ulcerative colitis limited to the rectum)
Ulcerative proctitis (ulcerative colitis.description: A form of ulcerative colitis confined to the rectum, causing continuous mucosal inflammation, rectal bleeding, urgency, tenesmus, and sometimes painful defecation.

Crohn disease with perianal involvement.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can involve any gastrointestinal segment and may cause perianal fissures, skin tags, rectal inflammation, pain, bleeding, fistulas, and abscesses.

Asymptomatic microscopic hematuria.description: Presence of a small amount of blood in urine detected on dipstick or microscopy without visible blood or urinary symptoms; it may be transient or reflect an underlying urinary tract condition.

Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder.description: Cancer arising from the lining of the bladder, often presenting with painless microscopic or visible hematuria, especially in older adults.

Renal cell carcinoma.description: A kidney cancer that can cause microscopic or gross hematuria and is sometimes discovered incidentally before causing pain or systemic symptoms.

Nephrolithiasis (kidney or ureteral ston.description: Formation of urinary tract stones that can irritate the lining of the kidney or ureter and cause microscopic hematuria.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia.description: Noncancerous enlargement of the prostate that commonly affects older men and can occasionally be associated with microscopic hematuria from prostatic bleeding.

Congenital dysfibrinogenemia.description: An inherited qualitative fibrinogen disorder in which fibrinogen antigen is present at a normal level but the fibrinogen molecule functions poorly, causing impaired clot formation and prolonged coagulation tests.

Congenital hypodysfibrinogenemia.description: An inherited fibrinogen disorder characterized by both reduced functional fibrinogen activity and an abnormal fibrinogen molecule; antigen levels may be normal or variably reduced depending on the mutation.

Congenital afibrinogenemia.description: A severe inherited deficiency of fibrinogen, usually caused by biallelic fibrinogen-gene variants, resulting in absent or extremely low fibrinogen and potentially severe bleeding from birth.

Acquired dysfibrinogenemia due to liver.normalized_text: Acquired dysfibrinogenemia due to liver disease or a paraprotein disorder
Acquired dysfibrinogenemia due to liver.description: An acquired qualitative fibrinogen abnormality that can occur with significant liver disease, plasma-cell disorders, or other systemic illnesses and may cause impaired fibrinogen function with prolonged clotting times.

Factor XIII deficiency.description: A rare inherited coagulation disorder caused by deficiency of factor XIII, which stabilizes fibrin clots. It can produce severe bleeding from birth, including umbilical stump bleeding and delayed postoperative bleeding.

diagnoses.name: Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the lung
diagnoses.normalized_text: Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the lung

Pulmonary pleomorphic carcinoma (sarcoma.normalized_text: Pulmonary pleomorphic carcinoma (sarcomatoid non-small-cell lung carcinoma)
Pulmonary pleomorphic carcinoma (sarcoma.description: A rare, aggressive non-small-cell lung cancer characterized by poorly differentiated epithelial tumor cells with pleomorphic and/or giant-cell features. It commonly occurs in older heavy smokers and may form a large central lung or mediastinal mass.

Small-cell lung carcinoma.description: An aggressive neuroendocrine lung cancer strongly associated with cigarette smoking. It often arises centrally, spreads early to mediastinal lymph nodes, and frequently causes superior vena cava syndrome.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.normalized_text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.description: A non-small-cell lung cancer closely linked to tobacco smoking. It commonly arises in the central bronchi, can cause endobronchial obstruction and lung collapse, and may invade mediastinal structures.

Lung adenocarcinoma.description: The most common type of non-small-cell lung cancer. Although often peripheral, advanced adenocarcinoma may involve mediastinal lymph nodes or directly invade mediastinal structures, producing airway and superior vena cava obstruction.

Primary mediastinal lymphoma.description: Lymphoma involving mediastinal lymph nodes or thymic-region lymphoid tissue can create a bulky mediastinal mass and cause superior vena cava syndrome through compression of the vena cava and adjacent airways.

BCL11B-related severe combined immunodef.description: A rare developmental immunodeficiency caused by pathogenic BCL11B variants. BCL11B is essential for T-cell development and also affects neurodevelopment, craniofacial structures, skin, teeth, and skeletal development.

22q11.2 deletion syndrome with complete.normalized_text: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome with complete DiGeorge syndrome
22q11.2 deletion syndrome with complete.description: A chromosomal disorder that can cause thymic aplasia or severe thymic hypoplasia, resulting in profound T-cell deficiency. It is commonly associated with congenital heart disease, facial differences, and developmental abnormalities.

CHARGE syndrome with thymic hypoplasia o.normalized_text: CHARGE syndrome with thymic hypoplasia or aplasia
CHARGE syndrome with thymic hypoplasia o.description: A multisystem developmental disorder usually caused by CHD7 variants. Some affected infants have severe T-cell lymphopenia due to thymic hypoplasia or aplasia, along with heart defects, hypotonia, and central nervous system abnormalities.

PAX1-related otofaciocervical syndrome t.normalized_text: PAX1-related otofaciocervical syndrome type 2 with severe T-cell immunodeficiency
PAX1-related otofaciocervical syndrome t.description: A rare autosomal-recessive developmental syndrome caused by PAX1 deficiency. It can produce absent or poorly developed thymic tissue with severe T-cell immunodeficiency, along with facial, skeletal, and sometimes cardiac abnormalities.

RAG1/RAG2-associated severe combined imm.normalized_text: RAG1/RAG2-associated severe combined immunodeficiency or Omenn syndrome
RAG1/RAG2-associated severe combined imm.description: Defects in RAG1 or RAG2 impair V(D)J recombination and can cause severe combined immunodeficiency with absent TRECs and profound T-cell lymphopenia. Hypomorphic variants may cause Omenn syndrome, characterized by inflammatory erythroderma and immune dysregulation.

Primary rectal extranodal marginal zone.normalized_text: Primary rectal extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma)
Primary rectal extranodal marginal zone.description: An indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising from mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. In the rectum it can produce submucosal nodules, erosions, or ulcerated lesions; biopsy commonly shows small lymphoid-cell infiltration with lymphoepithelial lesions and B-cell-marker positivity.

Rectal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the rectum that often causes altered bowel habits, rectal bleeding, mucus production, obstructive symptoms, and tenesmus.

Ulcerative proctitis or ulcerative colit.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease causing continuous mucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum. Rectal-predominant disease can cause urgency, tenesmus, mucus, and bleeding.

Intestinal or rectal tuberculosis.description: Gastrointestinal infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis that may produce ulceration, strictures, mass-like lesions, abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, and constitutional symptoms. Prior pulmonary tuberculosis increases clinical consideration, although rectal involvement is uncommon.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the rec.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the rectum
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the rec.description: An aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that can involve the gastrointestinal tract as an ulcerated or mass-like lesion and may cause tenesmus, bleeding, pain, or obstruction.

Acute left iliofemoral deep vein thrombo.normalized_text: Acute left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
Acute left iliofemoral deep vein thrombo.description: A blood clot in the deep veins of the left pelvis and leg, causing impaired venous drainage and risk of embolization to the lungs.

Acute pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries by embolized thrombus, usually originating from a lower-extremity or pelvic DVT; the chest CT image is consistent with pulmonary arterial filling defects.

May-Thurner syndrome (left iliac vein co.normalized_text: May-Thurner syndrome (left iliac vein compression syndrome) with thrombosis
May-Thurner syndrome (left iliac vein co.description: Compression of the left common iliac vein by the overlying right common iliac artery, predisposing young women to extensive left-sided iliofemoral DVT and pulmonary embolism; the pelvic imaging is suggestive of left iliac venous thrombosis.

Cellulitis of the left lower extremity.normalized_text: Cellulitis of the left lower extremity
Cellulitis of the left lower extremity.description: A bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue that commonly causes a warm, red, swollen, painful limb.

Exercise-related muscle strain or delaye.normalized_text: Exercise-related muscle strain or delayed-onset muscle soreness
Exercise-related muscle strain or delaye.description: Muscle injury or soreness after strenuous exercise, typically causing localized pain and tenderness after activity.

X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (.normalized_text: X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (CGD, CYBB-related NADPH oxidase deficiency)
X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (.description: A primary immunodeficiency in which neutrophils cannot generate an effective oxidative burst to kill certain bacteria and fungi. Abnormal dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry and a CYBB mutation pattern support this diagnosis.

Severe congenital neutropenia.description: An inherited disorder characterized by persistently very low neutrophil counts, causing early recurrent bacterial infections, oral ulcers and pneumonia.

Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1.description: A primary immunodeficiency caused by defective leukocyte adhesion and migration into tissues, leading to recurrent serious bacterial infections and impaired wound healing.

Hyper-IgE syndrome.description: A primary immunodeficiency, commonly involving impaired STAT3 signaling, characterized by recurrent pneumonias, eczema, skin abscesses, elevated IgE and eosinophilia.

Primary ciliary dyskinesia.description: An inherited mucociliary-clearance disorder causing chronic wet cough, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, bronchiectasis and sometimes situs abnormalities.

Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: A primary cancer of the bile ducts within the liver, typically forming infiltrative adenocarcinoma glands in dense fibrous stroma and often associated with elevated CA 19-9.

Metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcin.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the pancreas that commonly produces CA 19-9 and can spread to the liver, where it appears as multiple metastatic lesions with gland-forming adenocarcinoma histology.

Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma.description: Cancer of the colon or rectum that frequently metastasizes to the liver and may show infiltrating malignant glands with fibrotic stroma. CA 19-9 can be elevated in some cases, although CEA is more commonly elevated.

Metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma.description: A stomach cancer that can produce CA 19-9 and spread to the liver. Histology often shows infiltrating adenocarcinoma, sometimes with prominent stromal fibrosis.

Metastatic mucinous ovarian carcinoma.description: A mucin-producing epithelial ovarian malignancy that can elevate CA 19-9 and may metastasize to the liver or liver capsule. It may present with abdominal pain and can show glandular adenocarcinoma histology.

Primary leiomyosarcoma of the parotid gl.normalized_text: Primary leiomyosarcoma of the parotid gland
Primary leiomyosarcoma of the parotid gl.description: A rare malignant smooth-muscle tumor arising in or near the parotid gland, typically composed of intersecting fascicles of spindle cells and often showing smooth-muscle immunohistochemical marker expression.

Parotid gland schwannoma.description: A benign peripheral nerve-sheath tumor that may arise from branches of the facial nerve or adjacent sensory nerves and can present as a slow-growing parotid-region mass.

Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland.normalized_text: Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland
Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland.description: The most common benign salivary-gland tumor, usually presenting as a painless, slowly growing, mobile parotid mass with mixed epithelial and myoepithelial elements.

Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the parotid.normalized_text: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the parotid gland
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the parotid.description: A malignant salivary-gland tumor composed of mucous, epidermoid, and intermediate cells; it may cause a painful enlarging parotid mass and, in advanced cases, facial nerve dysfunction or nodal disease.

Myofibrosarcoma of the parotid region.description: A rare malignant spindle-cell tumor showing myofibroblastic differentiation, often with infiltrative fascicular growth and potential local recurrence or metastasis.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type III (Sanfilip.normalized_text: Mucopolysaccharidosis type III (Sanfilippo syndrome), especially type A or B
Mucopolysaccharidosis type III (Sanfilip.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by impaired degradation of heparan sulfate. It produces progressive neurodevelopmental regression, behavioral/cognitive deterioration, coarse facial features, hearing impairment, and white-matter abnormalities on brain MRI.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type II (Hunter sy.description: A lysosomal disorder due to iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency causing dermatan- and heparan-sulfate accumulation. Severe forms cause developmental delay or regression, coarse facies, macroglossia, hearing loss, joint and skeletal disease, and progressive neurologic involvement.

GM1 gangliosidosis type II (late-infanti.normalized_text: GM1 gangliosidosis type II (late-infantile GM1 gangliosidosis)
GM1 gangliosidosis type II (late-infanti.description: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by beta-galactosidase deficiency, leading to GM1 ganglioside accumulation in the brain and other tissues. Late-infantile disease commonly causes developmental regression, dystonia or spasticity, hearing impairment, coarse features, and progressive white-matter involvement.

Alpha-mannosidosis.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-mannosidase deficiency. It can cause developmental delay, progressive intellectual disability, hearing loss, coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, immune dysfunction, ataxia, and later spasticity.

Mucolipidosis type II/III (GNPTAB-relate.description: A lysosomal trafficking disorder in which multiple lysosomal enzymes fail to reach lysosomes, causing accumulation of storage material. It may produce coarse facies, gingival or tongue enlargement, developmental impairment, hearing loss, skeletal abnormalities, and progressive motor disability.

diagnoses.name: Bilateral vocal cord paralysis
diagnoses.icd11_title: Paralysis of vocal cords or larynx[Bilateral]

Bilateral vocal fold paralysis.description: Impaired movement of both vocal folds, often leaving them near the midline and producing a critically narrowed glottic airway. In neonates it may be congenital or associated with hypoxic-ischemic injury.

Unilateral vocal fold paralysis.description: Loss of movement of one vocal fold due to recurrent laryngeal nerve or central neurologic dysfunction. It usually causes a weak cry, hoarseness, aspiration, or milder stridor than bilateral paralysis.

Post-intubation posterior glottic stenos.description: Scarring or fixation of the posterior glottis after endotracheal intubation, causing reduced vocal-fold abduction and a narrow airway that can mimic bilateral vocal fold paralysis.

Post-extubation laryngeal edema.description: Swelling of the laryngeal mucosa caused by endotracheal tube irritation or traumatic intubation, producing temporary narrowing of the glottic or subglottic airway.

Laryngomalacia.description: The most common congenital cause of neonatal stridor, caused by dynamic collapse of supraglottic tissues during inspiration.

Pyriform sinus fistula (fourth branchial.normalized_text: Pyriform sinus fistula (fourth branchial pouch anomaly)
Pyriform sinus fistula (fourth branchial.description: A congenital tract arising from the apex of the pyriform sinus that commonly presents on the left side with recurrent neck infections or abscesses, often near the thyroid gland.

Third branchial cleft sinus or fistula.normalized_text: Third branchial cleft sinus or fistula
Third branchial cleft sinus or fistula.description: A rare congenital branchial anomaly that can form a sinus tract in the lower lateral neck and cause repeated infections or abscess formation.

Infected second branchial cleft cyst.description: A congenital cystic neck lesion that typically occurs along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and may become infected, causing painful swelling and fever.

Acute suppurative thyroiditis.description: A bacterial infection of the thyroid gland, often associated with an underlying pyriform sinus fistula in younger patients and usually involving the left thyroid lobe.

Recurrent cervical deep neck abscess or.normalized_text: Recurrent cervical deep neck abscess or suppurative cervical lymphadenitis
Recurrent cervical deep neck abscess or.description: A bacterial infection of cervical lymph nodes or deep neck spaces causing localized swelling, fever, and possible abscess formation; recurrent disease should prompt evaluation for an underlying congenital tract.

Drug-induced serum sickness-like reactio.description: A delayed immune-mediated reaction to a medication or supplement, characterized by urticarial eruptions, fever, joint symptoms, and sometimes angioedema; complement levels are often normal in serum sickness-like reactions.

Normocomplementemic urticarial vasculiti.description: A small-vessel cutaneous vasculitis presenting with urticarial lesions that are painful or burning, persist for more than 24 hours, and may resolve with bruising or hyperpigmentation. Systemic symptoms such as fever, arthralgia, myalgia, and angioedema can occur.

Acute drug-induced urticaria with angioe.description: An acute hypersensitivity reaction causing transient itchy wheals and localized swelling, often triggered by medications, supplements, foods, or infections.

DRESS syndrome (drug reaction with eosin.normalized_text: DRESS syndrome (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms)
DRESS syndrome (drug reaction with eosin.description: A severe delayed drug hypersensitivity syndrome, usually occurring 2 to 8 weeks after exposure, with fever, widespread rash, facial edema, hematologic abnormalities, and internal-organ involvement.

Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis.description: A systemic immune-complex vasculitis with recurrent urticarial lesions lasting more than 24 hours, often accompanied by low complement levels, arthralgia, angioedema, and potential renal, pulmonary, or ocular disease.

Rapunzel syndrome.description: A large gastric trichobezoar (hair ball) with a tail extending beyond the stomach into the small intestine, potentially causing intermittent gastric outlet or intestinal obstruction. The imaging appearance is highly characteristic.

Gastric trichobezoar.description: An accumulation of swallowed hair in the stomach that forms a dense, matted mass. It can cause gastric outlet obstruction, mucosal injury, anemia, and abdominal pain; this may be confined to the stomach or represent the gastric component of Rapunzel syndrome.

Small-bowel obstruction due to bezoar.description: Mechanical obstruction of the small intestine caused by a bezoar or a tail of a gastric trichobezoar. Obstruction may be intermittent initially and progress to more frequent pain and vomiting.

Peptic ulcer disease or erosive gastriti.normalized_text: Peptic ulcer disease or erosive gastritis
Peptic ulcer disease or erosive gastriti.description: Inflammation or ulceration of the stomach or duodenum can cause epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and iron-deficiency anemia from chronic occult blood loss.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Inflammation of the pancreas that typically produces severe persistent epigastric pain with nausea and vomiting, often radiating to the back.

Disseminated tuberculosis with intestina.description: Hematogenous Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection involving the lungs, ileum, and kidney, with ulcerative ileal disease causing perforation and tuberculous peritonitis. Histology showing granulomatous inflammation and acid-fast bacilli strongly supports this diagnosis.

Miliary tuberculosis.description: A disseminated form of tuberculosis caused by hematogenous spread, classically producing innumerable tiny nodules in the lungs and potentially involving the gastrointestinal tract, kidneys, and other organs.

Disseminated nontuberculous mycobacteria.description: Systemic infection with environmental mycobacteria, such as Mycobacterium avium complex, which can cause pulmonary disease and disseminated granulomatous infection, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum that may produce pulmonary nodules and granulomatous disease, with gastrointestinal ulceration in disseminated cases.

Crohn disease with intestinal perforatio.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that commonly affects the terminal ileum and can cause deep ulcers, transmural inflammation, strictures, fistulas, and bowel perforation; noncaseating granulomas may be present.

Vasovagal syncope (cardioinhibitory neur.description: A reflex-mediated autonomic event causing hypotension and sometimes marked sinus bradycardia or transient sinus arrest, often triggered by pain, nausea, vomiting, emotional stress, or medical procedures.

Acute myopericarditis.description: Inflammation of the myocardium and/or pericardium, commonly following a viral illness, which can cause chest pain, electrocardiographic ST-segment abnormalities, arrhythmias, and occasionally hemodynamic instability.

Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.description: Acute coronary artery obstruction causing myocardial ischemia and injury, classically presenting with central chest pressure, autonomic symptoms, and ST-segment elevation in anterior precordial ECG leads.

Coronary vasospasm (vasospastic or Prinz.description: Transient spasm of a coronary artery causing episodic myocardial ischemia, often with transient ST-segment elevation and chest pain that can resolve spontaneously.

Acute gastroenteritis with nausea-induce.normalized_text: Acute gastroenteritis with nausea-induced vagal reaction
Acute gastroenteritis with nausea-induce.description: An acute gastrointestinal viral illness can cause epigastric pain, vomiting, and nausea; gastrointestinal distress can trigger a strong vagal reflex with hypotension and transient bradycardia or sinus arrest.

Spontaneous pneumomediastinum (Hamman sy.description: Free air within the mediastinum occurring without trauma or an invasive procedure, often caused by alveolar rupture with air tracking into the mediastinum and neck tissues.

Esophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndro.description: A full-thickness tear of the esophagus that can release air and gastrointestinal contents into the mediastinum, causing pneumomediastinum and potentially severe mediastinitis.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax.description: Accumulation of air in the pleural space without trauma, most often in young adults, producing sudden pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath.

Tracheobronchial injury with air leak.description: A tear in the trachea or major bronchi can allow air to enter the mediastinum and subcutaneous tissues, typically after major blunt trauma, intubation, or airway procedures.

Acute pericarditis.description: Inflammation of the pericardial sac, commonly viral or idiopathic, causing sharp chest pain that often varies with position or breathing and may be associated with a pericardial friction rub.

Lyme disease (erythema migrans).description: Early localized infection with Borrelia bacteria transmitted by Ixodes ticks. Erythema migrans is an enlarging red patch or annular rash, often with central clearing, and may occur without a recalled tick bite.

Tinea corporis (ringworm).description: A superficial dermatophyte fungal infection of the skin that commonly causes an itchy, enlarging ring-shaped rash with a more active red edge and relative central clearing.

Erythema annulare centrifugum.description: A reactive inflammatory skin eruption characterized by slowly expanding annular red patches or plaques, sometimes triggered by infections, medications, fungal disease, or an unidentified cause.

Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis.description: Inflammation of the skin caused by contact with an allergen or irritant, such as clothing materials, topical products, plants, adhesives, or occupational exposures.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign inflammatory skin condition that produces ring-shaped papules or plaques, usually without scale. It may occur on the hands and feet but can also appear on the trunk.

Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina) w.normalized_text: Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina) with myocardial injury
Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina) w.description: Transient coronary artery spasm causing episodic myocardial ischemia, often occurring at rest in the early morning and strongly associated with smoking. Spasm can cause ECG ischemic changes and a small troponin rise despite nonobstructive coronary arteries between episodes.

Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.description: Acute myocardial infarction caused by myocardial ischemia and necrosis, typically identified by elevated cardiac troponin with ischemic chest symptoms and/or ECG changes. It may result from plaque disruption, coronary spasm, embolism, or supply-demand imbalance.

Myocardial infarction with nonobstructiv.normalized_text: Myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA)
Myocardial infarction with nonobstructiv.description: A working diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction in which coronary angiography does not show an obstructive epicardial coronary lesion. Potential mechanisms include coronary vasospasm, plaque erosion or rupture, coronary embolism, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, and microvascular dysfunction.

Wellens syndrome (critical proximal left.normalized_text: Wellens syndrome (critical proximal left anterior descending coronary artery ischemia pattern)
Wellens syndrome (critical proximal left.description: An ECG syndrome characterized by biphasic or deeply inverted T waves in the anterior precordial leads, classically indicating critical proximal left anterior descending artery stenosis and high risk of anterior myocardial infarction. Similar ECG changes can also occur with coronary spasm as pseudo-Wellens syndrome.

Type 2 myocardial infarction due to oxyg.normalized_text: Type 2 myocardial infarction due to oxygen supply-demand mismatch from iron-deficiency anemia
Type 2 myocardial infarction due to oxyg.description: Myocardial injury or infarction caused by inadequate myocardial oxygen supply relative to demand rather than acute coronary thrombosis. Significant anemia can contribute to ischemic chest pain and troponin elevation, particularly when another trigger such as coronary vasospasm is present.

Acetazolamide embryopathy.description: A pattern of congenital malformations potentially associated with fetal exposure to acetazolamide, including limb-reduction defects, digital anomalies, and occasionally craniofacial or dental developmental abnormalities.

Ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-clefti.description: A genetic disorder characterized by split hand/foot malformations, missing teeth or abnormal tooth enamel, ectodermal abnormalities, and frequently cleft lip and/or palate.

Nonsyndromic split-hand/foot malformatio.description: A congenital limb-malformation phenotype involving central digital absence or clefting of the hands and feet, sometimes accompanied by hypodontia or oligodontia without the ectodermal and clefting features of EEC syndrome.

Orofacial-digital syndrome.description: A heterogeneous group of genetic disorders causing digital malformations and dental abnormalities, often associated with oral frenula, tongue lobulation, cleft palate, facial changes, and sometimes intellectual or renal abnormalities.

Thalidomide-like limb reduction embryopa.description: A teratogenic embryopathy characterized by congenital limb-reduction defects, including absent or malformed digits and limbs; dental developmental defects can occur in some fetal drug-exposure syndromes.

Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.description: An intermittent supraventricular arrhythmia characterized by uncoordinated atrial electrical activity and an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm; episodes terminate spontaneously.

Alcohol-triggered paroxysmal atrial fibr.normalized_text: Alcohol-triggered paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (holiday heart syndrome)
Alcohol-triggered paroxysmal atrial fibr.description: Atrial fibrillation precipitated by acute alcohol intake, often occurring in people without severe structural heart disease but more likely in those with cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension.

Frequent premature atrial contractions (.description: Early atrial beats arising outside the sinus node that can cause skipped beats, fluttering, or palpitations and may trigger atrial fibrillation.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia.description: A sudden-onset, sudden-termination fast rhythm originating above the ventricles, commonly causing episodic palpitations and dyspnea.

Atrial flutter.description: A macroreentrant atrial tachyarrhythmia that can produce palpitations, dyspnea, and rapid ventricular rates; it may coexist with or alternate with atrial fibrillation.

Primary colorectal extranodal NK/T-cell.normalized_text: Primary colorectal extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type
Primary colorectal extranodal NK/T-cell.description: An aggressive Epstein-Barr virus-associated cytotoxic lymphoid malignancy that can rarely arise in the colon and produce destructive ulcerative colitis-like lesions.

Monomorphic epitheliotropic intestinal T.description: A rare aggressive intestinal T-cell lymphoma, often composed of monomorphic cytotoxic lymphocytes, which may cause multifocal ulceration, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss.

Ulcerative colitis.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon, causing congestion, edema, loss of vascular pattern, friability, and ulceration.

Crohn disease involving the colon.description: A chronic transmural inflammatory bowel disease that can cause discontinuous colonic inflammation, deep irregular ulcers, diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and fistulizing complications.

Intestinal amebiasis (amebic colitis).description: Colonic infection with Entamoeba histolytica that may mimic inflammatory bowel disease or malignancy and can produce irregular, undermined, exudative colonic ulcers with diarrhea and weight loss.

Ruptured pulmonary hydatid cyst (echinoc.normalized_text: Ruptured pulmonary hydatid cyst (echinococcal cyst) with hydropneumothorax
Ruptured pulmonary hydatid cyst (echinoc.description: A parasitic Echinococcus cyst in the lung that ruptures into a bronchus or pleural space, producing an air-fluid level and detached internal membranes on chest radiography.

Left-sided hydropneumothorax.description: The simultaneous presence of air and fluid in the pleural space, which can compress the lung and cause acute respiratory symptoms.

Spontaneous pneumothorax.description: Air enters the pleural space without trauma, causing partial or complete lung collapse and acute pleuritic chest pain with dyspnea.

Pleural empyema with bronchopleural fist.description: Infected pleural fluid (empyema) may communicate with the bronchial tree, creating a hydropneumothorax and respiratory compromise.

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.normalized_text: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation or other cystic lung lesion complicated by infection or rupture
Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.description: A congenital cystic lesion of the lung can become infected, communicate with an airway, or rupture, potentially producing an air-fluid level and acute respiratory symptoms.

diagnoses.name: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver
diagnoses.normalized_text: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver

Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of.normalized_text: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver
Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of.description: A localized monoclonal plasma-cell tumor arising outside bone marrow; primary hepatic involvement is very rare and may occur without systemic multiple myeloma.

Multiple myeloma with hepatic plasmacyto.description: A systemic malignant plasma-cell disorder that usually involves bone marrow and may rarely produce focal or diffuse liver involvement.

Primary hepatic lymphoma.description: A lymphoma predominantly involving the liver, usually presenting as a solitary or multifocal hepatic mass; diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is a common subtype.

Hepatocellular carcinoma.description: A primary malignant tumor of hepatocytes, most commonly associated with chronic hepatitis B or C infection, cirrhosis, or other chronic liver disease.

Inflammatory pseudotumor of the liver.description: A rare benign inflammatory mass composed of inflammatory cells and fibrosis that can mimic a malignant liver tumor on imaging.

Chlamydia infection (Chlamydia trachomat.description: A common sexually transmitted bacterial infection that may cause cervicitis, vaginal discharge, bleeding, pelvic discomfort, or no symptoms.

Gonorrhea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae cervici.description: A sexually transmitted bacterial infection that can infect the cervix and cause increased or purulent vaginal discharge, urinary symptoms, pelvic pain, or no symptoms.

Trichomoniasis.description: A sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis, often producing vaginal discharge, irritation, odor, and discomfort with urination or sex.

Bacterial vaginosis.description: A disruption of normal vaginal bacteria that commonly causes thin vaginal discharge and a fishy odor; it is associated with sexual activity but is not usually classified as a conventional STI.

Vulvovaginal candidiasis (yeast infectio.description: An overgrowth of Candida yeast in the vagina that usually causes thick discharge, itching, burning, and vulvar irritation.

Vanishing lung syndrome (giant bullous e.description: A severe form of bullous emphysema characterized by giant air-filled bullae, usually in the upper lungs, that compress adjacent normal lung tissue. It is strongly associated with cigarette smoking and cannabis use.

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due t.normalized_text: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due to ruptured emphysematous bullae
Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due t.description: Air entering the pleural space because of rupture of a subpleural bleb or bulla, commonly occurring in people with smoking-related emphysema or giant bullous disease.

Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulm.normalized_text: Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with bullous emphysema
Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulm.description: Progressive airflow obstruction caused by smoking-related emphysematous destruction of alveoli, sometimes producing large bullae and markedly reduced lung function.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency-related e.description: An inherited cause of early-onset emphysema, often with lower-lobe-predominant panacinar emphysema and severe airflow obstruction, particularly in smokers.

Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome with cystic lung.normalized_text: Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome with cystic lung disease and spontaneous pneumothorax
Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome with cystic lung.description: A hereditary disorder causing multiple pulmonary cysts and recurrent spontaneous pneumothoraces; it may also be associated with skin fibrofolliculomas and renal tumors.

Sporadic Burkitt lymphoma.description: An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with a very high proliferation rate, often presenting as an abdominal mass and causing spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.description: The most common aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults; it may involve abdominal lymph nodes, bone marrow, kidneys, and other extranodal organs and can produce high LDH and tumor lysis.

Plasma cell myeloma (multiple myeloma),.normalized_text: Plasma cell myeloma (multiple myeloma), possibly aggressive/anaplastic with extramedullary disease
Plasma cell myeloma (multiple myeloma),.description: A malignant plasma-cell disorder producing a monoclonal immunoglobulin, classically causing hypercalcemia, renal dysfunction, anemia, and increased serum protein; aggressive variants may form masses and rarely cause tumor lysis.

High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and.normalized_text: High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangements (double-hit/triple-hit lymphoma)
High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and.description: A highly aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma, often occurring in older adults and presenting with bulky nodal or extranodal disease, marrow involvement, high LDH, and a substantial risk of spontaneous tumor lysis.

Lymphoblastic lymphoma/acute lymphoblast.normalized_text: Lymphoblastic lymphoma/acute lymphoblastic leukemia of B-cell lineage
Lymphoblastic lymphoma/acute lymphoblast.description: A precursor lymphoid malignancy that can involve bone marrow, lymph nodes, and abdominal organs; high tumor burden may cause cytopenias, elevated LDH, renal dysfunction, and tumor lysis syndrome.

Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneou.normalized_text: Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneous PAN) with mononeuritis multiplex
Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneou.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of small- to medium-sized muscular arteries in the skin, which can cause livedo-like rash, nodules or purpura and peripheral nerve ischemia. The biopsy appearance of inflamed, damaged vessel walls supports this diagnosis.

Systemic polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that may involve skin, peripheral nerves, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract and other organs. Mononeuritis multiplex and livedo reticularis are characteristic features.

ANCA-associated vasculitic neuropathy.description: Small-vessel vasculitis, such as microscopic polyangiitis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis, can cause ischemic nerve injury producing mononeuritis multiplex and may produce purpura or other skin lesions.

Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis, often associated with hepatitis C or autoimmune disease, that commonly causes palpable purpura, peripheral neuropathy, joint symptoms and renal disease.

Leprosy (Hansen disease), multibacillary.normalized_text: Leprosy (Hansen disease), multibacillary or borderline form
Leprosy (Hansen disease), multibacillary.description: A chronic infection with Mycobacterium leprae that can cause skin lesions and peripheral nerve involvement, especially affecting cooler superficial nerves such as the ulnar and common peroneal nerves.

Classical homocystinuria due to cystathi.normalized_text: Classical homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) deficiency
Classical homocystinuria due to cystathi.description: An autosomal-recessive disorder of methionine metabolism causing markedly elevated homocysteine and methionine. It produces a marfanoid skeletal phenotype, ectopia lentis, osteoporosis, and thromboembolic risk.

Marfan syndrome.description: An autosomal-dominant connective-tissue disorder, usually caused by FBN1 variants, characterized by skeletal overgrowth, chest wall deformity, scoliosis, lens dislocation, and aortic-root disease.

Loeys-Dietz syndrome.description: A hereditary connective-tissue disorder involving TGF-beta signaling that can cause arterial aneurysms, craniofacial abnormalities, scoliosis, pectus deformity, and cardiac findings.

Homocystinuria due to methylenetetrahydr.normalized_text: Homocystinuria due to methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) deficiency
Homocystinuria due to methylenetetrahydr.description: An inherited remethylation disorder that elevates homocysteine because conversion of homocysteine to methionine is impaired; it commonly causes neurologic and thrombotic disease.

Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or anoth.normalized_text: Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or another heritable Ehlers-Danlos connective-tissue disorder
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or anoth.description: A group of inherited collagen disorders characterized by tissue fragility, joint hypermobility or instability, skin findings, and variable skeletal or vascular complications.

Pontine cavernous malformation with acut.normalized_text: Pontine cavernous malformation with acute hemorrhage
Pontine cavernous malformation with acut.description: A cavernous malformation is a cluster of fragile, abnormal small blood vessels that can bleed repeatedly. In the pons, an acute hemorrhage can cause crossed motor, sensory, cerebellar, and ocular symptoms and may obstruct cerebrospinal-fluid flow.

Primary pontine intracerebral hemorrhage.description: Bleeding within the pons, often related to hypertension or an underlying vascular lesion, produces acute or subacute brainstem dysfunction with weakness, sensory deficits, ataxia, and ocular movement symptoms.

Vertebral artery dissection with posteri.normalized_text: Vertebral artery dissection with posterior-circulation ischemic stroke
Vertebral artery dissection with posteri.description: A tear in the vertebral artery wall can occur spontaneously in young adults and may cause posterior-circulation stroke affecting the brainstem or cerebellum. Neck pain or headache commonly precedes neurological deficits.

Brainstem glioma or other intrinsic pont.normalized_text: Brainstem glioma or other intrinsic pontine tumor
Brainstem glioma or other intrinsic pont.description: An intrinsic tumor of the pons can progressively disrupt corticospinal, sensory, cerebellar, and ocular motor pathways and can cause obstructive hydrocephalus if it enlarges.

Multiple sclerosis with a brainstem demy.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis with a brainstem demyelinating lesion
Multiple sclerosis with a brainstem demy.description: Multiple sclerosis is an immune-mediated demyelinating disease that can involve the pons and cerebellar pathways, causing sensory symptoms, weakness, diplopia, tremor, and ataxia in young adults.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: Systemic infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, often acquired by inhaling fungal spores. Disseminated disease can involve the reticuloendothelial system, bone marrow, gastrointestinal tract, lymph nodes, and occasionally the genitourinary tract. The marrow images are compatible with intracellular small yeasts within macrophages.

Visceral leishmaniasis.description: A systemic protozoal infection caused by Leishmania species and transmitted by sandflies. It may cause fever, constitutional symptoms, gastrointestinal complaints, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and macrophages containing intracellular amastigotes in bone marrow.

Acute bacterial prostatitis.description: Acute infection and inflammation of the prostate, usually due to enteric gram-negative bacteria such as Escherichia coli. It can cause fever, systemic illness, dysuria, pelvic or perineal pain, low back pain, and referred pain to the groin or scrotum.

Acute pyelonephritis or complicated urin.normalized_text: Acute pyelonephritis or complicated urinary tract infection
Acute pyelonephritis or complicated urin.description: A bacterial infection of the kidney and upper urinary tract that commonly produces fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, dysuria, and flank or back pain. Severe infection may cause sepsis and pelvic inflammatory changes.

Disseminated tuberculosis.description: Systemic infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can involve lymph nodes, bone marrow, abdomen, spine, and genitourinary organs. Genitourinary tuberculosis may cause dysuria, pelvic pain, and scrotal involvement, although disseminated disease is usually more subacute or chronic.

Medication-related osteonecrosis of the.normalized_text: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ), likely bisphosphonate- or denosumab-associated
Medication-related osteonecrosis of the.description: Progressive necrosis of jaw bone with persistent exposed bone, often occurring in patients receiving antiresorptive therapy for metastatic bone disease. It can affect reconstructed vascularized bone flaps as well as native jawbone.

Chronic osteomyelitis of the reconstruct.normalized_text: Chronic osteomyelitis of the reconstructed mandible
Chronic osteomyelitis of the reconstruct.description: Chronic infection and inflammation of bone that may cause bone destruction, sequestration, mucosal inflammation, and exposed necrotic bone, particularly after major mandibular surgery and reconstruction.

Recurrent or progressive metastatic clea.normalized_text: Recurrent or progressive metastatic clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma involving the mandibular reconstruction
Recurrent or progressive metastatic clea.description: Clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma can metastasize to bone and may cause destructive osteolytic lesions in the mandible. Local tumor recurrence or tumor involvement of a graft can result in bony destruction and mucosal breakdown.

Osteoradionecrosis of the mandible.description: Osteoradionecrosis is radiation-induced hypovascular, hypocellular bone injury that may lead to persistent exposed necrotic jawbone and chronic mucosal inflammation after head and neck radiotherapy.

Vascular compromise and delayed necrosis.normalized_text: Vascular compromise and delayed necrosis of the fibular free-flap reconstruction
Vascular compromise and delayed necrosis.description: Partial flap ischemia, venous congestion, or delayed failure of a vascularized bone graft can result in loss of flap viability, exposed bone, and necrosis. Late compromise may occur due to thrombosis, mechanical factors, wound breakdown, or impaired local healing.

Giant cell myocarditis.description: A rare, rapidly progressive autoimmune myocarditis characterized by myocardial inflammation, myocyte necrosis, and multinucleated giant cells on biopsy; it can cause fulminant heart failure, cardiogenic shock, arrhythmias, and chest-pain syndromes mimicking acute coronary syndrome.

Acute necrotizing eosinophilic myocardit.description: A severe form of eosinophilic myocarditis in which eosinophil-rich inflammation causes myocardial necrosis and rapidly progressive heart failure or cardiogenic shock. It may occur with drug hypersensitivity, allergic disease, infection, or without an identifiable trigger.

Fulminant viral lymphocytic myocarditis.description: Acute inflammation of the heart muscle, commonly following a viral illness, which can produce chest pain, ventricular dysfunction, acute heart failure, arrhythmias, and cardiogenic shock.

Acute anterior myocardial infarction wit.normalized_text: Acute anterior myocardial infarction with cardiogenic shock and acute ischemic mitral regurgitation
