Acute anterior myocardial infarction wit.description: Acute coronary occlusion can cause myocardial infarction, severe left-ventricular pump failure, pulmonary congestion, cardiogenic shock, and acute mitral regurgitation from papillary-muscle ischemia or ventricular remodeling.

Massive pulmonary embolism with obstruct.normalized_text: Massive pulmonary embolism with obstructive shock
Massive pulmonary embolism with obstruct.description: A large pulmonary arterial thromboembolism can abruptly increase right-sided cardiac pressure, causing dyspnea, tachycardia, elevated JVP, hypoxemia, hypotension, and obstructive shock.

Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long Q.normalized_text: Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long QT syndrome type 8)
Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long Q.description: A rare multisystem genetic disorder caused by pathogenic CACNA1C variants, classically associated with marked QT prolongation, malignant ventricular arrhythmias, syndactyly, distinctive facial features, and variable developmental abnormalities.

Congenital long QT syndrome type 1 (KCNQ.normalized_text: Congenital long QT syndrome type 1 (KCNQ1-related LQTS)
Congenital long QT syndrome type 1 (KCNQ.description: An inherited cardiac ion-channel disorder causing delayed ventricular repolarization and risk of torsades de pointes, syncope, and sudden cardiac arrest, often triggered by adrenergic stress.

CACNA1C-related isolated long QT syndrom.normalized_text: CACNA1C-related isolated long QT syndrome (non-syndromic LQT8)
CACNA1C-related isolated long QT syndrom.description: A CACNA1C-associated channelopathy that can produce QT prolongation and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias without the full extracardiac manifestations of classic Timothy syndrome.

Andersen-Tawil syndrome (KCNJ2-related l.normalized_text: Andersen-Tawil syndrome (KCNJ2-related long QT syndrome type 7)
Andersen-Tawil syndrome (KCNJ2-related l.description: A genetic potassium-channel disorder characterized by ventricular arrhythmias, periodic paralysis, and characteristic craniofacial or skeletal abnormalities; QT-U prolongation may be present.

Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricula.description: An inherited arrhythmia syndrome, usually caused by RYR2 or CASQ2 variants, in which adrenergic stress can trigger bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia despite a structurally normal heart and often normal resting ECG.

Strongyloidiasis (Strongyloides stercora.description: A soil-transmitted intestinal nematode infection acquired through skin contact with contaminated soil in tropical and subtropical regions. It can cause diarrhea, rash, marked eosinophilia, and chronic or intermittent gastrointestinal symptoms.

Hypereosinophilic syndrome.description: A disorder characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia that can infiltrate and damage multiple organs, including the gastrointestinal tract, skin, spleen, heart, lungs, and bone marrow. It may be idiopathic, clonal, or secondary to another condition.

Eosinophilic gastroenteritis/enterocolit.description: An eosinophil-predominant inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract that may cause diarrhea, abdominal bloating, weight loss, and peripheral eosinophilia. It can occur independently or alongside other inflammatory bowel disorders.

Hookworm infection (Ancylostoma or Necat.description: A soil-transmitted helminth infection acquired by skin penetration of larvae in contaminated soil. It may produce a pruritic skin eruption, eosinophilia during larval migration, gastrointestinal symptoms, and chronic weight loss or anemia.

Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama syndrome.normalized_text: Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama syndrome) or intestinal schistosomiasis
Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama syndrome.description: A trematode infection acquired through freshwater exposure in endemic areas. Acute infection can cause eosinophilia, rash, systemic symptoms, and gastrointestinal complaints; chronic intestinal disease can cause diarrhea and colitis.

Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (hemorrhagic.description: An aggressive diffuse astrocytic glioma that can present as a necrotic, ring-enhancing cerebral mass with substantial surrounding edema and occasional intratumoral hemorrhage. The reported GFAP and OLIG2 positivity with IDH1 negativity, retained ATRX, p53 expression, and elevated proliferative activity favor a high-grade IDH-wildtype astrocytic tumor.

High-grade astrocytoma (anaplastic astro.normalized_text: High-grade astrocytoma (anaplastic astrocytoma or diffuse astrocytic glioma)
High-grade astrocytoma (anaplastic astro.description: A malignant primary glial tumor arising from astrocytes. High-grade lesions may enhance, cause edema, provoke seizures, and sometimes bleed; definitive classification depends on histologic and molecular features.

Cerebral abscess.description: A focal intracranial infection consisting of a pus-filled cavity surrounded by a capsule. On MRI it often appears as a ring-enhancing lesion with extensive edema and can cause seizures and reduced consciousness.

Hemorrhagic brain metastasis.description: Metastatic cancer to the brain can form a sharply circumscribed enhancing mass with edema and intratumoral bleeding. Some metastases, especially melanoma, renal-cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, thyroid carcinoma, and lung carcinoma, bleed readily.

Cerebral arteriovenous malformation or c.normalized_text: Cerebral arteriovenous malformation or cavernous malformation with hemorrhage
Cerebral arteriovenous malformation or c.description: Vascular malformations may cause spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage and seizures in young adults. Cavernous malformations can have repeated small hemorrhages, whereas arteriovenous malformations may cause acute larger hemorrhage.

Cryptococcal vertebral osteomyelitis (di.description: A fungal infection caused by Cryptococcus species that can disseminate from the lungs to bone, producing destructive vertebral lesions and paraspinal soft-tissue masses. Histology may show round encapsulated budding yeasts with a surrounding clear halo.

Blastomycosis with vertebral osteomyelit.description: Blastomycosis is a systemic fungal infection caused by Blastomyces species, usually acquired through inhalation. Pulmonary infection may disseminate to bone, causing lytic vertebral lesions and chronic painful osteomyelitis.

Coccidioidal vertebral osteomyelitis.description: Disseminated coccidioidomycosis is infection with Coccidioides fungi that begins in the lungs and can later involve bone, including the spine. Vertebral disease may cause lytic lesions, pain, and paraspinal inflammatory masses.

Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease).description: Tuberculosis of the spine is a chronic granulomatous infection of vertebral bodies that can cause vertebral destruction, disc-space involvement, paraspinal abscesses, pain, constitutional symptoms, and possible neurologic compromise.

Metastatic malignancy involving the lumb.normalized_text: Metastatic malignancy involving the lumbar spine
Metastatic malignancy involving the lumb.description: Cancer metastatic to the spine, such as lung, prostate, renal, thyroid, or hematologic malignancy, may produce destructive vertebral lesions, persistent night pain, weight loss, and eventual neurologic compression.

Disseminated talaromycosis (Talaromyces.description: A systemic dimorphic fungal infection that can involve the lungs, lymph nodes, skin, subcutaneous tissue, bone marrow, and other organs; it is especially associated with immunosuppression but can occur in apparently immunocompetent individuals.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species, usually acquired by inhalation; disseminated disease can produce fever, weight loss, pulmonary infiltrates, lymphadenopathy, and skin or soft-tissue lesions.

Disseminated cryptococcosis.description: An invasive infection caused by Cryptococcus species that can involve the lungs and spread to lymph nodes, skin, bone, eyes, or the central nervous system, particularly in immunocompromised patients.

Disseminated blastomycosis.description: A systemic fungal disease caused by Blastomyces species, producing pulmonary infection with possible spread to skin, soft tissue, bone, genitourinary sites, and occasionally the orbit.

Pulmonary and disseminated tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection may cause chronic pulmonary disease and constitutional symptoms, with extrapulmonary involvement of lymph nodes, soft tissue, and rarely the orbit or eyelid.

Congenital Zika virus syndrome.description: Fetal infection with Zika virus acquired during pregnancy, which can cause severe brain abnormalities including ventriculomegaly, cortical malformations, intracranial calcifications, and microcephaly. Maternal infection often causes a mild febrile rash illness with conjunctivitis.

Congenital cytomegalovirus infection.description: CMV is a common congenital viral infection that can cause fetal ventriculomegaly, periventricular calcifications, abnormal brain development, growth restriction, hearing loss, and neurodevelopmental impairment.

Congenital toxoplasmosis.description: Congenital infection with Toxoplasma gondii can produce hydrocephalus or ventriculomegaly, diffuse intracranial calcifications, chorioretinitis, and neurologic impairment.

Fetal aqueductal stenosis causing obstru.normalized_text: Fetal aqueductal stenosis causing obstructive hydrocephalus
Fetal aqueductal stenosis causing obstru.description: Obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow at the cerebral aqueduct causes enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles, often with relative sparing of the fourth ventricle. It may be isolated or associated with genetic or structural CNS disorders.

Genetic fetal brain malformation, such a.normalized_text: Genetic fetal brain malformation, such as L1 syndrome or a tubulinopathy
Genetic fetal brain malformation, such a.description: Genetic neurodevelopmental disorders affecting neuronal migration, axon formation, or cerebrospinal fluid pathways can cause severe ventriculomegaly, hydrocephalus, abnormal commissural structures, and cortical malformations. L1 syndrome is a classic cause of X-linked hydrocephalus, while tubulinopathies can cause complex cortical and ventricular abnormalities.

diagnoses.name: Complex hereditary spastic paraplegia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Autosomal recessive complex hereditary spastic paraplegia

SPG11-related hereditary spastic paraple.normalized_text: SPG11-related hereditary spastic paraplegia (Spastic paraplegia type 11, Kjellin syndrome spectrum)
SPG11-related hereditary spastic paraple.description: An autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic SPG11 mutations. It commonly causes progressive spastic paraparesis, cognitive decline, dysphagia, peripheral neurologic features, and thinning of the corpus callosum on MRI.

SPG15-related hereditary spastic paraple.normalized_text: SPG15-related hereditary spastic paraplegia (ZFYVE26-associated spastic paraplegia)
SPG15-related hereditary spastic paraple.description: A complicated autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia that closely resembles SPG11. It can cause progressive spastic paraparesis, intellectual or cognitive decline, dysphagia, and a thin corpus callosum.

FA2H-associated neurodegeneration / SPG3.normalized_text: FA2H-associated neurodegeneration / SPG35 (fatty acid hydroxylase-associated neurodegeneration)
FA2H-associated neurodegeneration / SPG3.description: An autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by FA2H mutations. It may present with complicated spastic paraplegia, cognitive decline, dysphagia, white-matter disease, and sometimes brain iron accumulation.

KIF1A-associated hereditary spastic para.description: A hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by KIF1A variants, with either dominant or recessive inheritance. Complicated forms can include cognitive impairment, optic neuropathy, peripheral neuropathy, and progressive spastic gait.

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy / adrenomy.description: A peroxisomal disorder caused by ABCD1 mutations. Adult forms can produce progressive spastic paraparesis, gait impairment, bladder dysfunction, neuropathy, and, in cerebral disease, cognitive decline and white-matter lesions.

Functional mediastinal paraganglioma (ca.description: A rare extra-adrenal neuroendocrine tumor arising from sympathetic paraganglia in the mediastinum, often near the heart or great vessels. It can secrete norepinephrine and cause episodic catecholamine crises; the imaging appearance is consistent with a hypervascular mediastinal mass.

Pheochromocytoma.description: A catecholamine-secreting neuroendocrine tumor arising from adrenal medullary chromaffin cells. It classically causes episodic headache, diaphoresis, palpitations, and severe hypertension, including during pregnancy.

Preeclampsia with severe features.description: A pregnancy-specific hypertensive disorder occurring after 20 weeks of gestation, typically associated with proteinuria or maternal end-organ dysfunction. Severe hypertension and headache are common warning features.

Neuroblastoma or ganglioneuroblastoma wi.normalized_text: Neuroblastoma or ganglioneuroblastoma with catecholamine secretion
Neuroblastoma or ganglioneuroblastoma wi.description: Neuroblastic tumors derived from sympathetic neural crest tissue that can produce catecholamine metabolites, especially vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid. They are predominantly pediatric tumors but rarely occur in adults.

Catecholamine-secreting ganglioneuroma.description: A usually benign tumor of sympathetic ganglia that may arise in the posterior mediastinum or retroperitoneum. Most are nonfunctional, but a minority secrete catecholamines and can cause hypertension.

Nocardia brain abscess (cerebral nocardi.description: An opportunistic infection caused by Nocardia species that can produce a focal, often ring-enhancing brain abscess, particularly in patients receiving chronic immunosuppressive therapy. Histology may show suppurative inflammation with branching filamentous bacteria.

Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis.description: Reactivation of Toxoplasma infection in immunocompromised patients, causing focal necrotizing brain lesions, commonly with ring enhancement and edema.

Primary central nervous system lymphoma.description: A lymphoma confined to the brain, spinal cord, meninges, or eyes. It is more common in older adults and in immunosuppressed patients and can cause focal neurologic deficits and enhancing brain masses.

Pyogenic bacterial brain abscess.description: A localized collection of pus in the brain caused by bacterial infection, often producing a ring-enhancing lesion with vasogenic edema and focal neurologic deficits.

Cerebral aspergillosis.description: An invasive fungal infection caused by Aspergillus species that can involve the central nervous system in immunocompromised patients, producing infarcts, hemorrhagic lesions, or abscess-like enhancing masses.

Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumo.description: A severe atypical bacterial pneumonia caused by Legionella species, often acquired from aerosolized freshwater sources and capable of progressing from focal to bilateral patchy consolidation.

Community-acquired pneumococcal pneumoni.description: An acute bacterial pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, commonly producing abrupt fever, productive sputum, pleuritic pain, and lobar or segmental air-space consolidation.

Aspiration pneumonia.description: Pulmonary infection or inflammation caused by inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastric contents, often affecting dependent lower-lobe lung segments and sometimes causing polymicrobial infection.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: A chronic pulmonary infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can cause cough, fever, and radiographic infiltrates or cavitation; diabetes is a risk factor for active disease.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae atypical pneumonia.description: A common atypical community-acquired pneumonia that usually causes a gradual respiratory illness with fever, cough, and diffuse or patchy interstitial-to-air-space infiltrates.

CHRNE-related congenital myasthenic synd.normalized_text: CHRNE-related congenital myasthenic syndrome (primary acetylcholine receptor deficiency)
CHRNE-related congenital myasthenic synd.description: A postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by reduced function or number of acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, often presenting from birth with severe generalized weakness and respiratory involvement.

RAPSN-related congenital myasthenic synd.description: A postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by rapsyn deficiency, impairing clustering of acetylcholine receptors at the motor endplate. It commonly causes neonatal or infantile weakness, ptosis, bulbar dysfunction, and respiratory crises.

MUSK-related congenital myasthenic syndr.description: A congenital disorder of neuromuscular-junction development caused by biallelic MUSK variants. It can produce severe neonatal respiratory and bulbar weakness, facial weakness, ptosis, and impaired eye movements despite negative MuSK antibodies.

DOK7-related congenital myasthenic syndr.description: A postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by impaired agrin-MuSK signaling and abnormal neuromuscular-junction formation. It often produces limb-girdle, neck, and respiratory weakness with normal sensation and reflexes; ocular symptoms may be mild or absent.

COLQ-related endplate acetylcholinestera.description: A synaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by deficiency of acetylcholinesterase anchored at the motor endplate, resulting in prolonged acetylcholine action, fatigable weakness, respiratory involvement, and progressive skeletal deformity.

Ethylene glycol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion causing high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, elevated osmolal gap, calcium oxalate crystal deposition, acute kidney injury, and neurologic symptoms.

Methanol poisoning.description: Toxic methanol ingestion produces an elevated osmolal gap initially and later severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis due to formic acid accumulation; it can cause central nervous system toxicity and visual impairment.

Diabetic ketoacidosis.description: Diabetic ketoacidosis is a metabolic emergency caused by insulin deficiency, resulting in hyperglycemia, ketone production, dehydration, and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

Salicylate poisoning.description: Salicylate toxicity causes respiratory stimulation, metabolic acidosis, neurologic symptoms, and often a mixed respiratory alkalosis with high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

Propylene glycol poisoning.description: Propylene glycol toxicity, often associated with large intravenous exposures to medications containing this solvent, can cause elevated osmolal gap, lactic acidosis, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, central nervous system depression, and kidney dysfunction.

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Q.description: A self-limited inflammatory thyroid disorder, usually triggered by a viral upper respiratory infection, causing thyroid enlargement, neck discomfort, fever, and transient release of thyroid hormone.

Acute suppurative thyroiditis.description: A rare bacterial infection of the thyroid gland that can produce fever, thyroid swelling, neck pain, and sometimes thyroid abscess formation.

Viral thyroiditis associated with acute.normalized_text: Viral thyroiditis associated with acute viral infection
Viral thyroiditis associated with acute.description: Inflammation of the thyroid occurring during or shortly after a viral syndrome; it may overlap clinically with subacute granulomatous thyroiditis and can cause fever and diffuse thyroid enlargement.

Graves disease with thyrotoxicosis.description: An autoimmune disorder in which thyroid-stimulating antibodies cause diffuse thyroid enlargement and excess thyroid hormone production, often resulting in tachycardia and heat intolerance.

Thyroid lymphoma or other infiltrative t.normalized_text: Thyroid lymphoma or other infiltrative thyroid malignancy
Thyroid lymphoma or other infiltrative t.description: An infiltrative tumor of the thyroid can cause firm thyroid enlargement and compressive neck symptoms; lymphoma may occasionally produce systemic fever.

Celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enterop.description: An immune-mediated small-intestinal disorder triggered by gluten that causes malabsorption, chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and characteristic duodenal mucosal inflammation with increased intraepithelial lymphocytes and villous injury.

Drug-induced enteropathy or microscopic.normalized_text: Drug-induced enteropathy or microscopic colitis related to lipid-lowering therapy
Drug-induced enteropathy or microscopic.description: Medication-related intestinal injury can cause chronic watery diarrhea, weight loss, abdominal discomfort, and biopsy findings of lymphocytic inflammation or epithelial injury. Symptoms may worsen after an increased medication dose.

Whipple disease.description: A chronic systemic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei, usually involving the small bowel and producing diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, malabsorption, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy. It can also cause neurologic, cardiac, and joint manifestations.

Chronic mesenteric ischemia with acute e.normalized_text: Chronic mesenteric ischemia with acute exacerbation
Chronic mesenteric ischemia with acute e.description: Reduced intestinal blood flow from atherosclerotic mesenteric arterial disease can cause abdominal pain, food avoidance, diarrhea, early satiety, and weight loss. Acute worsening may cause severe abdominal pain and mild laboratory abnormalities.

Acute pancreatitis, possibly medication-.description: Inflammation of the pancreas typically causes acute upper abdominal pain radiating to the back with nausea and elevated amylase and lipase. Some medications can precipitate pancreatitis.

Staphylococcus aureus polyarticular sept.description: Acute bacterial infection of one or more joints, commonly caused by S. aureus. It produces painful, warm, swollen joints and can occur without fever, particularly in older adults or after corticosteroid exposure. The image is consistent with gram-positive cocci in clusters growing on blood and chocolate agar.

Disseminated gonococcal infection with g.normalized_text: Disseminated gonococcal infection with gonococcal arthritis
Disseminated gonococcal infection with g.description: Hematogenous dissemination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae can cause migratory polyarthralgia or septic arthritis, often affecting wrists, knees, ankles, and small joints. It may occur after unprotected sexual exposure and may have little or no genital symptomatology.

Reactive arthritis.description: A sterile inflammatory arthritis that develops after genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection, including Chlamydia trachomatis. It commonly causes asymmetric lower-extremity arthritis and enthesitis.

Rheumatoid arthritis.description: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory polyarthritis that typically causes symmetric small-joint synovitis, prolonged morning stiffness, and gradual progression over weeks to months.

Lyme arthritis.description: A late manifestation of Borrelia burgdorferi infection that causes intermittent or persistent swelling of large joints, especially the knee, in individuals exposed to ticks in endemic regions such as New England.

diagnoses.name: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type
diagnoses.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type

Primary adrenal lymphoma (bilateral diff.normalized_text: Primary adrenal lymphoma (bilateral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma)
Primary adrenal lymphoma (bilateral diff.description: A rare extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma that often presents as bilateral adrenal masses, constitutional symptoms, high LDH, and may later cause adrenal insufficiency.

Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma.description: An aggressive lymphoma in which malignant B cells proliferate within small blood vessels, often causing fever, cytopenias, very high LDH, liver abnormalities, and extranodal organ involvement without enlarged lymph nodes.

Disseminated histoplasmosis with adrenal.description: A systemic fungal infection that can involve the reticuloendothelial system and adrenal glands, producing fever, cytopenias, liver enzyme elevation, bilateral adrenal enlargement, and possible adrenal insufficiency.

Disseminated tuberculosis with bilateral.normalized_text: Disseminated tuberculosis with bilateral adrenal tuberculosis
Disseminated tuberculosis with bilateral.description: Hematogenous tuberculosis may involve both adrenal glands and lungs, causing prolonged fever, constitutional illness, bilateral adrenal masses or enlargement, and eventual adrenal destruction.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (seco.description: A severe hyperinflammatory syndrome, frequently triggered by lymphoma or infection, characterized by persistent fever, cytopenias, liver dysfunction, high LDH, and often hepatosplenomegaly.

Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).description: A congenital persistent connection between the descending aorta and pulmonary artery, producing a left-to-right shunt and increased pulmonary blood flow.

Patent ductus arteriosus with ductal ane.normalized_text: Patent ductus arteriosus with ductal aneurysm
Patent ductus arteriosus with ductal ane.description: An aneurysmal dilatation of a persistent ductus arteriosus, which may appear as a large vascular structure between the aortic arch/descending aorta and left pulmonary artery.

Aortopulmonary window.description: A rare congenital communication between the ascending aorta and pulmonary artery that causes a left-to-right shunt, pulmonary overcirculation, and potentially pulmonary hypertension.

Anomalous origin of the left pulmonary a.normalized_text: Anomalous origin of the left pulmonary artery from the aorta (hemitruncus arteriosus)
Anomalous origin of the left pulmonary a.description: A congenital anomaly in which one pulmonary artery, often the right but occasionally the left, originates from the aorta rather than the main pulmonary artery, causing excessive flow and pressure in the affected lung.

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (PA.description: An abnormal direct communication between a pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein that creates a right-to-left shunt; lesions can produce a bruit and appear as enlarged tortuous pulmonary vessels on contrast imaging.

IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis.description: An IgG4-related fibroinflammatory disorder causing plaque-like soft-tissue thickening around the abdominal aorta, iliac vessels, ureters, and/or inferior vena cava. Venous or lymphatic compression can cause severe bilateral leg edema.

Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Orm.description: A chronic inflammatory fibrosing condition characterized by retroperitoneal tissue surrounding the aorta and iliac vessels, often causing obstruction of ureters, veins, or lymphatics. Some cases are now recognized as part of IgG4-related disease.

Retroperitoneal lymphoma.description: Lymphoma can produce retroperitoneal soft-tissue masses or nodal conglomerates that compress the inferior vena cava, iliac veins, or lymphatic channels, resulting in bilateral lower-extremity edema.

Malignancy-associated retroperitoneal fi.normalized_text: Malignancy-associated retroperitoneal fibrosis or metastatic retroperitoneal malignancy
Malignancy-associated retroperitoneal fi.description: Solid tumors, including prostate, colorectal, gastric, pancreatic, renal, or urothelial cancers, can cause retroperitoneal infiltration or secondary fibrosis that obstructs major pelvic veins and lymphatics.

Erdheim-Chester disease.description: A rare non-Langerhans histiocytic disorder that may cause retroperitoneal infiltration, periaortic sheathing ('coated aorta'), renal or ureteric involvement, and vascular compression. It most often affects middle-aged or older adults.

Primary spontaneous left pneumothorax.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial or near-complete collapse of the left lung. This is common in otherwise healthy young men and the radiograph shows a hyperlucent left hemithorax with absent peripheral lung markings and a collapsed lung medially.

Large left pneumothorax.description: A large pneumothorax involves substantial pleural air and marked reduction in visible aerated lung on the affected side. The chest radiograph appearance is consistent with a large left-sided pneumothorax.

Tension pneumothorax.description: A life-threatening form of pneumothorax in which rising pleural pressure compresses the lung and may impair venous return and circulation. It is diagnosed clinically, often with radiographic mediastinal shift when imaging is obtained.

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.description: A pneumothorax caused by an underlying lung disorder, such as emphysematous bullae, asthma, cystic fibrosis, infection, or interstitial lung disease. It may resemble a primary pneumothorax radiographically.

Giant pulmonary bulla (bullous lung dise.description: A large air-filled space within the lung can create unilateral hyperlucency and may mimic a pneumothorax on chest radiography. Differentiation may require CT imaging, especially if a pleural line is uncertain.

Acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic car.normalized_text: Acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic carditis and mitral regurgitation
Acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic car.description: A post-streptococcal autoimmune inflammatory illness characterized by migratory polyarthritis and carditis. Carditis can cause valvulitis, most often involving the mitral valve, resulting in mitral regurgitation and heart failure.

Infective endocarditis with mitral valve.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis with mitral valve regurgitation
Infective endocarditis with mitral valve.description: An infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a cardiac valve. Valve destruction can produce acute mitral regurgitation and pulmonary congestion; immune phenomena can cause arthralgias or arthritis.

Disseminated gonococcal infection.description: Hematogenous spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae that commonly causes migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, and later septic monoarthritis, usually in sexually active young adults.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflam.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflammatory arthritis and cardiac involvement
Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflam.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause constitutional symptoms, migratory or symmetric inflammatory arthralgias/arthritis, serositis, myocarditis, and Libman-Sacks valvular disease.

Viral myocarditis or myopericarditis wit.normalized_text: Viral myocarditis or myopericarditis with viral polyarthritis
Viral myocarditis or myopericarditis wit.description: Viral infection can cause fever, fatigue, arthralgias, and myocardial inflammation leading to impaired cardiac function, dyspnea, and signs of heart failure. Some viruses, such as parvovirus B19, can cause prominent arthralgias.

Tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott disea.normalized_text: Tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott disease) with epidural/paraspinal extension
Tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott disea.description: Spinal tuberculosis is a chronic infection of vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs that can cause vertebral destruction, paraspinal or psoas collections, epidural extension, and nerve-root compression.

Pyogenic lumbar spondylodiscitis with ep.normalized_text: Pyogenic lumbar spondylodiscitis with epidural abscess
Pyogenic lumbar spondylodiscitis with ep.description: Pyogenic spondylodiscitis is a bacterial infection of an intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral endplates. It may extend into the epidural space or paraspinal tissues and produce radicular pain or neurologic deficits.

Brucellar spondylodiscitis.description: Brucellar spondylodiscitis is a subacute or chronic spinal infection caused by Brucella species, often involving the lumbar spine and causing back pain, endplate abnormalities, disc involvement, and occasionally epidural or paraspinal collections.

Lumbar spinal metastasis with epidural t.normalized_text: Lumbar spinal metastasis with epidural tumor extension
Lumbar spinal metastasis with epidural t.description: Metastatic cancer involving the lumbar vertebrae can cause destructive bone lesions, epidural soft-tissue extension, neural compression, and persistent back pain with radiculopathy.

Degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis or d.normalized_text: Degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis or disc disease with radiculopathy
Degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis or d.description: Degenerative disc disease, facet arthropathy, and spinal canal or foraminal stenosis can compress lumbar nerve roots, producing chronic low-back pain and pain radiating into one leg.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip with.normalized_text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip with regional lymph-node metastasis
Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip with.description: A malignant tumor of squamous cells, commonly affecting the lower lip or oral commissure. It may present as a persistent crusted ulcer and can spread to submental or submandibular lymph nodes.

Chronic herpes simplex virus type 1 infe.normalized_text: Chronic herpes simplex virus type 1 infection
Chronic herpes simplex virus type 1 infe.description: HSV-1 commonly causes painful recurrent vesicles and crusted erosions around the lips. Persistent, extensive, or nonhealing lesions can occur in people with impaired immunity.

Human immunodeficiency virus infection w.normalized_text: Human immunodeficiency virus infection with opportunistic oral herpes infection
Human immunodeficiency virus infection w.description: HIV causes progressive immune dysfunction and may present with fatigue, recurrent infections, persistent mucocutaneous herpes lesions, and enlarged lymph nodes.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including diffuse.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including diffuse.description: Non-Hodgkin lymphomas are cancers of lymphocytes that can cause persistent lymph-node enlargement, fatigue, recurrent infections, and occasionally extranodal lesions involving the oral cavity.

Basal cell carcinoma of the perioral ski.normalized_text: Basal cell carcinoma of the perioral skin
Basal cell carcinoma of the perioral ski.description: Basal cell carcinoma is a slow-growing skin cancer associated with ultraviolet exposure. It can produce a persistent ulcerated or crusted lesion near the lip, although spread to lymph nodes is uncommon.

Crohn disease.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract, often causing patchy transmural inflammation, ulceration, bowel-wall thickening, strictures, malabsorption, and extraintestinal joint manifestations.

Ulcerative colitis.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease limited to the colon and rectum, characterized by continuous superficial colonic inflammation, bloody diarrhea, anemia, hypoalbuminemia in severe disease, and possible peripheral arthritis.

Primary intestinal lymphangiectasia.description: A congenital or early-onset disorder of intestinal lymphatic drainage causing protein-losing enteropathy, diarrhea, malabsorption, edema, hypoalbuminemia, and sometimes iron deficiency. Endoscopy may show whitish villi, mucosal edema, or nodular changes.

Common variable immunodeficiency with no.normalized_text: Common variable immunodeficiency with nodular lymphoid hyperplasia/enteropathy
Common variable immunodeficiency with no.description: An immune-deficiency syndrome that can cause chronic infectious or inflammatory diarrhea, malabsorption, nodular lymphoid hyperplasia of the intestine, protein loss, anemia, and inflammatory arthritis-like symptoms.

Intestinal Behçet disease.description: A systemic inflammatory vasculitis that may produce deep intestinal ulcers, gastrointestinal bleeding, diarrhea, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and recurrent arthritis; it most commonly affects the ileocecal region.

Dupuytren disease (palmar fibromatosis).description: A benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia that forms nodules and cords, progressively causing flexion contractures, most often affecting the ring and little fingers.

Trigger finger (stenosing flexor tenosyn.description: Inflammation and thickening around the flexor tendon pulley, usually at the A1 pulley, causing painful catching, clicking, or locking of a finger during flexion and extension.

Flexor tendon adhesion or post-traumatic.normalized_text: Flexor tendon adhesion or post-traumatic flexion contracture
Flexor tendon adhesion or post-traumatic.description: Scarring of the flexor tendons or surrounding soft tissues after injury, surgery, infection, or immobilization, which can restrict finger extension and produce contractures.

Camptodactyly.description: A congenital or developmental condition characterized by a persistent flexion deformity, usually of the proximal interphalangeal joint of the little finger and sometimes other fingers.

Diabetic cheiroarthropathy (limited join.description: A complication of long-standing diabetes characterized by waxy thickened skin and painless limitation of finger extension due to periarticular connective-tissue glycation and fibrosis.

Syphilitic lymphadenitis due to secondar.normalized_text: Syphilitic lymphadenitis due to secondary syphilis
Syphilitic lymphadenitis due to secondar.description: Lymph-node involvement by Treponema pallidum during secondary syphilis, which can cause prominent regional or generalized lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms; spirochetes may be demonstrated in the node by immunohistochemistry.

HIV-associated multicentric Castleman di.description: A human herpesvirus 8-associated lymphoproliferative disorder in people with HIV, characterized by inflammatory flares, constitutional symptoms, and enlarged lymph nodes at multiple sites.

HIV-associated non-Hodgkin lymphoma.description: Aggressive B-cell lymphomas occur more often in people with HIV and may present with rapidly enlarging lymph nodes, fever, night sweats, and extranodal disease.

Mycobacterial lymphadenitis, including r.normalized_text: Mycobacterial lymphadenitis, including recurrent Mycobacterium avium complex infection
Mycobacterial lymphadenitis, including r.description: Mycobacterial infection can cause chronic lymph-node enlargement and constitutional symptoms in immunocompromised patients; disseminated MAC is particularly associated with advanced HIV immunosuppression.

Inguinal lymphadenitis from a local geni.normalized_text: Inguinal lymphadenitis from a local genital, perianal, or lower-extremity infection
Inguinal lymphadenitis from a local geni.description: Reactive or bacterial lymphadenitis develops when lymph nodes draining the lower abdomen, genital region, perianal area, or legs respond to infection or inflammation in those areas.

diagnoses.name: Rib osteosarcoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: Osteosarcoma of bone or articular cartilage of ribs, sternum or clavicle

Ewing sarcoma of the rib (chest-wall Ewi.normalized_text: Ewing sarcoma of the rib (chest-wall Ewing sarcoma)
Ewing sarcoma of the rib (chest-wall Ewi.description: A malignant small round-cell bone tumor that commonly affects adolescents and can arise from a rib, causing a chest-wall soft-tissue mass, pleural involvement, pain, and respiratory symptoms.

Askin tumor (thoracopulmonary primitive.description: An aggressive peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor within the Ewing sarcoma family that typically arises in the chest wall of children and adolescents and may involve ribs, pleura, and soft tissues.

Osteosarcoma of the rib.description: A primary malignant bone-forming tumor that rarely arises in the ribs and may present as focal chest-wall pain, swelling, cortical destruction, and an adjacent soft-tissue mass.

Primary bone lymphoma of the rib.normalized_text: Primary bone lymphoma of the rib
Primary bone lymphoma of the rib.description: A malignant lymphoid tumor involving bone that can cause persistent localized bone pain and may produce a chest-wall soft-tissue component; it is less common in adolescents than Ewing sarcoma.

Rib osteomyelitis with chest-wall inflam.normalized_text: Rib osteomyelitis with chest-wall inflammatory mass or empyema
Rib osteomyelitis with chest-wall inflam.description: Infection of a rib can cause focal pain and tenderness and may extend into adjacent soft tissues or pleural space, producing reduced chest expansion and breathlessness.

Primary splenic classical Hodgkin lympho.description: A rare form of classical Hodgkin lymphoma confined predominantly to the spleen, characterized by malignant Reed-Sternberg cells that are often CD30-positive and associated with constitutional symptoms.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving the spleen
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving.description: An aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma that can present as a splenic mass, constitutional symptoms, anemia, and elevated inflammatory markers.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma.description: A CD30-positive T-cell lymphoma composed of large pleomorphic malignant cells that may mimic Hodgkin lymphoma and can cause systemic B symptoms.

Primary splenic marginal zone lymphoma.description: An indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that commonly presents with splenomegaly, cytopenias, and little or no peripheral lymphadenopathy.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis secon.description: A severe hyperinflammatory syndrome, often triggered by lymphoma or infection, causing persistent fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, and markedly elevated ferritin.

Fabry disease with Fabry cardiomyopathy.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-galactosidase A deficiency, leading to globotriaosylceramide accumulation in the kidneys, heart, nervous system, and other organs. Cardiac involvement commonly causes concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy, conduction abnormalities, atrial arrhythmias, and myocardial injury.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: A genetic myocardial disorder characterized by abnormal myocardial thickening, often involving the left ventricle, which can cause diastolic dysfunction, ischemic chest pain, atrial fibrillation, and sudden arrhythmias. The imaging findings are compatible with substantial ventricular hypertrophy.

Hypertensive heart disease with left-ven.normalized_text: Hypertensive heart disease with left-ventricular hypertrophy
Hypertensive heart disease with left-ven.description: Chronic hypertension can produce concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction, resulting in an S4, repolarization changes on ECG, atrial enlargement, and atrial fibrillation.

Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction o.normalized_text: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction or acute coronary syndrome
Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction o.description: Acute myocardial ischemia caused by coronary plaque rupture, thrombosis, or supply-demand mismatch. It may present with chest pressure, gastrointestinal symptoms, arrhythmias, and elevated cardiac troponin without classic ST-segment elevation.

Cardiac amyloidosis.description: An infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular amyloid deposition in the myocardium. It commonly produces increased ventricular wall thickness, diastolic dysfunction, atrial arrhythmias, conduction disease, proteinuria, and renal impairment.

Neonatal arterial ischemic stroke (left.normalized_text: Neonatal arterial ischemic stroke (left middle cerebral artery territory)
Neonatal arterial ischemic stroke (left.description: An acute focal cerebral infarction caused by arterial occlusion, most often involving the middle cerebral artery in term neonates. Diffusion-restricted left hemispheric cortical injury and focal contralateral seizures strongly support this diagnosis.

Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.description: Brain injury caused by impaired oxygen delivery and/or cerebral perfusion around birth. It may cause neonatal seizures, although injury is more often diffuse or bilateral than a single arterial-territory lesion.

Neonatal intracranial hemorrhage (includ.normalized_text: Neonatal intracranial hemorrhage (including focal intraparenchymal hemorrhage)
Neonatal intracranial hemorrhage (includ.description: Bleeding within the brain, ventricles, or extra-axial spaces can provoke seizures in newborns. Hemorrhagic lesions may occur after birth trauma, coagulation abnormalities, or vascular injury.

Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST).normalized_text: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) with venous infarction
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST).description: Thrombosis of intracranial venous sinuses or cortical veins may cause neonatal seizures and can produce venous infarction, sometimes with hemorrhage. Dehydration, perinatal stress, and prothrombotic conditions may contribute.

Neonatal meningitis or encephalitis.description: Central nervous system infection can present with seizures in newborns, including bacterial meningitis or viral encephalitis. Illness may initially be subtle but usually develops systemic or neurologic signs.

Takayasu arteritis.description: A granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, most often in young women. It can cause aortic wall thickening, stenosis or aneurysmal change, aortic-root dilation with severe aortic regurgitation, and pulmonary hypertension.

Infective endocarditis with severe aorti.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis with severe aortic regurgitation
Infective endocarditis with severe aorti.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve, which may produce vegetations, valve destruction, severe regurgitation, heart failure, and inflammatory laboratory abnormalities.

Acute decompensated heart failure from s.normalized_text: Acute decompensated heart failure from severe aortic regurgitation
Acute decompensated heart failure from s.description: Severe leakage of the aortic valve causes volume overload of the left ventricle and elevated pulmonary venous pressure, resulting in pulmonary edema, hypoxemic respiratory distress, and reduced exercise tolerance.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries by thrombus, often causing acute or subacute dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxemia, pleuritic pain, and right-heart strain.

Post-COVID inflammatory cardiac disease.normalized_text: Post-COVID inflammatory cardiac disease (myocarditis or aortitis)
Post-COVID inflammatory cardiac disease.description: Inflammatory cardiovascular disease temporally associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection can cause myocardial dysfunction, vascular inflammation, tachycardia, dyspnea, chest symptoms, and elevated inflammatory markers.

Torsion with infarction of an accessory.normalized_text: Torsion with infarction of an accessory spleen (splenunculus)
Torsion with infarction of an accessory.description: An accessory spleen can twist on its vascular pedicle, causing impaired blood supply, infarction, and focal intra-abdominal inflammation. This is particularly relevant in a patient with previous splenectomy and known splenunculi.

Mesenteric panniculitis (sclerosing mese.description: Mesenteric panniculitis is an inflammatory disorder of mesenteric fat that may cause a painful inflammatory mass or 'misty mesentery' on CT, sometimes associated with prior abdominal trauma or surgery.

Superior mesenteric venous thrombosis wi.normalized_text: Superior mesenteric venous thrombosis with mesenteric inflammation or early bowel ischemia
Superior mesenteric venous thrombosis wi.description: Thrombosis of the superior mesenteric vein can cause impaired venous drainage of bowel and mesentery, producing abdominal pain, mesenteric edema, inflammatory marker elevation, and potentially bowel ischemia.

Epiploic appendagitis or focal omental i.normalized_text: Epiploic appendagitis or focal omental infarction
Epiploic appendagitis or focal omental i.description: Infarction or torsion of an epiploic appendage, or infarction of focal omentum, produces localized sterile inflammation and acute abdominal pain with fat stranding on CT. Omental infarction is more common in people with obesity.

Acute gastritis or peptic ulcer disease,.normalized_text: Acute gastritis or peptic ulcer disease, potentially medication-associated
Acute gastritis or peptic ulcer disease,.description: Gastritis or peptic ulcer disease causes epigastric pain and dyspeptic symptoms. Although orlistat more often causes lower gastrointestinal adverse effects, a temporal medication association may initially raise concern for drug-related gastrointestinal symptoms.

Hematometrocolpos due to imperforate hym.description: Accumulation of menstrual blood within the vagina and uterus caused by congenital obstruction at the hymen. Ultrasound commonly shows a large midline pelvic cystic mass with homogeneous low-level internal echoes.

Hematocolpos due to a transverse vaginal.normalized_text: Hematocolpos due to a transverse vaginal septum
Hematocolpos due to a transverse vaginal.description: A congenital transverse partition within the vagina can obstruct menstrual outflow, causing retained blood in the vagina, sometimes with extension into the uterus (hematometrocolpos).

Obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral re.normalized_text: Obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral renal anomaly (OHVIRA syndrome)
Obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral re.description: A Müllerian duct anomaly, usually involving uterus didelphys with an obstructed hemivagina, that leads to hematocolpos or hematometra after menarche and may be associated with absence of a kidney on the same side.

Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst.description: A functional ovarian cyst with internal bleeding that can produce acute or subacute pelvic pain and a complex cystic adnexal mass with internal echoes on ultrasound.

Acute appendicitis.description: Inflammation of the appendix, classically causing progressively worsening abdominal pain that often migrates to the right lower quadrant and may be associated with fever, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia.

Potocki-Shaffer syndrome (11p11.2 deleti.description: A contiguous-gene deletion syndrome involving 11p11.2, commonly including EXT2, ALX4, and PHF21A. It causes multiple osteochondromas/exostoses, enlarged parietal foramina, developmental delay/intellectual disability, hypotonia, craniofacial differences, and growth impairment.

Hereditary multiple osteochondromas (mul.description: An autosomal dominant skeletal disorder, usually caused by EXT1 or EXT2 variants, characterized by multiple cartilage-capped bony outgrowths near growth plates that develop during childhood.

Trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type II (.description: A contiguous-gene deletion disorder involving 8q24, typically including TRPS1 and EXT1. It is associated with craniofacial differences, sparse hair, short stature, cone-shaped epiphyses, and multiple exostoses.

Coffin-Siris syndrome.description: A neurodevelopmental disorder caused by variants in chromatin-remodeling complex genes, characterized by developmental delay, hypotonia, feeding/growth problems, microcephaly or postnatal growth failure, and coarse or distinctive facial features.

Cleidocranial dysplasia.description: A RUNX2-related skeletal dysplasia characterized by delayed closure of cranial sutures, persistent or enlarged fontanelles, clavicular hypoplasia, dental abnormalities, short stature, and other skeletal differences.

Crusted scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei infes.description: A severe, highly contagious form of scabies with a high mite burden, often occurring in immunocompromised patients. Mites and eggs are present in the stratum corneum and can cause crusted, erosive, or ulcerated lesions.

Ecthyma (ulcerative bacterial pyoderma).description: Ecthyma is a deeper form of impetigo, usually due to Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus, producing punched-out crusted ulcers. It is more common in patients with poor host defenses.

Pyoderma gangrenosum.description: Pyoderma gangrenosum is an inflammatory neutrophilic dermatosis that causes painful, rapidly progressive ulcerations with undermined violaceous borders and may be associated with hematologic disorders.

Disseminated cutaneous fungal infection.description: Invasive fungal infections, including fusariosis or disseminated candidiasis, can cause papules, nodules, necrotic ulcers, or eschar-like lesions in patients with prolonged severe neutropenia.

Cutaneous involvement by myelodysplastic.normalized_text: Cutaneous involvement by myelodysplastic syndrome or leukemia cutis
Cutaneous involvement by myelodysplastic.description: Leukemia cutis refers to infiltration of the skin by malignant hematopoietic cells and may occur with myelodysplastic syndromes transforming toward acute myeloid leukemia. Lesions are typically papules, nodules, or plaques and only rarely ulcerate.

Rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulo.description: A severe glomerular inflammatory syndrome characterized by extensive crescent formation on kidney biopsy and rapid loss of renal function over days to weeks.

Pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephrit.description: A necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis with little or no immune-complex deposition; it is often associated with ANCA but can occur despite negative ANCA testing.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane diseas.description: An autoimmune disease in which antibodies target the glomerular basement membrane, causing severe crescentic glomerulonephritis; some patients also develop pulmonary hemorrhage.

IgA nephropathy with crescentic transfor.description: An immune-complex glomerulonephritis caused by mesangial IgA deposition; severe cases may develop crescents and rapidly progressive renal failure.

Postinfectious glomerulonephritis with c.description: An immune-complex glomerulonephritis that usually follows an infection, commonly streptococcal skin or throat infection, and can rarely progress to crescentic renal failure.

Primary extranodal B-cell lymphoma of th.normalized_text: Primary extranodal B-cell lymphoma of the extrahepatic bile duct
Primary extranodal B-cell lymphoma of th.description: A rare non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in or infiltrating the bile duct, producing obstructive jaundice. Lymphoma cells are typically CD45-positive and lack T-cell markers.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving the biliary tract
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving.description: An aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that may rarely involve the hepatic hilum or extrahepatic bile ducts and mimic cholangiocarcinoma with obstructive jaundice.

Cholangiocarcinoma (hilar bile-duct canc.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the bile ducts, especially at the hepatic hilum, that commonly causes progressive obstructive jaundice and biliary dilatation.

Myeloid sarcoma involving the biliary tr.normalized_text: Myeloid sarcoma involving the biliary tract
Myeloid sarcoma involving the biliary tr.description: Myeloid sarcoma is an extramedullary mass of immature myeloid cells that can rarely involve the liver, gallbladder, or bile duct and may occur without detectable acute myeloid leukemia in bone marrow.

IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis.description: An immune-mediated fibroinflammatory disorder causing bile-duct wall thickening and strictures, often associated with autoimmune pancreatitis and elevated serum IgG4.
